articles.title: Russo-Ukrainian war, day 1651: Russia’s sixth day of attacks on Kyiv ends with massive ballistic missile strike on eve of school year
articles.body:
Exclusives
Military
Second drone brigade in two months: Ukraine is forming the 446th Unmanned Systems Brigade. It is the second brigade of this level stood up in 2026, following the 445th, and recruitment is already underway, per unofficial sources.
Drone attack damages Russia's Baltic oil port as drone crosses Latvia into Estonia. Finland separately restricted air and maritime traffic in the eastern Gulf of Finland. No drones entered Finnish territory.
Russia's 6-day attack on Kyiv that started two days after CIA head's visit to Moscow, culminates with massive ballistic missile strike on eve of school year. Three children were among the injured. Civilian infrastructure was damaged in five of Kyiv's ten districts.
800 jet drones in four days: Russia is now firing type Ukraine's interceptors cannot catch. Of more than 1,500 drones launched over four days, about 800 have been jet-powered.
"In intercepts, they're screaming": Russia occupied this spit to control Ukraine's ports. Military says it has now isolated 2,500-strong grouping and destroyed all its artillery. Drone strikes and remote mining have cut supply, the Ukrainian soldiers say.
Intelligence and technology
Russia's Starlink rival falters as latest satellite batch stalls in low orbit, ISW says. None of the 16 spacecraft launched in July reached the 550-kilometer benchmark, while two may reenter the atmosphere and be lost.
Fired Ukraine defense chief Fedorov launches defense-tech company with Palantir CEO backing. After leaving government, Mykhailo Fedorov has moved deeper into defense technology, raising money in the US and pitching new ways to turn Ukraine's battlefield experience into weapons and military systems.
Russia promised a scramjet superweapon. Ukraine says Zircon runs on solid fuel. Ukraine's military intelligence puts Zircon's highest recorded speed at Mach 6.8, below Moscow's Mach 9 claim, and says both its motors are solid-fuel. Its component catalogue also names two US-manufacturer chips inside.
Ukrainian company builds single device that detects FPV drone, reads its video feed, and jams it. Brama has passed lab and combat testing and is now going through codification.
About $150 for airframe, about $875 for finished glider: Ukraine's BlueBird is selling its drone at every stage of assembly. Units pick the control system, camera, and electronics themselves; the bare airframe starts near $150.
Fired Ukrainian minister offers to help build America's drone army— for Patriot missiles in return. Mykhailo Fedorov is courting US investors for a fund that would build defense tech companies itself, not just back them.
International
Germany blames Moscow for Leipzig drone attack, closes consulate and cultural center among sweeping diplomatic measures. One of three drones linked to the incident reportedly struck a Ukrainian Antonov without detonating. Berlin also plans tighter entry controls for Russian nationals and additional EU sanctions.
German politician wants to send Taurus missiles to Ukraine after Russian drone attack in Leipzig airport. Wolfgang Kubicki wants Berlin to warn Moscow that further sabotage in Germany could unlock long-range cruise missiles for Ukraine.
US welcomes Russia back to G20 but rules out economic relief, source says. Washington tied any economic relief for Moscow to the end of the war, while European officials resisted Russia's return to the G20.
Armenia drops Russia's 'strategic partner' label, but foreign minister says alliance remains. The comments come after Armenia's new five-year government program changed how it describes ties with Moscow.
Latvia blocks Russian and Belarusian books, clothes and toys. The national measure goes beyond EU sanctions, covers goods worth €12.5 million in 2025, and limits the entry of propaganda materials.
Indonesia is examining whether traffickers put its citizens into Russia's war on Ukraine. The country's Foreign Ministry has put its overseas missions on establishing how one of its nationals came to serve Moscow's forces.
Someone placed funeral wreaths near defense companies in Lithuania and Czechia. The head of a Lithuanian defense company called it "ordinary intimidation" by Russians.
The US built itself a Russo-Ukrainian drone-war drill—Poland is the first ally in. A Green Beret officer expects most of NATO's 32 members to want a look, as Ukraine's war experience reshapes how the alliance trains.
Russia's shadow war on Europe is widening—NATO still sees no attack coming. A Polish warning, a US spy chief's Moscow trip, and an explosive drone found beside a cargo plane at a German airport all preceded the alliance's assessment.
Humanitarian and social impact
Russian air attack interrupts lessons on first day of school in Ukraine. Around 240,000 Ukrainian children entered first grade, 10% fewer than last year. 200,000 students near the front will study entirely online.
UN counted 183 Ukrainian children killed or wounded in July, the highest since 2022. The Ukrainian military released the breakdown on the day many schools across the country stayed shut because of Russian strikes.
Russian drone struck a Ukrainian fire truck on its way to a house fire—four rescuers injured. The crew was answering a call in a village outside Zaporizhzhia, and all four men went to hospital with injuries of differing severity.
Political and legal developments
"Russian airspace will effectively be closing": Zelenskyy warns airlines Russian skies are no longer safe. Ukraine says civilian aviation is not a target, but warns airlines can no longer assume Russian skies are safe.
Former Ukrainian president has made offer to Zelenskyy amid Russia's new type of war on Kyiv. Petro Poroshenko has tabled a five-point plan for how the capital survives permanent air raid alerts.
Read our previous daily review here.

- 
						
Russo-Ukrainian war, day 1649: Russia keeps Kyiv under fire for a fourth day as Ukraine tests new interceptors and strikes back at Russian oil
- 
						
Russo-Ukrainian war, day 1648: Russia hunts Ukraine’s grain trains

articles.title: Massive tit-for-tat strikes between Iran and US again
articles.body:
US Central Command (CENTCOM) announced a wave of strikes against Iran. Iranian state media reported multiple explosions across southern locations, including Asaluyeh, Jiroft, Bandar Abbas, Qeshm Island, Konarak, Chabahar, Jask, Sirik, and Lavan—the attack in Sirik hit a home during a wedding celebration, killing at least four people, including a child, and injuring more than 50
Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said it has launched a "heavy" ballistic missile attack on Prince Hassan airbase and a US Marine base in Jordan in response to earlier US strikes. Kuwait, Iraq, and Bahrain also report attacks from Iran
Israeli attacks continue on Gaza, occupied West Bank, south Lebanon, and southern Syria despite any agreements or alleged ceasefires
An Israeli strike on south Lebanon killed one person on Wednesday, Lebanese official media said,.
"One person was killed and another wounded in a strike launched by an enemy drone" in the city of Nabatieh, Lebanon's state-run National News Agency (NNA) said, also reporting other Israeli strikes on the area.
Israel's army claimed the Iran-backed Hezbollah group overnight "launched two explosive drones" towards Israeli soldiers in Ali al-Taher Ridge area, reporting no troop casualties.
In response, the Israeli military said it struck Hezbollah infrastructure in the Nabatieh area.
Despite an alleged ceasefire in June, Israel has continued its attacks on south Lebanon, particularly in the Nabatieh area where the strategic Ali al-Taher ridge is located.
Hezbollah has not claimed any attacks on Israeli targets for weeks.
Last week, Israeli airstrikes killed a woman.
On August 15, Israeli strikes killed 11 people including several children.
Lebanon's health ministry says Israeli attacks have killed at least 8,920 people since hostilities erupted in October 2023.
Iran security chief says US to face new war strategy
Iran's security chief on Wednesday warned the United States would face a "new strategy" from Tehran in the US-Israeli war after the heaviest exchange of attacks between the foes in weeks.
"You will soon see that Iran's new strategy on the battlefield, in diplomacy and in confronting the economic blockade will shatter your foundations," Iran's Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei posted on X.
The Saudi Foreign Ministry condemned what it described as an Iranian attack on a Saudi tanker while it was passing through the Strait of Hormuz, adding that the attack "resulted in fatalities among the tanker’s crew".
Every diamond has a story. Yours likely began with a child knee-deep in Congolese mud, digging for stones that armed groups tax and smuggle. It passed through Dubai’s gleaming towers, where one billion carats of diamonds were exchanged last year – none mined in the UAE. It was cut in Surat, India, where exploited workers, prone to suicide, earn less than $5 a day polishing nine out of ten of the world’s gems; writes Zeenat Adam.
Pakistan said Wednesday it remains engaged with the United States and Iran, with support from regional countries, in efforts to bring Washington and Tehran back to the negotiating table.
Foreign Ministry spokesperson Tahir Andrabi told a weekly news briefing in Islamabad that Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif met Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, as part of those efforts.
Andrabi said Pakistani Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar also met his Iranian counterpart, Abbas Araghchi, on the sidelines of the summit.
Pakistan’s army chief, Field Marshal Syed Asim Munir, traveled to Iran last week as part of Islamabad’s diplomatic efforts to help end the conflict and revive efforts to reopen the strategic Strait of Hormuz, Andrabi said.
“Regional de-escalation, breaking the military stalemate and exploring a negotiated settlement to restore regional peace and stability were discussed” during Munir’s visit to Tehran, he said.
European gas prices surpass their highest level since 2023
European natural gas benchmark futures have reached their highest since January 2023 after the US launched strikes once again against Iran on Tuesday, according to Bloomberg.
What a new Black Sea grain crisis means for the Middle East
As Russia and Ukraine intensify strikes in the Black Sea, disruptions to grain exports are raising new concerns about food security in the Middle East, writes Christopher Solomon.
Israel's defence minister on Wednesday said his country was prepared to respond "with great force" if attacked by Iran, after Iranian forces targeted US military positions across the region.
Israel Katz said Israeli forces were prepared for a possible attack from Iran over the Jewish high holiday season, which begins in mid-September.
"For now, they are striking throughout the region except us," he told a conference hosted by Israeli news site Ynet and newspaper Yedioth Ahronoth. "But there is a possibility that they will attack us. We are prepared for that defensively."
If Iran attacks, Israel would "respond with great force, independently of anyone else", Katz said, adding that "our planes are ready to take off".
Wall Street futures dipped on Wednesday as bond yields and oil prices marched higher following US-Iran clashes, offering little incentive to buy equities during what has typically been a weak month for returns.
The latest strikes have pushed geopolitical tensions front and center, ending the uneasy calm of the past few weeks and reviving inflation concerns.
"If hostilities are going to increase, they are likely to increase within the next couple of weeks. The Iranians have their maximum leverage now before the midterm elections," said Ryan Isherwood, founder and CEO of Significance Capital.
Any flare-up could complicate the interest-rate outlook further. Over the past week, traders have sharply increased bets on a September rate hike, after Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh said taming price pressures is the central bank's chief focus.
"It's been a ping-pong match on rate expectations, but we still think a hike right before the election is unlikely," Isherwood said.
Renewed tensions could push oil prices higher and add to inflationary pressures by raising costs for consumers and businesses.
Such a situation would typically demand rate increases, but the Fed could be in a bind if higher costs also start slowing economic growth, Isherwood added.
The uneasy calm of the past few weeks has ended, reviving inflation concerns. [Getty]
Two dead after Monday attack on Saudi oil tanker in Hormuz
Two Filipino sailors were killed in an attack on an oil tanker in the Strait of Hormuz on Monday, Saudi Arabia's national shipping company Bahri said on Wednesday.
"Bahri confirms that its vessel SIDR was involved in a security incident while transiting the Strait of Hormuz" on the evening of August 31, the carrier said on X, confirming "the loss of its two Filipino seafarers as a result" of the attack.
Two oil tankers hit sea mines and were disabled while attempting to transit the Strait of Hormuz, Iran's Revolutionary Guards said on Wednesday, in a statement shared by state media.
The statement said the tankers had been forced to disembark their crews and were placed in the hands of US operatives to pass through what it called an "illegal route" in the strategic waterway, despite earlier warnings from the Guards' navy about the dangers of crossing the mined passage.
Three paramilitary Basij fighters killed in US strikes
Iran's top negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf calls the United States "Satan" of its strikes hit a wedding ceremony in the country’s south.
"Minab school: children massacred. Lamerd sports hall: kids slaughtered. Kuhestak wedding: children killed with families. If a power acts like Satan, picks targets like Satan, and kills like Satan, it’s Satan. Shields a junior Satan that does the same? It’s THE Great Satan," says Ghalibaf in a post on X.
The Iranian Red Crescent reported four people were killed, including a child, and over 50 were wounded after a US strike hit a home that was hosting a wedding in south Iran.
Kuwait: fire in residential complex after Iran drone
Iran's Revolutionary Guards also announced that they struck US bases with missiles and drones in Erbil in Iraq's autonomous Kurdistan region, state media reported.
The Guards said they "carried out a coordinated missile and drone attack on US bases in Erbil" that destroyed a maintenance centre, warehouses and the "guidance system of a US surveillance aerostat", according to a statement carried by state-run IRNA news agency.
Iraqi Kurdish counterterrorism forces said on Wednesday that "the coalition forces downed ten explosive-laden drones in the airspace of Erbil province between 01:13 and 03:31 am" local time, without causing casualties.
Global bonds hit multi-decade highs for second day
Government bonds sold off sharply on Wednesday, driving borrowing costs to multi-decade highs as the US and Iran trade blows, raising energy prices and inflation fears, according to Reuters.
It was the second day of the market challenges, which began after a US strike on Larak Island triggered the latest round of escalation.
The conflict drove up energy prices, fueling investor concerns about inflation and mounting government debt. Consequently, the 10-year government bond hit a near three-year high in the US, a 30-year high in Japan, and a 15-year high in Australia, while prices for German and French 10-year bonds fell to multi-year or record lows.
Iran army announces strikes on Jordan, Kuwait, UAE, Bahrain
The Iranian army announced in a new statement that dozens of its suicide drones targeted radar systems and locations of US forces at the Al Dhafra and Al Minhad bases in the UAE.
The statement also noted that the Iranian army renewed its targeting of radar installations and US forces’ gathering centers at the Sheikh Issa base in Bahrain, with intense attacks using “Arch” suicide drones, as well as Ali al-Saleem base in Kuwait.
The US attacks across southern Iran, Tuesday night and Wednesday, have so far left 11 dead and 71 wounded, according to Iranian data.
Local authorities in Hormozgan Province reported that targeting a wedding party in a house in the port of Kohestak in the Sirik district of the province led to the killing of at least 5 people, including a child, and 63 wounded people were taken to the hospital. The governor of the city of Sirik, Reza Shahedin, told Iranian television that 50 people wounded in the wedding party were children and women.
In addition, the Iran's Fars agency quoted the Deputy President of Khuzestan Province for Security Affairs, Valiollah Hayani, as saying that American attacks last night on three points in the province claimed the lives of 7 people and injured eight others.

articles.title: Russia Turned Crimea Into a Missile Launchpad; Ukraine Is Now Dismantling It. Here’s How
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia Turned Crimea Into a Missile Launchpad; Ukraine Is Now Dismantling It. Here’s How
As Ukraine works to isolate Crimea from Russia and disrupt logistics on the southern front, its strikes on the peninsula serve as a form of proactive air defense, eliminating Russian missiles and drone salvos at their source before they can be used against Ukrainian cities.
Across 40 relentless days and nights between late June and early August, Ukraine launched a sweeping long-range campaign to paralyze Russian oil refining, cripple arms production, and neutralize shadow fleet vessels in the Black Sea and Sea of Azov—all to pressure Moscow toward peace.
Strikes hit key economic targets feeding the Kremlin's war chest, sending dual-use Wildberries logistics centers over 1,700 kilometers away in Yekaterinburg up in smoke. Eleven of Russia's largest oil refineries were also set ablaze, with hits reaching a record 2,500 kilometers into the interior, causing widespread fuel shortages and emergency rationing nationwide.
However, Ukraine’s strikes are also delivering a major blow to Russia’s ability to strike Ukraine from Crimea and hold on to the peninsula.
Why Crimea matters for Russia’s air campaign
Beyond deep strategic economic strikes, Ukraine's campaign relied heavily on "middle strike" drones to dismantle Russian supply chains and air defenses. Nowhere was this more evident than across temporarily occupied Crimea.
Thanks to Ukrainian efforts to hit Russian air defenses, they have been able to exploit gaps better and strike missile and drone launch sites. It is what Tomáš Nagy, an air defense expert and analyst at GLOBSEC, called “passive air defense,” which means that “you harden everything that you can harden, you mobilize whatever you can mobilize, and yes, you strike the capabilities of the other side to create vulnerabilities. And the best that the Ukrainians can do is to try to cripple [Russian] production capacity as much as possible.”
"It all started with Crimea, and it will end with Crimea,” a former Norwegian Defense Attaché to Ukraine, Hans Petter Midttun, told us. He underscored the peninsula's ultimate role in Russia's war against Ukraine.
"Russia's illegal annexation of Crimea in 2014 had a dramatic and immediate positive effect on Vladimir Putin's popularity and perceived legitimacy among Russians," he said, adding that it served as "one of the most important turning points in his domestic political standing".
Polling tracked this shift directly, showing Putin’s trust and approval for the general direction of the country jumped notably by August of that year, while overall approval for Putin reached 86% by September.
For years, "Crimea was perceived as the 'unsinkable aircraft carrier', essential for Russian power projection in the Black Sea and beyond," while also enabling full Russian control over the Sea of Azov, Midttun said. "Ukraine has turned a strategic trophy into a strategic liability. The campaign aims to make Russian operations from Crimea unsustainable. Every Russian military installation on the peninsula–airfields, naval bases, logistical hubs, sensors and weapons–is today within range of Ukrainian missiles and drones.”
If Crimea is liberated, Putin will likely fall.
Hans Petter Midttun
Former Norwegian Defense Attaché to Ukraine
Ukraine has managed to scale up its drone launches against Russia in both occupied territories and Russia itself, which is redefining the war.
“In the first 16 days of August, the reported rate rose to at least 480 per day,” said Midttun. “With the seven-day average reaching about 540 by 16 August. Russia is presently unable to effectively protect itself against Ukrainian missiles and drones.”
What is Ukraine's active (or proactive) air defense?
While one of the main goals of targeting Crimean infrastructure has been disrupting Russian supply lines, the campaign serves a vital secondary role: proactive air defense.
“Crimea is well within range of southern Ukraine,” said Midttun. “It reduces Ukrainian warning time and ability to counter incoming threats. The maritime domain further increases Ukraine’s defensive challenges, making it hard to locate air defense threats." That geography makes Crimea particularly valuable as a launchpad for Russian missile and drone attacks.
Crimea gives Russia a platform to project its military power from the south, creating what Midttun described as a “near omni-directional” threat and preventing Ukraine from concentrating its forces in the north and east.
To counter this, Ukrainian mid-range strikes degrade threats directly at their launchpads.
How Ukraine targets Russian missile launch infrastructure
Under Operation Crimean Power Switch Off, Ukrainian drone waves methodically degraded Russia's launch capabilities across the peninsula, striking a key forward staging hub and suppressing the daily barrage directed at Ukrainian civilians, cities, and critical infrastructure.
Specifically, Ukrainian strike networks have targeted six distinct pillars of Russia's Crimean military infrastructure:
- Air defense—S-300/S-400 launchers, Pantsir-S1 point-defense batteries. This weakens Russia’s defense of military sites.
- Missile launch sites—the aforementioned S-300/S-400 launchers, which Russia can use to fire surface-to-air missiles in a secondary ground-attack role, as well as Bastion launch sites used to fire Zircon and Oniks missiles. Striking these systems can reduce missile salvos targeting Odesa, Mykolaiv, and southern frontline positions at the source.
- Drone networks and launchpads—Dzhankoi Orion drone relay systems, Cape Chauda Shahed staging grounds, UAV command infrastructure. This targets the infrastructure used to stage, launch, and control Russian drones. In the same coordinated waves that neutralized two S-400 batteries, Ukrainian strikes also destroyed Shahed and Geran drone storage depots.
- Radars and tracking arrays—96L6 target acquisition radars, Okhotnyche radar shelters, Nebo complexes. This strips Russian forces of real-time air and maritime tracking, blinding target-coordination networks.
- Forward aviation hubs—Belbek, Saky, Dzhankoi, and Hvardiiske airbases: Suppresses tactical jet sorties by striking airfield hangars. This destroys ammo/fuel depots and forces strike aircraft to evacuate further inland.
- Military grid infrastructure—Tavriyskaya TPP, 330 kV Simferopol/Sevastopol substations, Kuban-Crimea power bridge. This cuts high-voltage power to bases, forcing air defense batteries and radars onto fragile backup generators.
What Russia uses in Crimea to launch attacks against Ukraine
Tracking every launch from Russian-occupied Crimea is difficult. While no single public source provides a complete picture, UNITED24 Media compared reports from Ukrainian threat-monitoring channel Monitor with official Ukrainian Air Force data to identify changes in Russia's use of Crimea as a launchpad.
Between January and August 12, Monitor’s tracking data recorded at least 35 confirmed missile launches across 17 distinct dates and 14 explicit drone launch episodes originating from the peninsula. Ukrainian Air Forces data shows the number of missiles is significantly higher, as Monitor tracks attack launches as they occur, not after; by August, Monitor observes a decrease in ground launches after the 40-day campaign.
Iskander, Zircon, and Oniks missiles were used repeatedly from January through to July. That surge saw a massive spike in attacks from Crimea at the height of the 40-day campaign—mostly from air-launched Kh-56/69 missiles, though ground launches also continued. However, combining the Monitor and Ukrainian official data, it shows that in August, the attacks drop, with four specific instances of Oniks missile launches by August 27, consisting of 8 confirmed missiles. In addition, there is one attack with Iskanders from the Crimea/Black Sea region, though it is unclear if it came from Crimea.
If we compare the types of attacks from Crimea, UAV attacks generally increase in July from the previous two months, but drop by mid-August. At the start of the year, in January, the majority of attacks were from ballistics, yet this number had dropped.
Oniks missiles continue to be launched from Crimea. In August, they were the majority of verified ground-launched missiles recorded from the peninsula in the combined dataset. Originally designed as anti-ship cruise missiles, Oniks can also be used against land targets. The shift in type of missile, and the volume, shows that Ukraine has made an impact on Russia’s ability to use Crimea as a missile launchpad.
Why Crimea is a key part of Ukraine's defense strategy
Further strikes on Russian launch infrastructure could constrain Crimea’s role as a platform for attacks on Ukraine even more. While Crimea remains a crucial launchpad for Russian drones and missiles, further degrading its potential to launch strikes yields multiple strategic benefits.
Midttun listed the key impacts:
- Opens the Black Sea for maritime trade and activity
- Allows Ukraine to relocate forces and capacities towards Belarus and Russia
- Increases the protection of Ukrainian citizens and critical infrastructure
- Creates the precondition for the forthcoming liberation of the Crimean Peninsula
The operation “Logistics Lockdown” is not only affecting Russia’s ability to sustain operations from Crimea but also the Russian occupation forces in the Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions, says Midttun.
“During the last three months, Ukraine has destroyed an average of 13,456 trucks monthly across all sectors,” he said. “A majority of these, however, are destroyed in the south. Road and rail bridges are being destroyed at scale.”
Targeting such a crucial launchpad and eliminating weapons systems before they can fire eases pressure on the southern front. Odesa, Mykolaiv, and other southern cities stand to benefit most directly because of their proximity to the peninsula.
These operations put pressure on Russia’s forces across the occupied south. If Russia cannot transport troops, supplies, and military vehicles without a major risk, then they cannot reinforce and are less able to conduct large-scale offensive operations.
These strikes also divert Russian resources, forcing Moscow to either protect its military equipment on the peninsula by relocating it or transfer air defense systems from elsewhere—weakening Russian defenses on other parts of the frontline.
Further degrading Russia’s ability to launch Oniks missiles could reduce the missile threat to Odesa and southern Ukraine—protecting civilians, supporting frontline forces, and securing Black Sea grain corridors.
What does Ukraine need to increase and repeat these results?
In a recent interview, Unmanned Systems Forces commander Robert “Magyar” Brovdi revealed that his forces are operating at just 14% of full capacity, but could strike seven times as many military targets in Crimea if pledged Western funds arrived faster.
This operational constraint aligns directly with Midttun’s assessment that production readiness is not the issue, but financial backing: "Ukraine lacks the economy to ramp up its missile and drone production. That’s the only thing stopping Ukraine from increasing the scale and scope of the campaign."
Western support must increase to allow Ukraine to expand its impact and replicate these tactics across other fronts, Midttun said. Russia’s invasion is part of a broader hybrid war against Europe—one that will only escalate if Ukraine is forced to operate under persistent material constraints.
Another way to boost Ukraine’s capabilities beyond its own territories would be allowing Starlink use over Russian territory. Ukraine’s ability to use Starlink over Crimea enabled it to strike a wide range of Russian military targets across the peninsula. However, even with the impressive long-range strikes, the satellite system could be more impactful if it eased the transfer of communications to drones.
President Zelenskyy recently said that Ukraine has a “window of opportunity” to end the war, because of its many advantages on the battlefield and in the skies. Operations that degrade Russia’s military infrastructure in Crimea are part of that broader effort.
Empowering Kyiv to degrade Crimean launchpads and set the conditions for the peninsula's eventual liberation is not just a battlefield tactic; it directly fortifies wider European security.
Discuss this article:
In a Nutshell

articles.title: Faith in fakes: How anti-Russian hysteria is driving the EU’s drone hoax
articles.body:
Faith in fakes: How anti-Russian hysteria is driving the EU’s drone hoax
Is it a bird? Is it a plane? Is it a well-timed ploy to ramp up defense spending? Germany's evidence-free claim that a drone found lying between Ukrainian cargo planes on the canopy of Leipzig/Halle airport is part of a pattern.
Last year's late-autumn drone sighting hysteria that swept across Norway, Denmark, the Netherlands and Belgium, was used by the bloc to amplify and entrench an anti-Russia stance that has seen it throw hundreds of billions it cannot afford into weapons and a war its chosen side cannot win.
Tens of millions of Euro has since been spent on the back of a 'scare' that has been shown to have been irrational, exuberant and driven by vested interests.
The most bizarre national security scare in recent European history began at Copenhagen’s Kastrup Airport on September 2 last year. According to Denmark’s Frihedsbrevet news site, an airport employee told her supervisors that she saw two drones approach the area “stealthily,” adding that “they are big. They are not toys.”
The airport was temporarily shut down, and within hours, reports of a similar drone incursion came in from Oslo, Norway.
“I can only say that this is in my eyes a serious attack on Danish critical infrastructure,” Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said at the time. “I cannot in any way deny that it is Russia.” Her Norwegian counterpart, Gahr Store, came to a similar conclusion. “Russia has violated Norwegian airspace on three occasions this spring and summer,” he claimed. “We cannot determine whether this was done intentionally or due to navigation errors. Regardless of the cause, this is not acceptable.”
“It is clear we are witnessing a pattern of persistent contestation at our borders,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said. “Our critical infrastructure is at risk. And Europe will respond to this threat with strength and determination.”
Open-source investigators insisted that the sightings were a hoax from the outset. Sleuths on the Metabunk forums concluded that the ‘drone’ seen at Kastrup Airport in the above footage was actually a small single-engine plane. FlightRadar24 data showed one such plane – a Socata TB-20 Trinidad – passing over the airport’s main runway twice at the time of the sighting.
Where were drones spotted?
Nevertheless, panic spread across northern Europe as drones were supposedly spotted at the following airports, military bases, and infrastructure sites in the following days and weeks:
- September 23: Aalborg Airport, Denmark
- September 24: Aalborg Airport, Billund Airport, Sonderborg, Esbjerg and Skrydstrup airports, Denmark
- September 25: Billund Airport, Denmark; Thyssenkrupp factory, Schleswig-Holstein, Germany; University Medical Center, Kiel, Germany; Bundeswehr base, Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, Germany
September 26: Karup Air Base, Skrydstrup Air Base, Jutland Dragoon Regiment base, Denmark
- September 27: Orland Main Air Station, Norway
- September 28: Bronnoysund Airport, Norway; Borris Camp, Denmark
- October 2: Munich Airport, Germany; Elsenborn-Butgenbach Air Base, Belgium
- October 3: Munich Airport, Germany
- October 31: Berlin-Brandenburg Airport, Germany
- November 2: Bremen Airport, Germany; Kleine Brogel Air Base, Belgium
- November 6: Gothenburg Airport, Sweden; Brussels Airport, Antwerp Port, Belgium
- November 9: Liege Airport, Doel Nuclear Power Plant, Belgium
- November 22: Volkel Air Base, Netherlands
- December 1: In the Irish Sea off Dublin, during Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky’s arrival by plane
Police across northern Europe received thousands of additional drone reports from civilians. In Denmark alone, nearly 6,000 reports of suspected drones were filed.
Did the drones even exist?
Not only is there no proof that Russia was connected with these sightings, there is no evidence that any drones were present at all. No wreckage has been recovered, no perpetrators have been identified, and no footage of the drones exists, except for the video from Copenhagen that apparently shows a light aircraft.
Despite being certain that Denmark was under “hybrid attack,” Mette Frederiksen acknowledged in late September that there could be an “alternate explanation” for the sightings. Six months later, six government sources told Denmark’s TV2 that they don’t “have any technical evidence to support that Denmark was subjected to a hybrid attack with drones.” Frihedsbrevet’s sources came to a similar conclusion, with the airport employee who reported the initial sighting admitting that she could have been mistaken.
Airport management still insist that drones were present in the area on September 22, but police have not acknowledged any drones, only “reports” of drones.
Danish troops reportedly opened fire on a drone over Borris Camp on September 28. According to an investigation by TV2, the only aircraft operating in the area at the time was a turboprop passenger plane. The Danish military, if TV2’s reporting is correct, nearly shot down a civilian aircraft over a false alarm.
After interviewing witnesses and reviewing surveillance footage, Norwegian police closed their investigation on November 6, stating that they were “unable to confirm or deny whether drones were actually observed on the night of September 23.”
German police have not been able to confirm any drone activity; Dutch officials have identified no threat, with internal documents stating that there was “no indication of sabotage or attacks on vital objects.” Dutch and Belgian authorities have found no credible basis for panic, with Belgian Defense Minister Theo Francken issuing a half-apology last month for attempting to pass off a video of a police helicopter as evidence of nefarious aerial activity.
Did they just lie?
Out of every country involved, Denmark’s leaders were most insistent that Russia was behind the spate of sightings. Frederiksen, Defense Minister Troels Lund Poulsen, and Justice Minister Peter Hummelgaard all described the incidents as “attacks,” despite nothing being attacked and no attackers being present.
“I consider it a new reality that Denmark and Europe are under more violent and frequent hybrid attacks,” Frederiksen said in a televised address on September 25. “And even though the authorities cannot conclude who is behind the hybrid attacks…there is primarily one country that poses a threat to Europe's security – and that is Russia.”
The flood of tips and reports from the public can be written off either as mass hysteria, or – more charitably – as a natural reaction from Europeans primed by their politicians and media to believe that Russia is planning an all-out war on the continent. As for why Frederiksen would stoke this fear, however, some clues can be found in her actions.
At the time, Denmark was just over a year into an historic rearmament program. After a €5.4 billion military budget hike in 2024, Frederiksen announced last February that defense spending would be increased from 2.4% to 3% of GDP by 2030 (since increased to 3.5%). By late 2025, Denmark had purchased hundreds of armored combat vehicles, signed contracts for new air defense systems, increased annual conscription numbers, and, for the first time in its history, introduced compulsory military service for women.
Denmark, she said last February, needs to undergo a “massive rearmament,” because “We don’t know what [Russian President Vladimir Putin] is planning, but we know that he and Russia are in the process of rearming.”
Frederiksen referenced this rearmament again in her September address, declaring that “the events of recent days only emphasize how important it is.”
Denmark held the EU’s rotating presidency at the time, and Frederiksen added that the alleged drone threat would be made front and center when EU leaders met in Copenhagen the following week, and that she would push for “the establishment of an actual drone wall.”
The EU’s drone wall
Frederiksen kept her word. Published on October 16, the European Commission’s ‘Defense Readiness Roadmap’ stated that a ‘European Drone Defense Initiative’ – the so-called “drone wall” comprising sensors and interceptors – would be operational along the bloc’s eastern borders with Russia and Belarus by 2027.
🚨🇪🇺 “We need to act now”Ursula von der Leyen now wants to build a “Drone Wall” on the Eastern Flank of Europe to protect from the alleged Russian Aggression. pic.twitter.com/UAGH93fKRc
— Concerned Citizen (@BGatesIsaPyscho) October 1, 2025
Drones continued to dominate the agenda at a European Council summit in Brussels in December. “The European Council strongly condemns all recent hybrid attacks against the European Union and its Member States,” read a statement released after the meeting. “In the light of Russia’s and Belarus’ intensified hybrid campaign, it calls for accelerated efforts to strengthen resilience, protect critical infrastructure, and…decisively ramp up Europe’s defense readiness by 2030.”
None of this is to suggest that Denmark orchestrated the drone panic to justify its remilitarization, or to sell the EU’s “drone wall.” Both initiatives were already underway at the time. Instead, it illustrates how Danish and EU officials saw an opportunity not to let a crisis go to waste, and kept the drone threat alive even as their own police forces, to put it mildly, struggled to substantiate it.
Belgium's very own drone crisis
Frederiksen wasn’t the only national leader who saw an opportunity amid the panic. Remember Belgian Defense Minister Theo Francken? After police hotlines were flooded with more than 550 reports of drones between September and December, Francken bypassed the standard bidding process to authorize the purchase of €50 million worth of drone detection and jamming systems.
An investigation by Belgium’s VRT broadcaster has since found that none of the reports of drones were credible, and Francken has been hammered by the opposition for sharing an image of a ‘drone’ over Brussels Airport that turned out to be a police helicopter. VRT found that the defense ministry ignored warnings from Belgium’s Inspectorate of Finance and purchased detection antennas at an inflated price, and Francken is now the subject of an inquiry by the Brussels Public Prosecutor's Office.
The debacle is reminiscent of the Agusta-Dassault affair. During the 1980s, defense contractors Agusta and Dassault paid the equivalent of €4 million in bribes to secure no-bid contracts for AW109 transport helicopters and electronic warfare equipment. Once exposed, the scandal led to the criminal conviction of Belgian Defense Minister Guy Coeme and Foreign Minister and NATO Secretary General Willy Claes.
So did Russian drones spook the EU?
Nearly eight months after the first ‘drones’ were spotted over Copenhagen, the crisis is still being milked across Europe. In early May, long after the threat had been debunked in Denmark, Norway, Belgium, and the Netherlands, the Dutch defense ministry announced that it would acquire approximately 900 “electro-optical aiming devices” for use against UAVs, “without prior announcement due to the urgency of a crisis situation.”
Questioned by the Belgian parliament in April, Francken insisted that there is “no other plausible explanation” for the reports other than Russian drones, and that the only way to prove or disprove this is to invest in drone defense technology. “As long as you don’t have the means to detect and neutralize drones, it stands to reason that you cannot immediately produce physical evidence,” he told lawmakers.
The Dutch and Belgians aren’t letting a lack of evidence stop them from pursuing the defense deals that they wanted from this crisis, and the EU is unlikely to step in and pump the brakes.
The EU's censorious and paranoid media industry is the perfect environment for fake news to fester, as long as it suits the bloc. Remember, Commission President Ursula von der Leyen's claims of “GPS jamming” hitting her plane on a trip to Bulgaria last September, and how, despite it being roundly debunked within days, it has been allowed to fester to serve her political agenda.
Anti-Russian hysteria is the animating political force in the EU, and the bloc’s leaders clearly aren’t going to let police and media investigations, or common sense, put a stop to the show.

articles.title: USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier docks in Thailand after nine months at sea
articles.body:
USS Lincoln carrier docks near Thailand's Pattaya resort after nine months at sea
More than 5,000 US sailors and Marines arrived in Thailand Wednesday after nine months at sea on the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier. The carrier's long deployment in the Middle East during the US-Israeli war on Iran sparked reports of worsening mental health crises on board, including attempted suicides.
The USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier steamed into Thailand's Laem Chabang on Wednesday after more than nine months at sea, including a long deployment in the Middle East marred by reports of sailors' worsening mental health and deteriorating conditions on board.
The 5,000 sailors and Marines on board the ship are headed for the Thai resort of Pattaya, a rest-and-recreation stop for US troops since the Vietnam War.
Tugs guided the huge nuclear-powered carrier, dozens of warplanes lined up on its flight deck, towards the port of Laem Chabang on Wednesday morning, AFP reporters saw.
"Our arrival in Laem Chabang provides a well-deserved opportunity for our Sailors and Marines to rest and recharge," Rear Admiral Robert Loughran, commander of the US Carrier Strike Group 3, said in a statement.
Read moreMiddle East live: Iran says latest US strikes kill 11 people
The Lincoln's commanding officer, Captain Dan Keeler, added that its first port visit of the "historic deployment" – after 286 days at sea – would allow "our crew to enjoy this beautiful and historic country".
An official in Pattaya said it was due to dock shortly before lunchtime.
The Lincoln left California in November 2025 for duty in the South China Sea and was rerouted to the Middle East before US-Israeli attacks on Iran that began six months ago.
Reports of deteriorating living conditions and poor mental health on board – including attempted suicides – made headlines in the United States and provoked criticism of President Donald Trump's war against Iran.
Thailand became a US treaty ally in 1954, before being designated a major non-NATO ally in 2003. Thailand's armed forces have long been reliant on US defence hardware and both countries' militaries maintain strong relations and hold annual exercises together.
Bangkok has made clear the visit is for logistics and rest and recuperation in line with its treaty commitments and is not connected to the conflict in the Middle East.
Pattaya is hugely popular with foreign tourists, known for its beaches and a nightlife scene that has long drawn scrutiny over sex tourism.
Although illegal in Thailand, the sex industry operates openly in major tourism hubs, including parts of Bangkok and Pattaya.
Pattaya's mayor, Poramase Ngampiches, told AFP this week that there had been a recent crackdown on sex workers but denied it was linked to the US arrivals.
Outside one bar in the resort on Tuesday was a sign saying "Welcome all US military personnel. Thank you for your service".
'Things can get out of hand'
The mayor said buses have been laid on to transport the sailors from the ship to Pattaya and back until the carrier departs on Sunday.
"They come to relax," Poramase said in a video posted on Facebook.
"Our preparations will focus on safety and ensuring fair pricing, so we don't take advantage of them."
He said the sailors have been banned from water sports such as jet skis, and from taking advantage of Thailand's lax cannabis laws.
But he encouraged them to enjoy the city's many other attractions, from malls to religious sites.
"We're happy to get business from anybody," Nicko, the French owner of a go-go bar in Pattaya, told AFP this week.
"We'll have to be careful because as we know, things can get out of hand with alcohol involved."
Democratic lawmakers have called for an investigation into conditions on the USS Abraham Lincoln following reports of food shortages, broken plumbing and mental health crises.
But Trump dismissed the concerns, as well as the suggestion the ship had been deployed for too long.
"A small number of mental health cases were treated with no loss of life," acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao said in mid-August, blaming the media for "trying to paint our warriors as victims".
The carrier was replaced in the Middle East by the USS George Washington, which had been in Japan, as the US-Israel war with Iran drags on.
That ship in turn will be relieved by the USS Theodore Roosevelt, which will sail from San Diego in the coming weeks, according to private military association the US Naval Institute.
The US has maintained an aircraft carrier in the Arabian Sea for strike missions over Iran since the US and Israel launched the war at the end of February, and subsequently to enforce a naval blockade of Iranian ports.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP and Reuters)

articles.title: Putin on Kiev’s ‘terrorism,’ British ‘legitimate targets’ and a ‘military secret’ (KEY REMARKS)
articles.body:
‘Military secret’: Putin keeps Kiev and London guessing over Russia’s ‘legitimate targets’ (KEY REMARKS)
Russian President Vladimir Putin has outlined Russia’s accelerating battlefield gains in Ukraine, denounced Kiev’s increasingly desperate threats to civilian airlines as “state terrorism,” and warned that UK military facilities on Ukrainian soil would be legitimate targets.
Speaking to reporters in Bishkek, Putin also addressed Russian strikes on ships carrying weapons to Ukraine, contact with US intelligence and Trump’s envoys, relations with Germany, and the West’s “sharks of imperialism.”
Here are the key takeaways:
‘The enemy will crumble’
Putin said Ukrainian forces are steadily losing ground, while cautioning against predicting when the decisive turning point will come, as “war is cruel and difficult to predict.”
Russian troops are not merely advancing but “increasing the pace of the offensive,” he said, giving a brief rundown of developments across the front. Putin said Russian forces are approaching Slavyansk, Kramatorsk, and Druzhkovka, while claiming that around 5,000 Ukrainian troops have been encircled near the Krasnooskolskoye Reservoir. He also reported advances in Zaporozhye Region and toward Sumy.
“I have no doubt that the enemy will crumble. The question of timing is always very complicated.”
He also rejected proposals to freeze the conflict along the current front line.
“We don’t want to freeze it. We want to end the war and achieve a lasting, absolute peace – both in Ukraine and in Europe.”
‘No negotiations with terrorists’
Asked about Vladimir Zelensky’s threat to civilian airlines using Russian airspace, Putin said the remarks amount to “a bid for state terrorism,” contrasting them with Kiev’s calls for “negotiations and personal meetings.”
“You don’t negotiate with terrorists,” Putin said, warning that if attacks on civilian aircraft were actually carried out, Moscow would find a way to respond.
Asked whether Ukrainian political and military leaders could become targets, Putin said Russia has so far refrained from this because it may ultimately need people on the Ukrainian side to negotiate with.
“This is a bid for terrorism; it is not yet a transition to terrorism. If it comes to that, we will see how to respond. We will find the tools.”
‘They hit ours – they’ll get an answer’
Putin said the Russian military has been ordered to prepare “massive strikes” against Ukrainian energy facilities in response to attacks on Russian civilian and fuel infrastructure. Ukrainian drones once again attempted overnight to penetrate the air defenses of Moscow and St. Petersburg and strike three Russian oil refineries, but the attacks were repelled, according to the president.
“They hit ours – they’ll get an answer. That’s roughly how things stand.”
Putin also said a recent decree allowing temporary state management of poorly protected critical infrastructure was intended to force private companies and state agencies to cooperate more closely on defense against drone attacks, rejecting suggestions that it amounts to nationalization.
‘Kiev opened Pandora’s box’
Putin stressed that Russia has not attacked Ukrainian shipping at random, but only targeted vessels that bring weapons and ammunition into Ukraine, arguing that the secondary explosions following the attacks confirmed the nature of their cargoes.
“We did carry out precision strikes on certain vessels, but they were genuinely selective.”
The president said Russia expanded its maritime response after Zelensky launched his much-touted 40-day campaign against the Russian economy and logistics. According to Putin, Kiev failed to inflict any “critical damage” but hit around 100 vessels and killed several sailors, including foreign nationals.
“You yourselves opened Pandora’s box – now take what comes.”
Putin noted that the original Black Sea grain initiative was promoted as being essential to averting hunger in developing countries, particularly in Africa – yet only around 0.2% of Ukrainian grain exported under the arrangement reached developing markets, while most went to European countries.
Contact with the CIA and Trump’s ‘welcome guests’
Putin dismissed the idea that contact between Russian and American intelligence chiefs is unusual, noting that channels remained open even during the Cold War. He singled out Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, describing the Trump confidants as sincere interlocutors who have the US president’s trust.
“Mr. Kushner and Witkoff are always welcome guests here, and we work with them with pleasure.”
Moscow is open to additional participants in Ukraine talks if they can make a real contribution, he added, but not diplomacy in “meaningless mode.”
British targets and a ‘military secret’
Putin confirmed that any British military facilities established in Ukraine would be considered legitimate targets.
“Any military facilities in Ukraine are our legitimate targets – British or any others.”
Asked whether military-industrial facilities in the UK could become targets if British weapons are used to strike Russia, Putin declined to reveal Russia’s red lines.
“That’s a secret. A military secret.”
Germany just needs to ‘press the button’
Putin also rejected German accusations surrounding a drone incident in Leipzig, arguing that Berlin is invoking the threat of an “aggressive Russia” to distract from domestic political and economic problems.
He recalled earlier accusations that Russia sabotaged its own Nord Stream pipelines, calling the allegation absurd given Russia’s interest in selling gas to Europe.
Russia remains capable of supplying Germany with gas, he said.
“They only need to press the button.”
German leaders, however, lack the political will to do so because of US sanctions, Putin said, describing Berlin’s broader Russia policy as contrary to the interests of the German people.
Western ‘sharks of imperialism’
Putin was also asked to explain a recent analogy involving orcas, polar bears, and Russia’s confrontation with the West. He said comparing the Collective West to an orca would be unfair to the animal, describing killer whales as intelligent creatures. Instead, he revived an old Soviet expression: “the sharks of imperialism.”
“If someone tries to drag us down the food chain and gobble us up, they may get hit in the teeth. Russia is ready to do that, despite the rapidly growing appetites and teeth of these sharks.”

articles.title: US launches new strikes on Iran
articles.body:
Iran hits back after deadly US strike on wedding: As it happened
Iran has launched a new wave of missile and drone attacks on US military facilities in the Gulf region after Washington resumed strikes on southern Iran, killing civilians, including children.
The US military began striking Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) targets near the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday, saying the operation was launched in response to alleged Iranian attempts to attack commercial shipping and US troops in the region. President Donald Trump called the strikes “large and powerful” and warned Tehran that any retaliation would trigger an even harsher response.
The Iranian authorities said a US strike hit a residential building in Kuhestak, Hormozgan Province, where a wedding was taking place. At least five civilians were killed, including a four-year-old child and a 16-year-old teenager, and dozens more were injured.
Iran subsequently launched what it called a “punishing response,” claiming missile and drone attacks on US military facilities in Jordan, Bahrain, Kuwait, the UAE, and Erbil in Kurdistan Region, Iraq. The strikes targeted Camp Titin near Aqaba, Sheikh Isa Air Base in Bahrain, Ali Al Salem Air Base in Kuwait, and Al Dhafra and Al Minhad bases in the UAE.
The IRGC claimed US personnel were killed and military equipment was destroyed in some of the attacks.
Jordan said 13 ballistic missiles entered its airspace during the latest attacks, with ten intercepted and three falling away from populated areas.
The escalation follows an exchange of strikes over the weekend, after US forces hit Iran’s Larak Island in the Strait of Hormuz. Iran retaliated with ballistic missiles and drones targeting US military positions in Jordan. Trump subsequently vowed to “hit Iran hard.”
Washington has also stepped up economic pressure on Tehran, launching an “economic onslaught” and threatening to cut foreign institutions that deal with Iran off from the US dollar system. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Sunday that new secondary sanctions could be rolled out every week against foreign banks and companies that continue dealing with Tehran.
This live feed has now ended.
- 02 September 2026 07:40 GMTThe Iranian strikes came hours after the US resumed attacks on Iran on Tuesday. President Donald Trump warned Tehran against retaliating. “If Iran retaliates against these strikes, they will be hit again at a much harder and higher level,” Trump said, adding that an even larger attack is “waiting in the wings.” “When it is over, there will be very little left of the Islamic Republic of Iran.” Trump said the strikes are in retaliation for Iran’s “failed attempt” to lay mines in the Strait of Hormuz and launching eight missiles at a US military base in Jordan, which he said were all intercepted. In a phone call with Fox News later on Tuesday, Trump escalated the threat, saying Iran would be “totally wiped out” if it strikes back. “This is a very big hit today. If it goes a third time, they’re going to be totally wiped out as a country,” Fox News quoted him as saying.
- 07:34 GMTThe IRGC said it had also launched dozens of kamikaze drones at two US military bases in the UAE, expanding its retaliatory strikes across the region. The drones targeted radar systems and US forces at Al Dhafra and Al Minhad air bases, according to the IRGC. It described the Al Dhafra base as a key operational center of “criminal America in the region,” used for air operations, reconnaissance, surveillance, and support. The IRGC said the attacks were retaliation for US strikes on Iranian residential areas and the “targeting of a wedding ceremony” in southern Iran. Four people were killed in the US strike on the wedding gathering in Sirik county on Tuesday night, Al Jazeera reported, citing the Hormozgan governorate. The dead included a four-year-old child and a 16-year-old teenager, as well as two women aged 43 and 50.
- 06:52 GMTIran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said on Wednesday it had killed “a number of enemy elements” and destroyed several drones in a missile and drone attack on Kuwait’s Ali Al Salem Air Base. In a statement, the IRGC said its Ground Force carried out a “combined missile and drone attack” on the headquarters and residence of the US commander at the base. The strike reportedly set fire to a drone hangar and deployment ramp and destroyed several drones used in attacks on Iran. Kuwait earlier said it had intercepted Iranian missiles and drones but reported no casualties. The IRGC said the operation was carried out alongside strikes on US bases in Jordan, Bahrain and Erbil in retaliation for a US strike on a residential building in Sirik, southern Iran, where officials said a wedding ceremony was taking place. The IRGC said the strike killed four people, including a child. Addressing Kuwaitis, the IRGC said the attack targeted the “US military presence” rather than the Kuwaiti people and called for the removal of American forces from the country.
- 04:54 GMTOil prices surged after the latest exchange of strikes between Washington and Tehran renewed fears of supply disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz. Oil prices initially jumped the US announced its strikes on Tuesday, with Brent settling 4.6% higher at $94.65 a barrel and WTI gaining 5.2% to $90.22. Prices continued climbing early Wednesday, with Brent trading above $95 and WTI above $91.
- 04:31 GMTAll US personnel are accounted for following Iran’s retaliatory strikes, a senior American official told Fox News. The official said US forces intercepted “the majority of” missiles fired by Tehran, with most of the missiles and drones reportedly headed toward Jordan. No major damage has been reported at US bases across the Middle East, the official added.
- 04:03 GMTBrigadier General Yadollah Javani, the IRGC’s deputy for political affairs, has urged regional countries hosting American forces to expel them and reclaim US bases. “It would be better for you to expel the Americans from your countries and take back the bases,” Javani said, according to Tasnim. Otherwise, he warned, Iran would deliver “decisive and crushing responses” to any attack launched from Kuwait, Bahrain, Jordan or any other country. Iran Strikes U.S. Sites Across Four Countries — Ryan Rozbiani (@RyanRozbiani) September 2, 2026
 1) 🇮🇶 Iraq: Maintenance center, equipment warehouses, surveillance system and fuel tanks
 2) 🇯🇴 Jordan: Marine facilities, attack helicopters and drone hangars
3) 🇧🇭 Bahrain: Radar systems, fuel infrastructure and U.S. troop… pic.twitter.com/xMsJCVioWs
- 03:45 GMTBahrain’s Interior Ministry has issued a third alert over a “potential threat” in the past six hours, again urging residents to remain calm and move to the nearest safe location. The ministry also called on the public to follow updates through official channels. An alert of potential threat.The Ministry of Interior urged citizens and residents to remain calm, proceed to the nearest safe location, and follow news through official channels for the protection of public safety. — Ministry of Interior (@moi_bahrain) September 2, 2026
- 03:28 GMTUS forces struck around 100 targets during the latest round of attacks on Iran – including two government tankers anchored off Iran’s coast, north of the US naval blockade line, Axios reported, citing unnamed US officials. American drones fired missiles into the tankers’ engine rooms under what one US official described as a new “tanker for tanker” policy reportedly approved by President Donald Trump in response to Iranian attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.
- 03:12 GMTIsraeli warplanes launched multiple strikes on southern Lebanon, according to regional media reports. Al Mayadeen reported a heavy barrage targeting Nabatieh al-Fawqa, while Al Jazeera correspondents on the ground said the Israeli military carried out two air strikes on the outskirts of Kfar Ramman and Arab Selim. شنّ الطيران الحربي الإسرائيلي حزامًا ناريًا عنيفًا استهدف بلدة النبطية الفوقا، في الجنوب.#الميادين_لبنانpic.twitter.com/ATabyxPhcc — الميادين لبنان - AL Mayadeen Lebanon (@mayadeenlebanon) September 2, 2026
- 02:55 GMTAt least seven people were killed and eight others injured in separate US missile strikes on three locations in Iran’s southwestern Khuzestan Province, IRNA reported, according to Al Jazeera. The casualties are separate from those reported in the strike on Kuhestak in Hormozgan Province, where a wedding was underway.

articles.title: ‘Gifts are on the way’: Iran says it will no longer exercise restraint with US allies after strikes
articles.body:
Iran launched retaliatory strikes on US bases in Jordan, Kuwait and Bahrain, overnight from Tuesday to Wednesday, following the US's renewal of strikes against Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) targets in Iran on Tuesday.
Sirens sounded in Kuwait as the country's air defenses confronted attacks by hostile drones, "following the sinful Iranian aggression," Kuwait's army said in a post on X/Twitter on Wednesday morning.
"The sounds of explosions, if heard, are the result of air defense systems intercepting the hostile attacks."
Meanwhile, the Bahraini Interior Ministry announced "an alert of potential threat" in the country, with local sources telling Iranian state media IRIB that at least four consecutive explosions were heard.
Iran strikes Iraq
In a statement the IRGC claimed to have carried out a combined missile and drone attack on US bases in Erbil, Iraq.
The attack "destroyed a maintenance center and technical equipment warehouses belonging to the US military and destroying the US spy balloon guidance system at the base," the IRGC statement claimed.
"The Ground Force fighters also set the base’s fuel depots on fire and killed several of the US Forces," it added. "A large number of American troops were sent to hell."
IRIB also reported that explosions were heard near the US consulate in Erbil, Iraq. Local media also reported an impact.
Neither the US nor Iraq have confirmed such attacks.
Iranian semi-official news outlet Tasnim reported that loud explosions were heard in Sulaymaniyah, Iraq.
Jordanian army intercepted 10 of 13 Iranian ballistic missiles
Sirens sounded in Jordan as air defenses intercepted 10 of the 13 Iranian missiles that entered the country's airspace, the Jordanian Armed Forces confirmed in a statement on Wednesday. The three impacts were in remoted areas, away from population centers, the statement added.
There were no American casualties from Iranian attacks on US military bases in Jordan, two US officials told Reuters.
Iran targeted a US Marine base in Jordan with ballistic missiles, the IRGC spokesperson announced on Tuesday evening, claiming that "a large number of US forces were killed" at the Camp Titin base.
The IRGC "carried out a heavy ballistic missile attack on the US Marine base in Jordan known as Camp Titin, located on the shores of the Gulf of Aqaba, killing a large number of US forces and destroying several important facilities and attack helicopters."
An El Al flight from Tel Aviv to Bangkok was forced to turn around mid air due to Iranian fire towards Jordan, N12 News reported. The plane is now continuing on its way to Thailand.
In a later statement the IRGC spokesperson said that combatants from the IRGC "carried out a heavy ballistic missile attack on the hangars housing RQ-4 and MQ-9 long-range unmanned aircraft at the US air base in Jordan known as Prince Hassan."
"Several drones were destroyed, and several pilots and flight technical crew members were killed," the IRGC claimed, contrary to American reports. "Several of their technical infrastructure facilities were also set on fire."
Iranian military spokesperson threatens Bahrain, Kuwait
Shortly after the US strikes began, Iranian military spokesperson Ebrahim Zolfaghari stated that Iran “will no longer exercise restraint regarding Bahrain and Kuwait” in a post on X/Twitter.
“Gifts are on the way,” Zolfaghari warned.
Saudi-owned news outlet Al Arabiya, citing an Iranian military official, reported that Iran had begun launching missiles and drones towards US-linked targets.
Tasnim shared an additional statement from Zolfaghari in which he reportedly said Iran will "deliver crushing and devastating blows to the despicable and malevolent American enemy."
Iran "launched a massive strike using kamikaze drones a few hours ago, targeting radar facilities and concentrations of American terrorist forces at the Sheikh Isa Air Base in Bahrain," the IRGC spokesperson claimed on Wednesday morning.
"Combatants of the IRGC have delivered a crushing and sweeping response to the enemy's hostile actions," the statement added."
There has not been any confirmation from Bahrain or the US of the attack.
Trump warns there'll be 'little left of Islamic Republic of Iran' should it respond
CENTCOM and US President Donald Trump confirmed the strikes, noting that they are being carried out in retaliation for Iranian attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and the recent attack on US troops stationed in the region.
"The United States is, as we speak, striking Iranian Targets near the Strait of Hormuz," he wrote. "The strikes are large and powerful, and in retaliation for the Iranians’ failed attempt at adding sea mines to the Strait, which currently has no mines (They have been completely removed or detonated!), and the Iranians shooting eight missiles, all successfully knocked down, at our Military Base in Jordan."
Trump threatened Iran that, should it respond to the "very justified attack," it will be hit "again at a much harder and higher level, but it will not be the biggest attack of them all, that is waiting in the wings and, when it is over, there will be very little left of the Islamic Republic of Iran!"
Iranian state media reported that several explosions were heard in the eastern area of the city of Bandar Abbas and across southern Iran.

articles.title: Iran launches retaliatory strikes after latests US airstrikes
articles.body:
Tasnim and Fars news agencies have reported that the Iranian armed forces fired missiles and drones towards aggressor US bases in the region.
The IRGC public relations office said in a sttaement issued on Tuesday night that the "regret-inducing response" to the aggression by the US military had begun.
The IRGC also said that the US aggression latest of which happened on Tuesday night would strengthen the lock on the Hormuz Strait.
There were reports of missiles being fired from Karaj next to Tehran, Kermanshah and Aligoudarz in Lorestan Province in the west of Iran.
There were also reports of civilian casualties in Hormuzgan province as a resut of the US aggression.
Mehr News Agency also reported later that sound of air defense were heard in the east of the capital Tehran on Tuesday midnight.
Meanwhile, Barak Ravid, American news website "Axios" reporter said in a post on social media that the US base in Jordan came under attack by Iranian ballistic missiles.
