							Ukraine’s Security Service says it foiled FSB plot to assassinate Russian opposition leader in Kyiv – several wounded in street shootout
- 
						
							Putin calls Zelenskyy’s airspace warning “state terrorism” as shares in Russia’s national airline fall 5%
- 
						
							“Russian airspace will effectively be closing”: Zelenskyy warns airlines Russian skies are no longer safe

articles.title: This is what the post-Western world looks like
articles.body:
This is what the post-Western world looks like
The Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit in Bishkek will be remembered less for its formal group photo than for the leaders in attendance – and the political significance of bringing them together. Seated around the same table were Russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, and the leaders of Central Asian nations, Iran, Pakistan, and Belarus. They were joined for the expanded session by leaders of partner countries, including Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, as well as representatives of international organizations, among them UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres.
This was no longer simply a regional gathering focused on security in Central Asia. The SCO’s ten member states now cover roughly a quarter of the world’s landmass, account for more than 42% of its population, and generate over 23% of global GDP. In other words, nearly half of humanity was represented in Bishkek. The simultaneous presence of the leaders of Russia, China, and India was especially significant: They represent the world’s largest country by area, its second-largest economy, and its most populous nation. Together with the SCO’s other members, they form a demographic, resource, industrial, and political bloc without which any serious discussion of reshaping the international order is now impossible.
That is why the summit in Kyrgyzstan should be seen as more than another entry on the diplomatic calendar. It demonstrated that multipolarity is no longer an abstract formula but is beginning to acquire a clear institutional shape. The SCO is one of the platforms where a new balance of power is emerging not only in speeches and declarations, but in practice – through regular meetings between leaders, security coordination, settlements in national currencies, new transportation corridors, energy cooperation, and the gradual development of independent mechanisms for growth.
From the Shanghai Five to Greater Eurasia
Over the past quarter-century, the SCO has evolved from a confidence-building mechanism along the former Soviet-Chinese border into the largest association in Greater Eurasia. Its original agenda – combating terrorism, separatism, and extremism – remains in place, but it is no longer the organization’s sole focus. Trade, energy, transportation, digitalization, food security, humanitarian exchanges, and the reform of international institutions have all been added to the list.
The Bishkek summit cemented that evolution. The leaders adopted the Bishkek Declaration along with 27 other documents. The package included decisions on responding to emerging security challenges, combating drug trafficking, developing ports and logistics hubs, nuclear safety, energy, and emergency response. The SCO also introduced a single partner status, merging the previously separate categories of observer state and dialogue partner. On the surface, this may look like an administrative reform. Its political significance, however, is much broader: The organization is streamlining its external framework and preparing for more systematic engagement with countries that want to cooperate without immediately becoming full members.
The practical side of multipolarity is also visible in the economic sphere. Putin said national currencies now account for more than 98% of Russia’s settlements with other SCO countries. This does not yet amount to a common currency or a unified financial system, but it points to a sustained trend: The organization’s members are seeking to reduce their mutual trade’s dependence on external payment infrastructure. Discussions about an SCO Development Bank, new investment instruments, and the integration of Eurasian transportation routes are part of the same effort.
At the same time, the SCO’s emergence as a genuine center of global politics will depend on how quickly it can turn declarations into working projects. The organization already possesses immense collective potential, but there is always a gap between potential and real influence. Final communiqués alone will not close it. Banks, transportation routes, payment systems, security centers, and resilient trade networks will.
SCO Plus: Expanding without endlessly adding members
The defining political development of the Bishkek summit was the consolidation of the SCO Plus format. The first summit-level meeting under that name was held in Astana in 2024. In Bishkek, it moved beyond the experimental stage and became a distinct element of the summit itself. Representatives of 17 countries and six international organizations took part in the SCO and SCO Plus events. The expanded session focused on the role of the United Nations and the SCO countries’ contribution to building a fair multipolar world order.
The logic closely resembles that of BRICS Plus. In both cases, the goal is to build a broad circle of partners around a permanent core. This model allows the organization to expand its geographic reach without turning the admission of new members into an endless process or overburdening its decision-making machinery. Countries can participate in discussions of major issues, advance economic and political initiatives, and develop ties with members while retaining their freedom of maneuver.
There is, however, a difference between the two formats. BRICS Plus is primarily focused on the global economy, development, and reform of international financial governance. SCO Plus has emerged from a Eurasian agenda centered on security, transportation connectivity, and political dialogue. Over time, the two mechanisms could complement one another: BRICS can provide the broader global framework, while the SCO builds a dense network of cooperation across Greater Eurasia.
Türkiye’s participation in the meeting was particularly revealing. Ankara remains an SCO partner rather than a full member, while also belonging to NATO and pursuing an independent policy in Eurasia. Its presence demonstrates that the SCO does not force its partners to make a rigid geopolitical choice. Instead, it offers a platform to countries that do not want to confine themselves to a single bloc and are seeking to diversify their foreign relationships.
This is one of the defining features of the emerging multipolar system. It does not necessarily mean replacing the old closed camp with a new one. Rather, it is a system of overlapping formats in which countries can cooperate on some issues while disagreeing on others. SCO Plus is becoming the institutional expression of precisely that model.
Iran, Pakistan, and Türkiye: The SCO’s new geography
The presence of Iran, Pakistan, and Türkiye gives the SCO a significance that extends far beyond Central Asia. Their respective statuses, however, differ – and that distinction matters. Iran and Pakistan are full members: Islamabad joined alongside India in 2017, while Tehran completed the accession process in 2023. Türkiye participates in the SCO’s broader orbit as a partner.
The admission of Iran and Pakistan redrew the organization’s political map. It brought South Asia, Afghanistan, the Persian Gulf, and the Middle East directly into the SCO’s purview. At the same time, it brought together countries with serious disagreements of their own. That complicates efforts to forge a common position, but it also makes the organization more valuable. Dialogue is needed most not by those who already agree, but by those whose interests regularly collide.
In the Bishkek Declaration, the participants reaffirmed their support for Iran’s sovereignty and territorial integrity, condemned the military strikes on Iranian territory, and called for a political and diplomatic settlement of the conflict. This was an important outcome for Tehran. Iran’s SCO membership has acquired practical value by allowing the country to place its own security on the collective political agenda of a major Eurasian organization.
Pakistan’s role is equally significant. Islamabad is not an invited participant but a full member – and Pakistan will assume the SCO chairmanship after Kyrgyzstan. This underscores the organization’s shift from its original Central Asian core toward a broader Eurasian configuration. The simultaneous membership of India and Pakistan does not eliminate their disputes, but it preserves a common channel of communication even during periods of severe tension.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian’s remarks at the SCO Plus session captured the central meaning of the gathering. The emerging order, he argued, must not amount to replacing one center of hegemony with another. Multipolarity can be fair only if it rests on sovereign equality, multilateralism, and international law. This is an important caveat: Simply increasing the number of power centers does not automatically make the international system more stable. It also requires rules, representative institutions, and mechanisms for reconciling competing interests. Pezeshkian separately emphasized the potential of SCO Plus as a platform for shaping the future international order.
This also explains the criticism of the effectiveness of the UN and its Security Council voiced in Bishkek. SCO countries are not proposing that the United Nations be abandoned. On the contrary, they insist that it must retain its central role. But that role should be supported by updated representation that reflects the actual distribution of political, economic, and demographic weight in the world. Otherwise, the gap between the formal architecture of the mid-20th century and the realities of the 21st will only continue to widen.
Russia’s opportunity: A bridge, not an arbiter
For Russia, the Bishkek summit mattered not only because it reaffirmed the country’s place among Eurasia’s leading power centers. Moscow possesses a rare network of relationships that allows it to serve as a bridge between different groups within the SCO. Russia has a strategic partnership with China, a special and privileged partnership with India, stable ties with Pakistan, allied relations with the countries of Central Asia, a comprehensive strategic partnership with Iran, and an ongoing political dialogue with Türkiye.
This network gives Moscow an opportunity to help resolve conflicts and reduce tensions. That does not mean turning the SCO into a supranational court or imposing ready-made solutions on its members. The organization operates by consensus, and bilateral disputes have traditionally been kept out of the center of its formal agenda. Russia’s most realistic role is therefore to offer its good offices, keep channels of communication open, facilitate informal consultations, encourage confidence-building measures, and create conditions in which direct dialogue becomes possible.
The historical parallel is obvious. In 1966, Soviet mediation led to the signing of the Tashkent Declaration, which brought an end to the 1965 war between India and Pakistan. That experience cannot simply be transplanted into the present day, but it serves as a reminder that Moscow can be useful to both sides precisely because it maintains working relations with both New Delhi and Islamabad.
A similar approach could be applied to other flashpoints, from tensions surrounding Iran and security in the Persian Gulf to Afghanistan and border disputes in Asia. Russia’s contribution could be to translate the SCO’s general commitment to political and diplomatic conflict resolution into specific mechanisms: contact groups, expert consultations, communication channels between military officials and diplomats, joint threat assessments, and agreements to protect transportation and energy infrastructure.
The organization’s capabilities should not be overstated, however. The SCO is not a military-political bloc, does not impose alliance discipline, and brings together countries with very different concepts of security. The Kashmir conflict between India and Pakistan remains unresolved, India and China continue to have border disputes, and the members’ positions on many international crises do not always align. Yet the SCO’s ability to keep these countries within a common negotiating framework is itself one of its most important assets.
A multipolar world is not a world of universal agreement. It is an order in which no single power center can dictate the rules on its own, forcing states to construct a complex system of compromises. The SCO fits this logic better than many traditional alliances: It does not demand ideological conformity, impose a single model of development, or require its members to rally against a common enemy.
The bottom line from Bishkek
The summit’s most important outcome was that the SCO has definitively moved beyond seeing itself solely as a regional security organization. The Bishkek Declaration, deeper financial and transportation cooperation, the new unified partner status, and the consolidation of the SCO Plus format are creating a broader framework – political, economic, and, most importantly, institutional.
An impressive geographic reach alone does not guarantee effectiveness. The SCO still needs to accelerate the development of project-financing mechanisms, give its new security centers substantive responsibilities, improve transportation links, and learn to play a more active role in de-escalating tensions among its own members. But the direction of travel is already clear.
Bishkek presented multipolarity not as a slogan but as a political reality. Russia, China, and India were in the same room; Iran and Pakistan participated as full members; Türkiye attended as a key partner in the expanded format. These countries do not constitute a unified bloc, nor do they seek to subsume their individual interests into a common line. But they are creating a space in which security, development, and global governance can be discussed without outside supervision or compulsory submission to a single center of power.
In this sense, SCO Plus is more than a successful adaptation of the BRICS model. It is a bid to build an open political framework around Greater Eurasia. If the organization can translate its demographic and economic scale into functioning institutions, platforms like this will shape not only the debate about a multipolar world, but also the way that world operates in practice.

articles.title: Air defense downs 141 of 174 Russian drones; missile, UAV hits recorded at 16 locations
articles.body:
On Wednesday night, the Defense Forces of Ukraine neutralized 141 Russian drones, but hits by drones and missiles were recorded at 16 locations, the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported.
"As of 08:30, air defense shot down/suppressed 141 targets: 3 S8000 Banderol; 138 Russian UAVs of the Shahed type (including jet-powered), Herbera, and drones of other types," the report states.
In total, overnight into September 2 (from 18:00 on September 1), Russia attacked with two Iskander-M ballistic missiles, two Kh-59/69 guided air missiles, as well as 174 strike UAVs of the Shahed type (about half being jet-powered), S8000 Banderol, Herbera, and Parodiya-type decoy drones.
The downing of ballistic and air missiles was not reported.
The air attack was repelled by aviation, anti-aircraft missile troops, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of the Defense Forces of Ukraine.
Meanwhile, hits by Russian missiles and strike UAVs were recorded at 16 locations, as well as the fall of shot-down targets (debris) at four locations. In addition, part of the enemy strike means did not reach their targets, with information regarding them currently being clarified.
Thus, the effectiveness of air defense performance on drones alone amounted to about 81%, and on all air targets, given the lack of missiles for anti-ballistic air defense systems, 79.2%.
As reported, the previous massive strike launched by Russia against Ukraine occurred overnight into June 2, when 602 out of 656 drones and 40 out of 73 missiles were neutralized, with hits recorded at 38 locations. The most massive strike was launched by Russia over the course of May 13-14 using 1,428 strike UAVs, of which air defense neutralized 1,362, bringing air defense effectiveness against UAVs to 95.38%.
The highest percentage of neutralized drones and missiles was recorded overnight into July 9, when 718 out of 729 drones and missiles launched by the occupiers were neutralized, yielding an effectiveness of about 96.9%.

articles.title: Ukrainian pilot details fight against jet-powered Shaheds
articles.body:
- A Ukrainian fighter pilot told Waypoint that jet-powered Shahed drones remain a difficult but viable target for crewed fighter jets despite the cost.
- He said Ukraine's main constraint is funding and procedural delays, not a failure of its layered air defense system.
A Ukrainian fighter pilot who runs the social media channel “Sonyashnyk” told the outlet Waypoint that jet-powered Shahed drones remain difficult to stop even as Ukraine’s air defense system continues to evolve, arguing that focus on the small number of drones that get through overlooks the far larger number destroyed before they reach populated areas.
The pilot, whose name was not disclosed, was asked where Ukraine’s air defense system fails most against jet-powered Shahed drones. He said no country’s air defense system could withstand the volume of daily Russian strikes, and pushed back on the idea that Ukraine’s system is failing.
“The amount of resources the enemy uses daily is colossal. Civilians focus on the number of targets that got through some echelon of our defense, but forget that downing enemy targets starts back over the swamps,” the pilot said.
He said Russia has adapted its tactics over the course of the war after realizing it could not overwhelm Ukraine’s defenses carelessly, now preparing major strikes with extensive resources and support from what he called allied “tyrants.” He said Russia has found gaps Ukraine currently lacks the means to close, including exploiting national borders and launching mass strikes during periods of worsening weather.
“In my opinion, our Achilles heel is funding, both from partners and locally. Many important initiatives and ideas have to pass through a hundred procedural councils before anyone hears them,” the pilot said. “As for allies, the world is still moving too slowly into World War III. That’s where the shortage of ammunition and other resources comes from.”
Asked whether it still makes sense to send crewed fighter jets after jet-powered Shaheds, given the cost involved, the pilot said the mission remains within a fighter jet’s core role of air dominance and integrated air defense work.
“From a fighter’s perspective it makes sense, because that’s literally our specialty: air dominance and working within the air defense system,” the pilot said. He said the older Geran-1 and Geran-2 drones had been a persistent nuisance for a period, but described the jet-powered Shahed as a comparatively good target given its flight characteristics.
“Financially it’s painful, but that’s our purpose,” he said. “In a single sortie even an old MiG can take out a dozen or so. You have to understand that since there aren’t many other options, you end up relying on skill and experience.” He added that some enemy targets fly at altitudes where cheaper interceptors simply cannot reach them or arrive in time.
Asked for two or three real priorities for countering jet-powered Shaheds systematically rather than case by case, the pilot said destroying the launch sites themselves is not realistic, since Russia can rebuild or relocate them, including launching from mobile platforms.
“Of course we need to conduct operations on enemy territory, hunt launch sites and logistics, factories and workshops,” he said. “But I also think that if all our forces are directed toward that alone, the enemy will simply move faster to operate from underground.” He said the more logical approach is parallel work: building out a layered, unified air defense system, even if unified only by sector or “line,” while continuously pressuring the enemy’s capabilities.
“If we’re given a sufficient quantity of interception means and expand the authority of commanders and leaders on the ground, then with competent coordination everything will be fine,” he said. He pointed to a shift he said Ukrainians witnessed roughly six months earlier, when, with sufficient interception resources available, only a pair of drones out of hundreds launched toward Kyiv managed to get through.

articles.title: Scott Ritter: The CIA never comes to Russia in peace
articles.body:
Scott Ritter: The CIA never comes to Russia in peace
CIA Director John Ratcliffe traveled to Moscow last week.
What we know: Ratcliffe met with Sergey Naryshkin, the director of Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service. This has been confirmed by Naryshkin himself, who described the meeting as “routine.” We also know that the US spy chief did not meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
“The meeting took place, there is nothing unusual in this,” Naryshkin stated afterwards. “In the practice of special services, meetings of managers, personal meetings or online are part of our work. So, the meeting with John Ratcliffe is a working format.”
Naryshkin refused to state what issues were discussed, explaining that they were within the competence of the intelligence services. “And the competence of the intelligence services is such a rather delicate and special thing,” the Russian spy chief said.
What we don’t know: literally anything else.
Rumors abound about additional attendees, as well as the agenda – or lack thereof – that was pursued by Ratcliffe during a meeting which appeared to be anything but routine. But the fact is, any meeting between Ratcliffe and Naryshkin, given the nature of the times we live in, could never be described as “routine.”
A quick reminder: John Ratcliffe’s CIA is currently at war with Russia. Literally.
Ratcliffe assumed his current position on January 23, 2025. Prior to this, he did a short stint as national intelligence director during the last year of Trump’s first term in office. He was a Texas congressman for a few years, as well as a small-town mayor and acting US attorney for the Eastern District of Texas.
He is a politician, not a spy.
But he is fully cognizant of the CIA’s secret war against Russia, having been fully briefed while serving as DNI. As a member of Congress, Ratcliffe was a leading policy maker on national security issues serving as a member of the House Intelligence and Homeland Security committees.
Any effort to portray him as some sort of “innocent abroad” fails on the face of the facts.
The CIA has always been at war with Russia. During the Cold War, Moscow Station (the name of the CIA’s operation center based out of the US Embassy) was literally the front line of the spy-versus-spy antics taking place between the US and the Soviet Union.
The CIA headed up Operation Cyclone, a massive paramilitary-driven effort to create a Vietnam-like quagmire for the Soviet Union in Afghanistan. The goal of Operation Cyclone was to kill Russians.
I worked with people who were directly or indirectly affiliated with Operation Cyclone. ‘Kill more Russians’ was literally their mantra.
There was a time when the CIA hired genuine Russia-area experts. The analysts who populated the Office of Soviet Analysis (SOVA) in the Directorate of Intelligence at the height of the Cold War were some of the best experts on the Soviet Union imaginable.
I know because I worked with them. From 1988-1990, I received two classified commendations from the director of the CIA for my analytical work involving the Soviet Union. I was considered by the CIA leadership to be a top-notch Soviet analyst.
In 1992 the CIA actively recruited me for an analytical position within the predecessor to SOVA, the Slavic and Eurasian Office. I was brought in for a high-level interview, after which I was informed that the CIA would be passing on my application. When I asked why, I was told that I was too married to old school thinking about Russia – in short, I was a ‘Sovietologist’.
The CIA was looking for people who could imagine Russia ‘differently’. What this meant was divorcing oneself from the mindset that Russia (i.e., the Soviet Union) was a peer-level opponent worthy of respect (my view), and instead adopting a stance that Russia was a defeated foe that needed to be kept down by any means necessary.
In the 1990s, the CIA’s task was to use Boris Yeltsin as an agent of influence to weaken Russia and facilitate foreign control over its resources. The CIA actively infiltrated every aspect of the Russian economy and used ‘soft power’ resources funded by the likes of the National Endowment for Democracy and overseen by the US Agency for International Development (USAID) to hijack Russian democratic institutions and Russian social life, especially through media-related activities.
The CIA also was very active in working to break Russia up into more manageable fiefdoms, each ruled over by a CIA-controlled lackey. The Russian-Chechen conflict was a primary example of this activity.
When Boris Yeltsin stepped aside in favor of Vladimir Putin as Russia’s president on New Year’s Eve 1999, the CIA immediately made it its task to undermine Putin and replace him with someone from the Yeltsin camp willing and able to do the CIA’s bidding.
Putin’s resistance and resilience as a Russian leader operating independent of CIA control helped shape a new generation of Russophobes in the United States. The first generation were the ‘new Russian’ thinkers that replaced the old school ‘Sovietologists’ at the end of the Cold War. To them, Russia was a playground for which to launch experiments on economic and political domination with absolutely zero regard to the price being paid by the people of Russia.
This generation of Russophobes simply detested Russia and the Russian people, failing to attribute any normative human value to their lives. Millions of Russians lost their lives as a result, and tens of millions of others suffered greatly.
Michael McFaul, the former US ambassador to Russia, falls into this category. So, too, does Fiona Hill. And Beth Sanner. People whose educational background and Russian experience pre-dates Putin, people who know the truth about Russia but opted instead to embrace the hegemonic policies of superpower singularity and work to weaken and destroy Russia.
But Putin’s stubborn hold on power, despite concerted efforts by the CIA to oust him (think Navalny), led to the birth of a new generation of Russophobes, so-called ‘experts’ whose only claim to relevance is their undying hatred of Putin and everything Russian.
It is this generation that has gravitated to the upper levels of the CIA’s analytical community, and who openly hate all things Russia. People like Andrea Kendall-Taylor and Julia Gurganus.
It is this openly Russophobic CIA that John Ratcliffe oversees.
His relationship with Julia Gurganus is both instructive and illustrative of the sickness that pervades the CIA when it comes to Russia. Gurganus was the National Intelligence Officer for Russia back in 2016-17, at the height of the Obama-era Russiagate scandal that tried to make the case of collusion between then-candidate Donald Trump and Russia to steal the 2016 presidential election from Hillary Clinton.
Gurganus helped manufacture the intelligence that underpinned this false allegation. She was a vociferous critic of Trump, so much so that the CIA quietly exiled her to a think tank position during Trump’s first term in office.
When Trump was reelected, Ratcliffe oversaw the whitewashing of Gurganus’ role in falsely accusing Trump of collusion, leading to the elevation of Gurganus as the senior CIA briefer onboard Air Force One as Trump flew to Alaska to meet with Putin in August 2025. That’s right – Ratcliffe purposefully cleansed Gurganus of her anti-Trump credentials so she could personally brief the president before his meeting with Putin.
Tulsi Gabbard, in her role as DNI, exposed Gurganus as an anti-Trump operative and had her security clearances revoked, but not before the damage was done.
There was a time when the CIA’s Directorate of Operations Russia House was home to living legends. People like Milton Beardon, who helped run Operation Cyclone and was chief of the Soviet/East European Division at the time the Soviet Union fell. Gardner Hathaway and Berton Gerber, who ran some of the most successful CIA spying operations from Moscow Station in the late 1970s and early 1980s.
And Murat Natirboff, another legendary Russian hand who led the Moscow Station during the Nicholas Daniloff affairs in the 1980s. Natirboff is instructional in this regard. His father was an officer in the Russian White Army which fought the Bolsheviks during the Russian Civil War. Natirboff hated the communists. But he loved Russia. He was held in very high regard by the Soviet officers of the KGB which faced off against him during his tour in Moscow.
I can personally attest to Murat’s feelings toward Russia – I met him after he left Moscow in 1988, where we spoke about my experiences in Votkinsk as an INF Treaty weapons inspector.
The CIA no longer employs people of this caliber in its operational work regarding Russia. Gone are the days of the Russian romantics – people who took the time to learn about their enemies to bring to life Sun Tzu’s classic observation: “If you know your enemy as yourself, you need not fear the outcome of a hundred battles.”
The present-day Directorate of Operations is overrun with paramilitary operatives, men (and women) who cut their teeth during the heyday of the post-9/11 ‘Global War on Terror’, where they oversaw secret wars in Iraq, Afghanistan, Syria, and Iran.
They take their cue from veterans like Tom Sylvester, a former Navy SEAL who worked in the CIA’s Special Activities Branch as a Ground Branch operative. Tom headed the CIA’s efforts in Ukraine post-2022, when the Special Military Operation began. His job was literally to kill Russians.
People like ‘Santa Claus’, the nickname of the CIA’s Kiev Station Chief who sent Ground Branch to Ukraine post-2014 to train the Ukrainian intelligence special operations forces on how best to kill Russians.
Veterans of the CIA’s drone assassination programs now advise the Ukrainian drone operators on how to kill Russians and destroy Russian infrastructure.
In December 2025, the CIA helped direct Ukrainian drones toward a residence in Valdai where Putin was staying.
Yes – John Ratcliffe’s CIA tried to kill the Russian president. The CIA denies Putin was the target, but the data from the guidance chips extracted from Ukrainian drone debris appears to suggest otherwise.
Today, the CIA is knee-deep in the business of killing Russians. They continue to guide Ukraine’s expanded drone warfare campaign targeting Russia. And Russians.
This is John Ratcliffe. This is the organization he leads. So, when people reflect on the recent visit by Ratcliffe to Russia, never lose sight of his primary mission.
The statements, views and opinions expressed in this column are solely those of the author and do not necessarily represent those of RT.

articles.title: Germany successfully tests Israeli ballistic missile
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Germany successfully tests Israeli ballistic missile, officials say
Germany successfully tested an Israeli ballistic missile in the North Atlantic overnight, military officials said on Wednesday, as Western powers scramble to acquire long-range weapons to counter what they see as an increased threat from Russia.
The test of what officials said was a LORA missile built by Israel Aerospace Industries came hours after Berlin publicly blamed Russia for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport last month and ordered measures in response.
Germany does not currently have ballistic missiles, which fly at much higher speeds than the cruise missiles in its arsenal. The Israeli-built system has a range of up to 500 km (310 miles), Germany's defence ministry said.
Berlin is engaged in a number of multinational collaborations aimed at developing long-range missiles, and also looking at options to buy such weapons.
Navy chief Jan Christian Kaack said the test was a success.
"Our units can successfully deploy the system, and its potential range exceeds anything we have seen before," he said in a statement. "In terms of protecting Germany and our allies, this test marks a new chapter in deterrence and maritime defence readiness."
Germany is also working on an upgraded version of its Taurus cruise missile, currently its only weapon with a range of several hundred kilometres, with production scheduled to start in 2029.
The upgraded Taurus NEO missile will feature an extended range, improved shielding against interference, and advancements in navigation and seeker head technology, according to a budget document.
German forces have about 600 Taurus missiles with an official range of more than 500 km (310 miles) in their inventories, that can be launched from fighter jets such as the Tornado, the F-15 or the F-18.
The weapon, built by European defence company MBDA, is designed to destroy targets behind enemy lines such as command bunkers, ammunition and fuel dumps, airfields and bridges.

articles.title: Putin calls possibility of Russian strikes on UK "military secret"
articles.body:
Putin calls possibility of Russian strikes on UK "military secret"
Russian ruler Vladimir Putin has refused to rule out the possibility of Russian strikes on military facilities in the United Kingdom over its support for Ukraine.
Source: Putin at a press conference, as quoted by Russian Interfax
Details: Putin claimed that any military facilities on Ukrainian territory, including British ones if they exist, are "legitimate targets" for the Russian Armed Forces.
Meanwhile, he said he doubts that there are any British military facilities in Ukraine.
"Are there British military facilities in Ukraine?" the Kremlin leader asked.
When a journalist clarified that the question was hypothetical, Putin replied: "If there are, then definitely [they will become targets – ed.]."
Asked whether UK defence industry facilities located on British territory could become military targets, Putin replied: "That's a secret, a military secret."
Background:
- The Russian Foreign Ministry previously threatened that Russia could attack UK military targets in Ukraine and "beyond its borders" in response to Ukrainian strikes using British weapons.
- Moscow's threats came after UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced on 24 August that the UK would release Storm Shadow missile production technology to Ukraine.
- The following day, Andrei Fedorov, an adviser to Kremlin ruler Vladimir Putin, said that British factories producing drones and missile components could face attacks from "unknown sources".
- Moscow has repeatedly threatened London over its military assistance to Ukraine. Russia previously accused the UK of a "deliberate drive towards escalation" after media reports claimed that British-made drones had been used in strikes on targets inside Russia.
- Burnham responded by stressing that the UK would not allow itself to be intimidated by Russia.

articles.title: Ukraine's General Staff says 213 combat clashes occurred on front over past day
articles.body:
Ukraine's General Staff says 213 combat clashes occurred on front over past day
A total of 213 combat clashes have occurred on the battlefield over the past day.
Source: General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine on Facebook, information as of 08:00 on 2 September
Quote: "The enemy carried out one missile strike and conducted 93 airstrikes, dropping 313 guided aerial bombs. In addition, the invaders deployed 11,511 kamikaze drones and conducted 2,969 strikes on Ukrainian positions and settlements, including 57 from multiple-launch rocket systems."
Details: Over the past day, Ukraine's Air Force and Rocket Forces and Artillery units hit 10 clusters of Russian military personnel, six UAV ground control stations, five artillery pieces and another crucial facility belonging to the Russians.
On the North Slobozhanshchyna front and in the operational zone in Russia's Kursk Oblast, Ukrainian defenders stopped six Russian assaults over the past day.
On the South Slobozhanshchyna front, Ukrainian units repelled seven Russian attacks. The Russians attempted to advance towards the settlements of Volokhivka, Khatnie and Bochkove and near Vovchanski Khutory and Starytsia.
On the Kupiansk front, the Russians conducted six attacks towards the settlements of Radkivka, Kupiansk-Vuzlovyi, Kurylivka, Dovhenke and Kivsharivka.
On the Lyman front, Russian forces carried out nine attacks towards the settlements of Novoosynove, Drobysheve, Cherneshchyna, Olhivka, Lyman and Dibrova.
On the Sloviansk front, Russian troops conducted three assaults towards Ozerne and Mykolaivka and near Kryva Luka.
On the Kramatorsk front, the Russians launched one attack towards the village of Yurkivka.
On the Kostiantynivka front, 28 Russian attacks were recorded. The Russians tried to advance near the settlements of Kostiantynivka, Illinivka, Novoselivka, Stepanivka and Sofiivka and towards Novopavlivka and Vilne.
On the Pokrovsk front, a total of 25 attacks were recorded. The Russians attempted to advance towards the settlements of Novyi Donbas, Serhiivka, Novopidhorodne and Novopavlivka and near Udachne, Muravka, Molodetske and Horikhove.
On the Oleksandrivka front, the Russians did not conduct any offensive operations.
On the Huliaipole front, the Russians carried out 13 attacks, attempting to advance towards the settlements of Vozdvyzhivka, Rizdvianka, Verkhnia Tersa and Charivne.
On the Orikhiv front, Ukrainian defenders stopped two Russian attempts to advance towards Pavlivka.
On the Prydniprovske front, the Russians did not conduct any offensive operations.

articles.title: Middle East live: Iran says latest US strikes kill 11 people
articles.body:
Live: Iran launches retaliatory attacks, condemns alleged US strike on wedding as a ‘war crime’
Iran’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei on Wednesday said the US was guilty of a “war crime” after the Iranian Red Crescent reported that an overnight US air strike killed four people at a wedding celebration in the country’s south. Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said they had responded by attacking US assets in Kuwait, Bahrain, Jordan and Erbil in Iraqi Kurdistan. Follow our liveblog for all the latest developments.
Iraq boosts oil exports in August as low prices draw buyers
Iraq boosted its oil exports in August, with September shipments also set to climb, as wide profits and Iranian approval for its tankers to pass through the Strait of Hormuz have encouraged buyers, according
to industry sources and shipping data.
The recovery in exports for OPEC's second-largest producer, which had been severely curtailed by the near-closure of the Strait of Hormuz since the US and Israel started the Iran war on February 28, improves the supply of heavy high-sulphur crude to major importers China and India.
Iraq's oil exports rose to around 2.34 million barrels per day in August from about 1.35 million bpd in July, two Iraqi energy officials said on Wednesday.
Provisional data from shiptracking firms Vortexa and Kpler pegged Iraqi crude exports in August at 2.3 million and 2.17 million bpd, respectively, up from July's level but below February's pre-war level of 3.7 million and 3.362 million bpd.
"Iraq has been giving heavy discounts ... which has incentivised buyers to find shipping options to get the cargoes out," Sparta Commodities' senior analyst June Goh said.
Also, Tehran granted permission for a number of Iraqi oil tankers to pass through the Strait of Hormuz, Iran's state news agency IRNA reported last week.
While it is unclear whether the permission applies to all Iraqi cargoes, Iraq is the only Gulf producer that has explicitly received a permit, Sparta's Goh said.
Israeli strike on southern Lebanon kills one
An Israeli strike on south Lebanon killed one person, Lebanese official media said, while Israel said it targeted Hezbollah in retaliation for an attack targeting its soldiers in the south.
"One person was killed and another wounded in a strike launched by an enemy drone" in the city of Nabatieh, Lebanon's state-run National News Agency (NNA) said, also reporting other Israeli strikes on the area.
Israel's army said the Iran-backed Hezbollah group overnight "launched two explosive drones" towards Israeli soldiers in Ali al-Taher Ridge area, reporting no troop casualties.
In response, the Israeli military said it struck Hezbollah infrastructure in the Nabatieh area.
Israel has recently increased its attacks on south Lebanon, particularly in the Nabatieh area where the strategic Ali al-Taher ridge is located.
Lebanon's health ministry says Israeli attacks have killed at least 8,920 people since hostilities initially erupted in October 2023, after Hezbollah launched rockets at Israel in support of its Palestinian ally Hamas over the Gaza conflict.
Iran security chief says US to face new war strategy from Tehran after strikes
Iran's security chief warned the United States would face a "new strategy" from Tehran in the Middle East war after the heaviest exchange of attacks between the foes in weeks.
"You will soon see that Iran's new strategy on the battlefield, in diplomacy and in confronting the economic blockade will shatter your foundations," Iran's Supreme National Security Council secretary Mohsen Rezaei posted on X.
Iran foreign ministry calls US strike on wedding a 'war crime'
Iran's foreign ministry spokesman on Wednesday labelled a deadly attack on a wedding ceremony in the south of the country a "war crime".
"The truth of this unlawful war of choice – and the true face of the war crime – is in Sirik, where a wedding ceremony was brutally bombed as part of America's desperate struggle to conceal its failure," foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei posted on X.
What we know about the alleged US strike on a wedding in Iran
US forces launched fresh attacks on Iran Tuesday, including one that the Iranian Red Crescent said killed four people dead at a wedding celebration.
FRANCE 24's correspondent in Tehran Reza Sayeh has the latest.
Israel says it's prepared to 'respond with great force' if Iran attacks
Israel's defence minister said his country was prepared to respond "with great force" if attacked by Iran, after Iranian forces launched retaliatory strikes at US military positions across the region.
Israel Katz said Israeli forces were prepared for a possible attack from Iran over the Jewish high holiday season, which begins in mid-September.
"For now, they are striking throughout the region except us," he told a conference hosted by Israeli news site Ynet and newspaper Yedioth Ahronoth.
"But there is a possibility that they will attack us. We are prepared for that defensively," he added.
If Iran attacks, Israel would "respond with great force, independently of anyone else", Katz said, adding that "our planes are ready to take off".
Iran strikes back against latest US attacks, vowing ‘severe’ consequences
Iran struck US interests around the Middle East on Wednesday, vowing "severe" consequences for renewed American attacks on the Islamic republic, including a US strike it said killed five and wounded dozens of civilians at a wedding. FRANCE 24 reports.
Two oil tankers disabled after hitting mines, Iran's Revolutionary Guards say
Two oil tankers hit sea mines and were disabled while trying to cross the Strait of Hormuz, Iran's Revolutionary Guards said in a statement shared by state media.
The statement alleged the tankers had been forced to disembark their crews and were placed in the hands of US operatives to pass through what it called an "illegal route" in the strategic waterway, despite earlier warnings from the Revolutionary Guards' navy about the dangers of crossing the mined passage.
Saudi shipping company Bahri says two sailors killed in incident in Strait of Hormuz
Saudi Arabia's national shipping company, Bahri, said that two Filipino seafarers were killed in a security incident involving its vessel "SIDR" while it was transiting the Strait of Hormuz on Monday.
US attack on Iranian Gulf island killed three paramilitary personnel, Revolutionary Guards say
Iran's Revolutionary Guards said that three members of the paramilitary Basij force were killed in attacks overnight on an island in the Gulf.
"Three Basij fighters ... were martyred in last night's attack by the criminal US on Lavan Island" in the Gulf, a local IRGC commander was quoted by the Mehr news agency as saying.
Iran's top negotiator calls US 'Satan' after deadly attack on wedding
Iran's top negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf on called the United States "Satan" after an attack on a wedding ceremony in the country's south.
"Minab school: children massacred. Lamerd sports hall: kids slaughtered. Kouhestak wedding: children killed with families. If a power acts like Satan, picks targets like Satan, and kills like Satan, it's Satan. Shields a junior Satan that does the same? It's THE Great Satan," said Ghalibaf in a post on X.
Iran Revolutionary Guards say four personnel killed in US attacks in western province
Iran's Revolutionary Guards said that a US attack on the western province of Kermanshah killed four of their personnel.
"Four fighters of the IRGC Aerospace Force in Kermanshah province were martyred in an attack by the US regime," the Guards said in a statement carried by Fars news agency, using their acronym.
Pakistan says it remains engaged with US and Iran on talks to end conflict
Pakistan is engaged with the US and Iran on talks to end their conflict and is positive that the countries "will return to the table for dialogue", foreign ministry spokesperson Tahir Andrabi said at a regular media briefing.
Pakistan's Chief of Defence Forces Asim Munir's visit to Tehran last month created "considerable momentum" on the issue of the Strait of Hormuz, he said.
France calls for EU mission to support Palestinian elections
French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot called for the European Union to deploy a mission to support Palestinian elections.
Kuwait says it extinguished a fire after an Iranian drone targeted a 'residential complex'
Kuwait on Wednesday said an Iranian drone attack caused a fire in a residential complex in the capital but there were no casualties and it was brought under control.
"A fire that broke out in a residential complex in the Capital Governorate has been brought under control. The complex had been targeted by a hostile drone launched as part of the nefarious Iranian aggression," Kuwait's official KUNA news agency said quoting a fire department spokesman, adding there were no casualties.
USS Abraham Lincoln arrives in Thailand after reports of worsening conditions on board
Iran’s Revolutionary Guards say they attacked US assets in Kuwait, Bahrain, Jordan and Erbil in Iraqi Kurdistan
Bahrain says air defences intercepted and destroyed several Iranian aerial attacks
Iran says 11 dead in US strikes on its territory: state media
Iran said Wednesday that US strikes on its territory killed 11 people, state media reported, after a fresh attack in the southwestern province of Khuzestan.
"The Deputy Governor of Khuzestan Province for Security and Law Enforcement Affairs said that last night's US missile attack on three locations in the province left seven people dead and eight injured," state-run IRNA said.
It came after the Iranian Red Crescent said Tuesday that four people including a child were killed and more than 50 people wounded by a US attack at a wedding in southern Sirik county.
Stocks fall as US-Iran flare-up sends oil prices and bond yields higher
Stocks fell and bond yields held at multi-decade highs as investors ramp up rate hike bets amid a fresh flare-up in Middle East tensions that has sparked another surge in oil prices.
Crude jumped more than two percent and has spiked around 10% this week after the United States hit an Iranian island in the Strait of Hormuz, sparking a series of tit-for-tat attacks in which Tehran has targeted American interests in several regional countries.
The latest round of military action comes after weeks of relative calm during which peace talks went nowhere and Washington said it would aim for the "economic asphyxiation" of the Islamic republic.
Yesterday's key developments:
- The US launched fresh air strikes on Iran, including one that the Iranian Red Crescent said left four people dead at a wedding celebration.
- Israeli air strikes in Gaza killed at least four people during what the Israeli military said was an operation to seize a Hamas official.
- The US military attacked two Iranian government tankers, Axios reported.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP, AP and Reuters)

articles.title: Air defence downs 82 attack drones during the day, including 57 jet-powered UAVs
articles.body:
Air defence downs 82 attack drones during the day, including 57 jet-powered UAVs
The Ukrainian Air Force has reported that Russian forces attacked Ukraine with 99 strike UAVs during the day on 1 September, 72 of which were jet-powered.
Source: Ukrainian Air Force
Details: Early reports indicate that between 06:30 and 18:00, Ukrainian air defence forces shot down or jammed 82 strike UAVs, including 57 jet-powered drones.
As of 18:30, around 10 jet-powered strike UAVs remained in Ukrainian airspace. New groups of drones were also entering the country.
The Air Force urged people not to ignore air-raid warnings.

Strikes were recorded at 28 locations.

articles.title: Russia secretly aiding Iran in development of supersonic cruise missile technology - report
articles.body:
Russia has been secretly helping Iran develop supersonic cruise missiles, London-based outlet The Financial Times reported on Wednesday morning, which experts say would likely have been intended for anti-ship and land attacks.
The program, codenamed C430L, began in 2023 and was arranged by Russia's state arms exporter, Rosoboronexport, in coordination with the US-sanctioned NPO Mashinostroyenia, FT reported.
According to FT, Russian arms export officials and senior NPO Mashinostroyenia engineers traveled to Iran repeatedly in 2023.
Among the engineers who conducted these trips were Alexander Dergachev, chief designer for sea-launched missiles and cruise missile complexes; Alexander Chebakov, head of NPO Mashinostroyenia’s design department for air-breathing propulsion units and a specialist in supersonic ramjet propulsion for cruise missiles; and Yuri Prokhorchuk, head of the aerodynamics and ballistics department.
FT also learned that Vladislav Kuzmichev, head of Rosoboronexport’s department of defense technologies and space, accompanied the delegation on its third trip to Iran, and later negotiated the C430L contract with Iran.
By 2025, NPO Mashinostroyenia had received various Iranian technical materials, which Russian engineers analyzed and responded to with various questions.
In correspondence seen by FT from April 2025, Rosoboronexport proposed sending a delegation of Russian specialists to Iran and asked Tehran to answer the engineers' questions before the trip.
“People often think about technology transfers as being solely about sending blueprints, parts, or entire missiles," Fabian Hinz, an Iranian missiles expert and senior analyst with Conflict Armament Research, a UK-based weapons-tracing organization, told FT, "but getting a 60-year-old engineer to fly over and problem-solve, using their experience, is hugely valuable.”
Iranian president thanks Putin for support against United States
On Tuesday, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian thanked Russian President Vladimir Putin for Moscow's position on the war in Iran and resulting sanctions, and said that together, Moscow and Tehran can resist what he called US "unilateralism."
The two leaders spoke on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in the Kyrgyz capital Bishkek.
During the meeting, Putin told Pezeshkian that Moscow stood in solidarity with the Iranian people in the fight for their interests.
Putin also said that Russia and Iran will maintain their economic and trade relationship despite the current military and political environment.
“During this difficult period, we are striving to provide you with the necessary assistance - as we have discussed - and are supplying you with essential goods,” Putin said.
Pezeshkian accuses US of violating international law
Pezeshkian, in turn, said that the US does not have the right to impose sanctions "whenever they please," and accused them of violating international law and committing acts of aggression.
Russia and Iran, he said, would find ways to circumvent the US sanctions.
"Within frameworks like the SCO and other organizations, we can bypass unilateral measures and cooperate on a multilateral basis,” he stated.
Notably, the US sanctions Pezeshkian was referring to, including Washington’s latest measures targeting Iranian financial networks and IRGC-linked assets, are not in themselves prohibited under international law. Economic sanctions also do not constitute an “act of aggression” under the UN definition.
Reuters contributed to this report.

articles.title: Kyiv, Odesa Hit in Massive Russian Attack as 10 People Are Wounded
articles.body:
Kyiv and Odesa came under a massive Russian missile and drone attack overnight on Wednesday, Sept. 2, leaving at least 10 people wounded and damaging civilian infrastructure, Ukrainian officials said.
In Kyiv, a fire broke out in an open area in the Holosiivskyi district after debris from a Russian drone fell there, Mayor Vitaliy Klitschko reported on Telegram.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Kyiv Post correspondents heard explosions in the city shortly after 7 a.m. At around 8 a.m., local Telegram channels reported thick smoke over the capital following the explosions and a large fire on the outskirts of the city.
“Kyiv residents, close your windows: the capital is being filled with thick smoke,” one local channel reported.
The Holosiivskyi district had also been targeted during the previous evening’s Russian attack, when debris caused a fire in an open area. A private house in Kyiv’s Solomianskyi district also caught fire.
Two wounded in Kyiv region
Two people were wounded in the Kyiv region during the morning attack, according to Regional Military Administration head Tymur Tkachenko.
In the Bucha district, a man suffered a shrapnel wound to his thigh. In the Brovary district, a woman sustained shrapnel wounds to her arm and shoulder. Both are receiving medical treatment.
Damage was reported in the Bucha, Brovary and Boryspil districts.
Warehouses caught fire in the Bucha district, where a private house was also damaged. Another private house was damaged in the Brovary district, while a warehouse building was damaged in Boryspil.
Sporting Diplomacy in Odesa: Ukrainian Servicemen Take on Italian Pacifists
Rescuers continue to work at the sites and clear the aftermath of the attack.
Odesa hit overnight
Odesa also came under a massive Russian attack overnight, according to the head of the Odesa City Military Administration, Serhiy Lysak.
“It’s been a difficult night for Odesa. The enemy has again launched a massive attack on the city,” Lysak wrote on Telegram at around 7 a.m.
He said eight people were wounded, including one child. Two of the injured were hospitalized.
A 24-story residential building was damaged, with apartments on several floors destroyed. Windows were blown out in nearby buildings, and cars were damaged.
Office buildings and two educational institutions were also damaged in the attack.
Experts are continuing to assess the damage across several areas of the city. Emergency and utility crews are working at the scene, while energy workers are restoring power supplies.
Emergency assistance centers have also been set up for residents affected by the attack.
Air Force: Russia launched 174 drones and missiles
According to the Ukrainian Air Force, Russia launched a massive overnight attack beginning at 6 p.m. on Sept. 1, using missiles and 174 attack drones.
The attack included two Iskander-M ballistic missiles and two Kh-59/69 guided aircraft missiles.
Russia also launched 174 drones, including Shahed-type attack UAVs – about half of which were jet-powered variants – as well as S8000 Banderol, Gerbera and Parody decoy drones. The main targets were the Kyiv and Odesa regions.
As of 8:30 a.m., Ukrainian air defenses had destroyed or suppressed 141 aerial targets, including three S8000 Banderol drones and 138 Shahed, Gerbera and other unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs).
Debris from missiles and downed drones fell at 16 locations, while additional debris from intercepted targets was recorded at four other locations. Some weapons failed to reach their targets, with the circumstances still being clarified.

articles.title: Putin brushes off mobilization reports as 'absolute nonsense,' threatens mass strikes on Ukraine’s energy sector
articles.body:
Putin brushes off mobilization reports as 'absolute nonsense,' threatens mass strikes on Ukraine’s energy sector
Russian President Vladimir Putin on Sept. 1 dismissed reports of a possible new wave of mobilization in Russia as "absolute nonsense," while saying he had ordered preparations for large-scale strikes against Ukraine's energy infrastructure.
Putin made the remarks during a press conference following the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit in Kyrgyzstan, where he was asked about reports that Moscow could announce another mobilization after upcoming State Duma elections.
"This is absolute nonsense. This is an information attack on Russia," Putin said, interrupting a journalist before the question was finished.
The remarks follow warnings from President Volodymyr Zelensky that the Kremlin could resort to another mobilization drive, with Zelensky recently saying Moscow intends to recruit around 300,000 personnel in 2026 and another 300,000 in 2027.
During the same press conference, Putin said he had instructed the Russian military to prepare "massive strikes" against Ukraine's energy facilities, portraying them as retaliation for Ukrainian attacks against Russian oil refineries and other infrastructure.
Putin claimed he had been briefed on Sept. 1 that a large number of Ukrainian drones attempted to penetrate air defenses around Moscow and St. Petersburg and strike three oil refineries.
"Keeping all this in mind... the armed forces of Russia have been instructed to prepare and launch massive strikes on Ukraine's energy facilities," Putin said. "They are hitting ours, they will get a response."
Russia has repeatedly targeted Ukraine's power grid and other civilian energy infrastructure since launching its full-scale invasion in 2022, with attacks intensifying during the colder months in an effort to disrupt electricity and heating.
The Russian Defense Ministry has also recently threatened further large-scale attacks against Ukraine's energy sector, similarly framing them as retaliation for Ukrainian strikes on Russia's fuel and energy infrastructure.

articles.title: Russia targets Ukraine’s rail network as war enters deadly new phase
articles.body:
Russia has opened a deadly new phase in its war against Ukraine by deliberately targeting the country’s railway network, with six employees killed on Tuesday in the latest strikes on Kyiv.
Ukraine’s state-owned railway company, Ukrzaliznytsia, said its workers died when a ballistic missile plunged into a locomotive depot. The Russians hit other railway facilities, it added, during a massive bombardment of Kyiv and the Kyiv region. At least 12 people died, with a dozen wounded, including three children.
“An unbearably difficult night for the entire railway family. Railway staff have been working at the scene since early this morning. The attack has caused significant damage. Rescue workers are still putting out a number of fires,” said Ukrzaliznytsia’s chair, Oleksandr Pertsovsky.
The grim strike took place as Russia escalated its attacks on the Ukrainian capital. It has carried out continuous raids for six days, beginning last week, in an attempt to disrupt daily life and demoralise the city’s inhabitants. The onslaught took place hours before Ukrainian children began a new school year.
Since Russia’s full-scale invasion, 58 railway staff have been killed and at least 318 injured. One wounded railway employee, Volodymyr, was taken to hospital on Tuesday, with people urged to donate blood if they were B positive – his group. “Our colleagues are by his side,” Ukrzaliznytsia said, adding it would support victims’ families.
Ukraine’s railway network is Europe’s third largest, with 15,000 miles (24,000km) of track. It has been a lifeline for the country’s wartime civilians, transporting four million people and an estimated 120,000 pets. It has brought world leaders to Kyiv, including Joe Biden and Andy Burnham, who arrived last week on an overnight service from Poland.
Serhih Leshchenko, a member of Ukrzaliznytsia’s supervisory board, described the railway as the “backbone of Ukraine’s economy”. It was the main logistical supplier for the country’s army and industry, and every week transported 600,000 people, he told the Guardian. With 170,000 workers, it was also Ukraine’s biggest company.
For these reasons Russia was trying to destroy railways, he added. In the first year of the war it attacked bridges, which could be easily replaced. Next, it targeted rails and electricity substations. Ukraine then switched to using diesel engines. This year, Russia started “direct attacks on civilian locomotives”, he said – an insidious tactic, at a time when Ukraine is short of air defences.
Several drivers have been killed and locomotives targeted inside depots. Leshchenko said that if a Shahed drone came within 50km of a train, it had to be evacuated, and could only continue once the threat has passed. So far this year Russia has hit the network more than 1,500 times – a higher figure than in the whole of 2025. Overall, 249 carriages and 492 locomotives have been damaged.
Once known for their punctuality, trains now suffer regular delays, sometimes lasting as long as 12 to 15 hours. Amid air raid sirens, passengers are forced to disembark and take cover, including during winter. Writing on Facebook, the Ukrainian journalist Tetiana Zaiets described how she hid in April when Russian drones flew overhead.
“It was hell. The train stopped at night somewhere in central Ukraine. I don’t even know the name of the town. Half asleep, I just heard the conductor say ‘evacuation’. We took only our personal belongings and valuables with us. It was raining outside. Thank you to the conductors for handing out blankets,” she posted.
She added: “That’s how we held out for two hours. While kamikaze drones were buzzing overhead, we crawled under a goods wagon. The last carriage in the train was full of children. They were being taken back from hospital. They were crying in their sleep. I thought I’d ended up in some sort of horror film. But no, this is our life.”
Since the incident, Zaiets said she was too frightened to travel by train. “Until the war is over, I won’t be using it,” she said, stressing she respected Ukraine’s “courageous” railway workers.
Last week, an enemy drone hit a train in the Odesa region with 600 people on board, including 15 children. “The train was stopped, we were kicked out. We heard explosions, everything was burning. It was scary,” one passenger, Andriy, told the website Suspline.
Another passenger, Eva, said she was evacuated twice, and “dropped off in a field”. “We sat there and heard something flying. Then we saw a drone very close by.” She managed to collect her belongings and was eventually picked up by a bus, she said.
Leshchenko admitted the Russian strikes were hurting Ukraine’s economy and had slowed the export of grain from its under-fire Black Sea ports. He said Kyiv needed air defences from western partners, so it could protects its trains from marauding missiles and drones. “If the whole country is under attack, they will attack railways for sure,” he said.
Up until this year more than 90% of Ukrainian trains arrived on time. This was in part down to the fact engines never go especially fast, rolling at 55mph. Carriages are clean and comfortable: the best way of getting around a vast country. Stewards look after night train customers and bring them morning tea in filigree holders. There is a trolley on day trains, and patchy wifi.
On international services, border guards scrutinise male passengers, while dogs roam up and down corridors. Since the invasion, men between 18 and 60 have been forbidden from leaving the country, with some exemptions. On trains from Kyiv to Przemyśl, a railway hub in eastern Poland, most travellers are women. Since 2022 about six million people have departed abroad, many exiting by train.
In recent days Russia has launched over 1,500 drones at Ukraine, 800 of them jet-fuel models, which are harder to shoot down. In the past, Moscow would send a swarm of drones a couple of times a week, usually at night. Now the attacks continue without a pause, with one or two drones dispatched every hour, paralysing ordinary life. Air raid sirens in Kyiv are non-stop.
Pertsovsky, Ukrzaliznytsia’s boss, described the loss of his employees on Tuesday as “terrible”. “We are in touch with their loved ones. Everyone is with them to get through this extremely difficult time. The night is bitter with impossibility,” he wrote.

articles.title: US and Iran trade fire as hostilities flare again
articles.body:
US and Iran trade fire as hostilities flare again
The US military hit targets in Iran on Tuesday as Tehran reponded with retaliatory strikes as hostilities between the two countries flared once again in an intermittent war that has lasted more than six months. One US strike hit a home hosting a wedding, killing four people and wounding dozens, local officials said.
US forces struck Iran on Tuesday and President Donald Trump vowed a "much harder" response to any counterattacks, as exchanges of fire between the two sides threatened to reignite their smouldering conflict.
The Iranian Red Crescent said on Tuesday that four people including a child were killed and over 50 people were wounded by a US strike on a home hosting a wedding in the south.
Washington hit Iranian targets on Sunday in its first known strikes in several weeks, after which Tehran's forces targeted US troops in Jordan and the United Arab Emirates, and projectiles struck two oil tankers in unclaimed attacks.
More US strikes came on Tuesday, with Iranian state television reporting that explosions were heard in the country's south along the strategic Strait of Hormuz waterway and on an island in the Gulf, and that US forces hit an airport in the southern province of Kerman.
The official IRNA news agency said that "four projectiles hit areas within the counties of Chabahar and Konarak", without specifying whether there was any damage.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Iranian state television reported that several people attending a wedding were wounded by a US attack in the country's south. It added that the US attack hit a "residential area" in Bandar Kuhestak in Sirik county.
US Central Command (CENTCOM) said on X that the strikes followed "recent attempted attacks by (the Guards) against commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and against American service members deployed to the region".
Trump said the "large and powerful" strikes were "in retaliation for the Iranians' failed attempt at adding sea mines to the Strait" and "the Iranians shooting eight missiles, all successfully knocked down, at our Military Base in Jordan".
"If the failed Nation of Iran retaliates for this very justified attack, they will be hit again at a much harder and higher level," he said in a post on his Truth Social platform.
Read moreStrait of Hormuz accessibility at the centre of US-Iran war flare-up
Revolutionary Guards spokesman Hossein Mohebi warned on X that Washington "will regret its new attacks", saying that "severe punishment awaits the aggressors".
Iran's Tasnim news agency later said a "decisive operation by Iran's armed forces in response to the US enemy has begun", and that "US bases and interests in the region are being targeted by Iranian missiles and drones."
Tankers attacked
After six months of war, the foes remain at an impasse, with Iran keeping the Strait of Hormuz closed and the United States persisting with a counter-blockade of Iranian ports.
Washington said its forces attacked Iranian rocket launchers on the island of Larak on Sunday to prevent Tehran planting mines in the strait's key shipping lanes.
The Middle East war began in late February with the US and Israeli attacks on Iran that killed its former supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.
Read moreIran discovers major new gas reserves amid war-hit energy sector
Attacks on commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz, through which one-fifth of world oil supplies flowed before the war, previously led to the collapse of a ceasefire between the United States and Iran.
Greek maritime risk management firm Marisks said Tuesday that two crude tankers were hit by "unknown projectiles" late the previous day.
One of the incidents had been publicised earlier by the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency, which added that no casualties or environmental effects had been reported.
Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian meanwhile vowed Tuesday to match any US move to return to a deal aimed at ending the war.
He also warned that a return by the United States to "a policy of pressure and threats could derail the path of diplomacy".
(FRANCE 24 with AP and AFP)

articles.title: Drone Incident in Leipzig: the Trail Leads to Russia
articles.body:
The German Government is holding Russia responsible for the attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport. The findings of the intelligence agencies clearly point to “Russian involvement”, Germany’s Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said, and announced further sanctions, including the closure of the Russian consulate in Bonn and the termination of the lease for the Russian House in the centre of Berlin. We are not at war with Russia, but we are a “target of war”, he stated. What comes next?
Europe must go a step further
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
A response to the Russian attacks was long overdue, says Frankfurter Rundschau (Germany) :
“It also sends a signal to EU citizens to take the Russian threat more seriously and not just see it as a distant war against Ukraine. Sanctions alone are not enough. Germany and its partners will have to do more than before to mitigate the consequences of Russia’s hybrid war, which encompasses sabotage and disinformation campaigns. ... The EU should go a step further. Spain and Greece should hand over their Patriot missile defence ammunition to Ukraine so that the invaded country can better protect itself against Russian attacks.”
Measured response from Berlin
The Tages-Anzeiger (Switzerland) praises the response:
“This is a moderate signal to Putin, a cautious one even, since Berlin has refrained from involving Nato. Yet it is also a measured response because Chancellor Friedrich Merz thus retains the option to resort to the means of escalation: firstly, Article 4, which provides for consultations within the defence alliance if ‘the territorial integrity or security’ of an ally is threatened. And if the Russian bully still does not cease his provocations, Nato could then activate Article 5, the collective defence clause – at which point war in Europe would not be far off. Rationally speaking, Putin can have no interest in things going that far. But this warlord has not been behaving particularly rationally for some time now.”
Machine-Gun Pickup Escorts Putin Convoy in Vladivostok
Now the last buffer is gone
Unfortunately, the time for purely diplomatic responses is over, De Standaard (Belgium) stresses:
“Germany and its Nato allies must now do everything in their power to break free from the logic that military action is the only possible next move. Perhaps the concept of ‘hybrid defence and deterrence’ can buy some time, with a combination of diplomatic and economic sanctions and the accelerated expansion of their own defence capabilities. But the little diplomacy that had tentatively been pursued so far will be destroyed as a result. Positions will inevitably harden. There is no longer any buffer to prevent a reaction.”
Bureaucrats provoked into hasty measures
Journalist Sergei Aslanjan (Russia) makes light of Germany’s reaction on Facebook:
“Russia has acted treacherously, even though it knows that the Bundeswehr is not online at night and only wages war during working hours, in daylight from 8 am to 5 pm and with a lunch break. Russia’s military operations on German territory disrupt the Chancellor’s schedule, throw his staff’s work into disarray and prevent a well-considered response, thereby provoking the government into taking hasty measures. This has a significant impact on Germany’s defence capabilities, deprives Bundeswehr soldiers of their statutory benefits, disrupts their workflow and hinders their combat training.”
Leipzig was part of a campaign
Russia is pursuing a grand plan with small-scale actions, writes military expert Alexandru Grumaz (Romania) in Adevărul:
“Moscow is targeting the system that is helping Ukraine to continue its fight. ... This is the fundamental problem for Nato. A large-scale attack on a member state is relatively easy to assess, both politically and militarily. A drone found near an airport, a suspicious fire in a factory, a damaged cable, a CCTV camera that has been tampered with or a saboteur recruited via Telegram are far more difficult to deal with. Taken individually, these incidents may be too minor to warrant a major response. Taken together, however, they can add up to a campaign. That is the essence of hybrid warfare.”
