articles.title: Middle East crisis live: US military says it’s striking targets in Iran as hostilities flare
articles.body:
Iran says ‘regretful response’ to US attacks has begun after state TV reports four killed at wedding in Sirik region – as it happened
The US and Iran have exchanged fire for the first time in a month, with missiles and drones fired at Iranian rocket launchers on an island in the strait of Hormuz
At least four people including a young child have been killed and over 50 injured after the US resumed strikes against Iran on Tuesday. According to the Iranian Red Crescent, shrapnel from a US missile attack hit a residential home where a wedding was taking place inthe coastal city of Kuhestak, in Sirik county of Hormozgan province.The United States has yet to comment on the incident.
It comes several hours after the US military announced it was launching strikes on Iran, quashing hopes that an exchange of fire last weekend might not presage a wider renewal of hostilities. US Central Command said it was striking targets in Iran over attempted attacks on shipping and against US service members in the region. Explosions were reported in several locations across southern Iran.
Donald Trump warnedthat if Iran retaliated against the US’s latest strikes, “they will be hit again at a much harder and higher level, but it will not be the biggest attack of them all, that is waiting in the wings and, when it is over, there will be very little left of the Islamic Republic ofIran.” That very ominous last part is starkly reminiscent of threats Trump has made in the past that could amount to war crimes if carried out. He added that the strikes were “in retaliation” for Iran’s “failed attempt” to lay mines in the strait of Hormuz and for Iran’s (retaliatory) attacks on the US military base in Jordan (which were intercepted).
In a call with Fox News, Trump reportedly reiterated that Iran would be “totally wiped out” if it launches retaliatory strikes against the US. “This is a very big hit today. If it goes a third time, they’re going to be totally wiped out as a country,” Fox News quoted the US president as saying.
In response to the attacks, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said it had begun a “regretful response to the aggressors”, state broadcaster IRIB reported. And IRGC spokesperson Sardar Mohebi said in a post on X that “severe punishment” awaited the aggressors and that the US “will regret its new attacks”.
Jordan’s army said that 10 out of 13 Iranian ballistic missiles were intercepted and the other three fell in remote areas. It followed claims from the IRGC that it had killed “a large number of US forces”, while destroying “several installations and enemy attack helicopters” in a ballistic attack on US Marines’ barracks at Camp Titin, a military site near Aqaba. Reuters and Al Jazeera have since both reported, citing US sources, that there were no injuries or damage to the barracks.
A reminder that this phase of fighting began when the US military said it had struck rocket launchers on Larak Island in the strait of Hormuz on Sunday, in its first strikes on Iran since July, after it detected the Iranians were planning to deploy fresh mines in the critical waterway. Tehran responded by launching missiles at US sites in Jordan, which were intercepted, and the United Arab Emirates, which said it had stopped an Iranian drone over its territorial waters. Trump had threatened further action on Monday, telling Fox News: “We’re going to hit them hard. There will be a response.” These strikes, 24 hours after Trump’s comments, are that response.
Meanwhile, in a statement, the Jordanian army has said it intercepted 10 of the 13 ballistic missiles that entered the kingdom’s airspace, while the remaining three fell in remote areas, away from population centres.
IRGC claims attack on US military barracks in Jordan
The IRGC has claimed that it killed “a large number of US forces”, while destroying “several installations and enemy attack helicopters” in a ballistic attack on US Marines’ barracks at Camp Titin, a military site near Aqaba, Jordan.
In a statement, carried by Iranian broadcaster IRIB, the IRGC said its retaliation would continue.
There was no immediate comment from the US military. We’ll bring you more on this as we get it.
The Iranian state broadcaster IRIB shared video footage showing extensive debris and damage at what it said was the site of the wedding in Sirik following the US strike, with rescuers rushing through the scene and people heard screaming in the background.
The Iranian Red Crescent said that four people including a child were killed and over 50 people were wounded.
Alarm sirens have been activated in Jordan’s Mafraq and Aqaba governorates, state TV reported, as Tehran launched retaliatory attacks against US interests and bases in the region.
Sirik death toll rises to four including child, says Iran Red Crescent
The Iranian Red Crescent said that four people including a child were killed and over 50 people were wounded by a US attack while attending a wedding in the south.
“Following a US missile attack, shrapnel hit a residential home in the city of Kuhestak, in Sirik county of Hormozgan province, where a wedding celebration was taking place,” the Red Crescent said in a post on X.
“More than 50 people were injured and four people, including a young child, were martyred.”
IRGC says ‘regretful response’ to US attacks has begun
A short while ago, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said it had begun a “regretful response to the aggressors” amid the fresh US attacks on southern Iran, state broadcaster IRIB reported.
In a statement, the IRGC said that “in blind and desperate attacks”, the US had bombed several locations, including civilian areas. It went on:
Attacks that tightened the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz and strengthened the determination of the fighters to suppress the foreign forces interfering in the strait of Hormuz.
The brave warriors of the IRGC have begun a regretful response to the aggressors, and in the first action, using the new aerospace defence system, they shot down the 50th advanced MQ9 drone of the invading American army.
At least two people killed at wedding in US attack on Sirik, Iranian state tv reports
At least two people were killed and several others wounded at a wedding in the coastal city of Bandar Kuhestak in Iran’s southern Sirik county during the US attacks, Ahmad Nafisi, deputy governor of Hormozgan province, told Iranian state television in a phone call.
“A residential home was attacked while people were holding a wedding ceremony,” Nafisi said, adding that “two people were reported martyred and a number of others wounded”.
The situation at Jiroft airport in Iran’s Kerman province is “under control”, a deputy governor said in comments carried by Iran’s Fars News Agency, after a US projectile landed outside the airport’s runway.
There were no casualties or damage to airport structure, he said.
Iran may target 'Americans throughout the world', US says in new travel alert
Renewed tensions between Iran and US forces have prompted heightened travel alerts for the Middle East.
In a post on X, the US state department said:
“Due to tensions in the Middle East, the security environment remains complex with the potential for unforeseen escalation. Americans currently in the Middle East should exercise heightened vigilance and be aware of potential flight cancellations, airspace closures, and travel disruptions.”
The advisce, covering all countries in the region, is similar to that given during previous points of heightened conflict with Iran. It also warns Iran and its supporters may target US interests “and Americans throughout the world, including US businesses and other institutions”.
We’re getting some more details from Iranian media on the US strikes on Jiroft airport in southern Iran.
Fars news agency, quoting the governor of Kerman province, said the attack caused “no casualties and did not damage the runway or the airport buildings.”

articles.title: West lacks adequate defence against drone swarms
articles.body:
Western militaries do not currently have an adequate defence against the autonomous drone swarms that could emerge as unmanned warfare moves beyond systems requiring individual human pilots, General David Petraeus has warned in an address to the House of Lords, the UK Defence Journal understands.
Speaking on 1 September, Petraeus argued that the war in Ukraine is demonstrating a change extending well beyond the adoption of drones themselves. He described a battlefield in which large numbers of relatively expendable unmanned systems are linked with sensors, software, electronic warfare, artificial intelligence and increasingly rapid targeting processes, while military technology and tactics are being modified continuously during combat.
Petraeus said: “Much of the discussion has understandably focused on individual technologies—unmanned systems, artificial intelligence, electronic warfare, cyber capabilities, precision strike, battle management systems, and others. Each matters. But the principal lesson is larger: the very concept of warfare is changing.”
He continued: “We are witnessing the convergence of technological, operational, industrial, and organizational change into an entirely new way of conducting war. Information is collected, analyzed, disseminated, and acted upon at unprecedented speed. Sensors and battle management systems are connected to vast numbers of attritable unmanned systems capable of precision effects across every domain.”
Petraeus said commercial innovation was also moving directly onto the battlefield, with software, hardware and operational methods adapted during fighting and an increasingly close relationship developing between military operations and the industrial base.
The former US commander said remotely controlled systems are already changing the role of conventional formations by taking over tasks previously performed by personnel in some of the most exposed parts of the battlefield.
He said: “And remotely operated unmanned systems on the ground, in the air, and at sea are increasingly displacing humans from many of the most dangerous functions of front-line combat and profoundly changing the role of traditional combined-arms formations.”
Petraeus also made a strong claim about the scale of drone employment in Ukraine, telling peers that remotely piloted systems now account for the overwhelming majority of Russian casualties and that established land systems are operating under persistent threat from surveillance and precision weapons.
He said: “Those changes will encounter fierce resistance from advocates of existing force structures and legacy systems, many of which are becoming extraordinarily vulnerable on the battlefield we see in Ukraine. Remotely piloted systems, employed there in enormous numbers, already inflict the overwhelming majority of Russian casualties. Tanks and artillery increasingly operate only under extraordinary threat from ubiquitous surveillance and precision strike.”
His warning went further with the development of fully autonomous systems. Petraeus argued that removing the requirement for an individual human pilot for each platform would allow unmanned formations to increase dramatically in size, potentially producing swarms considerably larger than those possible with today’s remotely operated systems.
He said: “And the advent of fully autonomous systems in the months and years ahead will represent another profound development. Removing the constraint imposed by the number of human pilots will make possible unmanned operations at vastly greater scale—including swarms for which we presently possess no adequate defense.”
Petraeus argued that military advantage would consequently depend on institutional adaptation as well as technical development, particularly the ability to incorporate battlefield lessons rapidly into doctrine, force design, training and acquisition.
He said: “In this environment, decisive advantage will belong not simply to those who innovate technologically, but to those whose institutions learn faster than their adversaries. Warfare is becoming a continuous competition in institutional learning and adaptation—the ability to identify lessons, incorporate them rapidly into doctrine, force design, procurement, training, and leader development, and repeat the process before the adversary catches up.”

articles.title: Russia attacked Ukraine with 4 missiles with ballistic missiles; 141 of 174 drones neutralized
articles.body:
Russia attacked Ukraine with 4 missiles with ballistic missiles; 141 of 174 drones neutralized
Kyiv • UNN
During the night, Russia launched 174 drones and four missiles at Ukraine. Air defense destroyed or suppressed 141 unmanned aerial vehicles; hits were recorded at 16 locations, including missile strikes.
On the night of September 2, Russia launched four missiles at Ukraine, including two Iskander-M ballistic missiles, and 174 drones, 141 of which were shot down or suppressed. No reports have been made of Russian missiles being neutralized, but some of the enemy’s weapons did not reach their targets. UNN reports this, citing data from the Ukrainian Air Force on September 2.
What Russia used to attack
According to the Ukrainian Air Force, on the night of September 2 (since 18:00 on September 1), the enemy attacked with:
-  2 Iskander-M ballistic missiles from the temporarily occupied territory of Crimea; 
-  2 Kh-59/69 guided air-launched missiles from the airspace over the Black Sea; 
-  174 Shahed-type attack UAVs (approximately half of them jet-powered), S8000 “Bandarol,” Gerbera, and Parodiya-type decoy drones launched from the following areas: Orel, the temporarily occupied territory of Donetsk region, Hvardiiske – the temporarily occupied territory of the Autonomous Republic of Crimea. 
What were the main directions of Russia’s attack
The main directions of the attack were Odesa and Kyiv regions, the Air Force reported.
How air defense performed
The air attack was repelled by aviation, anti-aircraft missile forces, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of the Defense Forces of Ukraine.
According to preliminary data, as of 08:30, air defense shot down/suppressed 141 targets:
-  3 S8000 “Bandarol”; 
-  138 enemy Shahed-type UAVs (including jet-powered ones), Gerbera drones, and drones of other types. 
"Hits by enemy missiles and attack UAVs were recorded at 16 locations, as well as the falling of downed targets (debris) at 4 locations. In addition, some of the enemy’s weapons did not reach their targets; information concerning them is being clarified," the Ukrainian Air Force stated.
The attack, as reported, is ongoing, with enemy UAVs in the airspace.

articles.title: Why doesn’t Russia kill Ukraine’s leaders? Putin says he needs ‘some kind of negotiators’ left in Kyiv — in case they decide to settle.
articles.body:
Why doesn’t Russia kill Ukraine’s leaders? Putin says he needs ‘some kind of negotiators’ left in Kyiv — in case they decide to settle.
Russian President Vladimir Putin spoke at a press conference following the Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit in Bishkek. Just before 3 a.m. local time, he took reporters’ questions about Germany’s decision to close Russia’s consulate general, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky’s statement on the safety of Russian airspace, and the likelihood of another mobilization after Russia’s elections. Here’s what he said, in a nutshell.
On Russia’s next targets in Ukraine
Russia’s armed forces have been given instructions to prepare and carry out large-scale strikes on Ukraine’s energy facilities.
On Zelensky’s threats to the safety of Russian airspace
I haven’t heard any such statements, but if that was said out loud, that amounts to state terrorism. And they’re asking us to resume negotiations, asking for in-person meetings. You don’t negotiate with terrorists. If tragedies happen, we’ll find a way to respond.
On strikes against Ukraine’s leadership
As you can see, we aren’t carrying out strikes like that. We work on the assumption that we need some people there, if they come to realize that they want to settle things peacefully. We need some kind of negotiators.
On mobilization after Russia’s elections
That’s a load of nonsense. It’s a disinformation campaign against Russia.
On negotiations over Ukraine
If someone is making, or can make, a concrete contribution, we’re all for it. The one thing we’d rather avoid is having the whole thing spin its wheels. The negotiating process […] is, to a certain extent, frozen as of today.
On the decree to protect critical infrastructure
You need to get nationalization out of your heads; nationalization was never even on our minds. You know the saying: people don’t act until disaster strikes. So the enemy started striking our facilities, including oil refineries — and sure enough, it did damage, because those facilities weren’t protected. I met with businessmen, and they started saying that this was the responsibility of law enforcement and the army. But we talked it over, and they realized they had to pitch in too.
On the CIA director’s visit to Moscow
There have always been contacts between intelligence officials, even during the Cold War. We recently handed over to the United States an American citizen who had been serving a prison sentence. There are always contacts.
On Germany’s decision to close Russia’s consulate general
This has to do with Germany’s domestic political situation. The chancellor is in a difficult spot; he isn’t defending his country’s national interests. You have to stand up to an aggressive Russia — but where’s the evidence? Well, so they planted the evidence. Given falling poll numbers and the upcoming elections, this raises the question of the political future of Germany’s ruling elite. That’s what this is about.
On killer whales and bears
If someone tries to drag us down the food chain, to gobble us up, to wolf us down, they just might catch one in the teeth.

articles.title: ‘Drone-infested skies are no place for civilian aviation’: Zelensky tells airlines still flying into Moscow to get out, days after ordering 1,000 drone attacks a day
articles.body:
‘Drone-infested skies are no place for civilian aviation’: Zelensky tells airlines still flying into Moscow to get out, days after ordering 1,000 drone attacks a day
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky warned airlines that Russian airspace is becoming unsafe because “there will simply be drones in Russia’s skies on a scale that has to be taken into account.”
“Today, we want to warn every airline that uses Russian airspace, every insurer, and everyone who still uses Russia’s key airports: Russian airspace is becoming completely unsafe,” Zelensky said in his evening video address.
Zelensky said that Ukraine “does not threaten civilian aviation as such,” but that Ukrainian drone attacks mean “Russian airspace will effectively be closing”:
We in Ukraine do not want innocent lives to be lost. That is why we are warning our partners: the safe days in Russia’s skies are over. It is important that this is heard by the ambassadors of countries represented here in Ukraine, as well as by ambassadors working in Moscow. Every one of them knows exactly what Russia’s war means for our country and our people, and they must convey this information to their capitals.
It is important that the airlines currently flying to airports primarily in Moscow, St. Petersburg, and other key destinations in Russia hear this as well. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Ukraine and our other institutions will provide international organizations with full information about the dangers in Russian airspace. Drone-infested skies are no place for civilian aviation.
Volodymyr Zelensky said on August 28 that he had ordered Ukrainian troops to launch 1,000 drones a day at Russia. “Today I held a meeting of the Staff. The key thing is to maximize production of our weapons to defend against Russian strikes on Ukraine. […] The task is 1,000 drones for long-range sanctions a day against Russia,” he said.

articles.title: Budanov: Ukrainian drones and missiles will operate in the skies over the Russian Federation until the aggression ends
articles.body:
Budanov: Ukrainian drones and missiles will operate in the skies over the Russian Federation until the aggression ends
Kyiv • UNN
Budanov said that systematic strikes on military targets in the Russian Federation would be carried out in response to the aggression. Ukraine allows pauses only for the sake of genuine steps toward peace.
As long as Russia’s aggression continues, Ukrainian drones and missiles will operate in Russian skies. This was stated by Head of the Office of the President of Ukraine Kyrylo Budanov, UNN reports.
Details
According to him, the Kremlin deliberately chose the path of escalation, turning September 1 into yet another day of terror against Ukrainian children and civilian infrastructure.
Guided by the right to self-defense, Ukraine will deliver a tough and proportionate response. I fully support the decision of President and Supreme Commander-in-Chief Volodymyr Zelenskyy. Russian skies are no longer safe. This is the new reality, about which we are officially warning international airlines, insurers, and partners. Our long-range capabilities will systematically strike military targets on the enemy’s territory
He added that Kyiv respects the diplomatic efforts of its partners and is ready to ensure targeted pauses "exclusively for genuine steps toward ending the war."
Context
The day before, President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned every airline using Russian airspace that "Russian skies are becoming completely dangerous" and "will de facto be closed."
In response, Russian dictator Putin called Zelenskyy’s words "a bid for state terrorism" and promised that Russia "will find a way to respond."

articles.title: What do Canada and Iran have in common? The US bullies both
articles.body:
What do Canada and Iran have in common? The US bullies both
Canada has very few similarities with Iran – to Canada’s own shame.
Let’s leave aside the basic differences, such as location, demographics, weather, and cuisine, and focus on the essentials: Historically, Iran is old and firmly based on an ancient civilization; Canada, like the US, is young and a little accidental, a leftover of the British Empire in its settler-colonial-ethnic-cleansing variant.
In terms of religion, Iran is shaped by pious Shia Islam; Canada displays the flaccid mix of an emasculated Christmas-and-jingle-bells-only Christianity and aggressive anything-goes consumerist secularism typical of the contemporary West.
Geopolitically, Iran is a proud and victorious opponent of the US and Israel; Canada is a fairly ordinary vassal in the American empire.
Accordingly, Canada is deeply and proudly involved in the West’s proxy war against Russia by way of using up Ukraine. Indeed, the Canadian contribution is particularly ironic because it also serves a frenetic and powerful nationalist Ukrainian lobby, rooted in deliberately privileged fascist World War Two runaways and Cold War conspirators. Iran, on the other side, has long helped Russia and, for its efforts, been directly attacked by Kiev’s Zelensky regime. In return, Western sources claim, Moscow has been helping Tehran with its ongoing defense against the US and Israel.
Most importantly, Iran is a country on the side of elementary decency, fundamental human ethics, and international law and therefore against the genocide committed by Israel, the US, UK, Germany, and various other Western accomplices against the Palestinian nation. Canada – Israeli murders of Canadian citizens and some cheap and, in effect, empty gestures from Ottawa notwithstanding – has been, at the very best, yet another camp follower of the Western genocide coalition.
And yet, strange as it may be, recent events have produced something that Iran and Canada have in common. Or to be precise, it’s Washington’s bizarre policies that have created this odd overlap: both Canada the long-standing vassal and Iran the steadfast antagonist are currently at the receiving end of both fresh attempts at coercion by economic warfare and escalating rhetoric from Washington.
Of course, there are orders-of-magnitude differences between the Trump administration’s ‘Operation Economic Outcast’ against Tehran and the latest round of tariff and trash-talk launched against Canada.
The ‘Operation’ targeting Iran, according to its mastermind and cheerleader Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, aims to combine a naval blockade, intelligence gathering, “mapp[ing] every node, every facilitator and every network that Iran” is using to trade abroad, and wide-ranging secondary sanctions to, in Bessent words, “asphyxiat[e]” Tehran. The declared end goal is to “collapse” Iran by inflicting an “Economic D-Day,” as President Donald Trump has put it.
There’s no such intention to wage total economic war in the case of Canada. Regarding Ottawa, Washington has merely initiated a pressure campaign within its empire. Its goal is not absolute destruction but the punishment and coercion of a wayward vassal.
In essence, the Canadian government under Prime Minister Mark Carney has rejected Washington’s offer of a crudely disadvantageous and interfering trade deal, featuring, according to the Financial Times, “ludicrous” American demands.
Faced with “clodhopping bullying” so extreme no leader could have submitted – except maybe, say, the EU’s Ursula von der Leyen or Germany’s Friedrich Merz – Carney had an excellent opportunity to make a stand. He declared that Canada is under US attack and, in effect, at war – all restricted to the economy, of course – and that his government will retaliate tit-for-tat, dollar-for-dollar.
Washington is striking at Ottawa with 50% tariffs on Canadian goods worth $20 billion, and, in return, Ottawa will give as good as it gets. That’s the plan at least. But while the Wall Street Journal reports that both sides are getting ready for a long fight, there also is still some time for last-minute off-ramps.
Things need to be kept in proportion: the new US tariffs would affect about 5% of Canadian exports to its overbearing southern neighbor. The Canadian retaliation would target about 6% of what the US sends north. Meanwhile, US rhetoric is surging. Trump has renamed Lake Ontario as Lake America and posted an extraordinarily odd AI-generated video about it, featuring (Canadian?) wild geese marching in lockstep under US flags and firing assault rifles. In Canada, for now at least, Carney’s hardline response is popular.
In short, what is really happening between Ottawa and Washington may well seem like a farce if compared to the state of things between Washington and Tehran. Unsurprisingly, the Iranian leadership has declared that it won’t budge. And why should it? It has already won two rounds of war against Washington. While its economy is certainly suffering, the American-Israeli aggression has, in effect, fully immunized Iranian society against any regime-change schemes.
Finally, Washington will not succeed in making key players submit to its secondary-sanctions blackmail. China, now the world’s great oil power, as The Economist concedes, and a crucial partner for Iran not merely in economic terms, has already made that much clear. Russia is very unlikely to be impressed either.
But take a step back and look at the picture as a whole. Here we are: the US is waging economic war – of different intensity – against both opponents and so-called allies. More importantly, it is meeting resistance in both cases. And most importantly, in both cases, there is no reason to assume that Washington will win. All of that is happening against a background of the US escalating its use of brute force: There is the fresh “deal” – really, steal – to siphon off 65 billion barrels of crude from the de facto US protectorate of post-Maduro Venezuela. Regarding the much-disturbed bond markets, meanwhile, Trump has openly threatened to use the US military to shape them to Washington’s advantage.
The idea is about as smart as trying to fix a microchip with a sledgehammer. But, with the US, that doesn’t mean it won’t be tried. For the red thread running through all of the above is a combination of slipping real power, escalating aggressiveness, and rising resistance from others. What makes this so dangerous is that Washington seems to have entirely lost the ability to realistically adjust its aims and demands to its declining capabilities. Think of it as a bully past his prime who is not only very violent but also not smart enough to see when being more flexible would be in his own best interest.
The statements, views and opinions expressed in this column are solely those of the author and do not necessarily represent those of RT.

articles.title: Von der Leyen and NATO secretary general will meet on 2 September to discuss rising hybrid threats from Russia
articles.body:
Von der Leyen and NATO secretary general will meet on 2 September to discuss rising hybrid threats from Russia
European Commission chief spokesperson Paula Pinho said that the meeting between European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte on 2 September will focus primarily on the growing hybrid threats posed by Russia to Europe and strengthening EU-NATO defence cooperation.
Source: European Pravda
Quote from Pinho: "Indeed, and it's frequently the case that meetings are added to the calendar of President von der Leyen also at short notice. Now, this meeting tomorrow between the president and Secretary General Rutte is to be seen in the context as we strengthen our defense cooperation within Europe and with NATO."
Details: The spokeswoman stressed that this is particularly important in light of the "increasing hybrid threats that we are seeing".
"So it's in this context that it's taking place. I cannot prejudge what will be discussed specifically," she added.
Asked whether Ukraine and its need for interceptor missiles would be discussed at the meeting, Paula Pinho noted that she does not "think that there can be such a discussion without referring to Ukraine, without referring to what is going on in Europe, which obviously has major consequences also for us in the EU".
Background:
- EU chief diplomat Kaja Kallas announced the creation of a high-level group made up of former political and military leaders from European countries and Ukraine, who will work on issues related to the bloc's defence capabilities.
- On 28 July, the US Department of Defense officially began a six-month review of its military presence in Europe, which could pave the way for a reduction in US troops on the continent.
- The Pentagon's review of the deployment of US troops in Europe, which is expected to be completed by 6 November, will create at least four possible courses of action for US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth.

articles.title: Second drone brigade in two months: Ukraine is forming the 446th Unmanned Systems Brigade
articles.body:
Ukraine's Armed Forces are forming the 446th Separate Unmanned Systems Brigade, which is recruiting servicemembers while formation continues, MilitaryLand reported. The new unit joins a force that hit 32,485 Russian personnel over the summer alone, the Unmanned Systems Forces (SBS) reported on 1 September.
Ukraine is facing a shortage of military personnel, yet the Armed Forces are forming their second separate unmanned systems brigade this year. The force's commander wants unmanned systems covering the entire front at tactical, operational, and strategic depths.
What is known about the 446th Brigade
Military personnel from other units can apply for a transfer through Army+, according to MilitaryLand.
The first of the two was the 445th Separate Unmanned Systems Brigade Chata, whose formation became known in July. Both units are recruiting for posts running from operators of ground robots, FPV, bomber, and interceptor drones to psychological-support officers, analysts, and accountants, Militarnyi reported.
The deployment of such units is part of the Ukrainian Armed Forces' broader effort to increase the number of unmanned systems in the military. Ukrainian drones accounted for about 96% of Russian casualties in March—33,988 of roughly 35,000 killed or severely wounded—Zelenskyy said in April.
Why Ukraine is turning to drones
The expansion of unmanned systems brigades is part of a broader effort initiated by Robert Brovdi, callsign Madyar, to increase the role of the SBS within Ukraine's Defense Forces, Militarnyi notes.
Brovdi told Reuters in June that he wants to raise the drone forces from about 2.5% of Ukraine's armed forces to 5%, a goal he first stated publicly in September 2025. At that share, the drone units accounted for roughly a third of Russian losses over the previous 12 months, according to figures the force gave Reuters, which said it could not verify them independently.
Then Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine Oleksandr Syrskyi described unmanned systems as one of the key factors shaping modern warfare. Current Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine Mykhailo Drapatyi stated that one of his priorities is the development and scaling of the unmanned component.
Overall, the SBS struck 58,465 targets in August, its own tally for 1–31 August shows.

articles.title: Katz warns: Iran may strike during Jewish holidays, Israel ready to respond
articles.body:
Defense Minister Israel Katz said Wednesday that Israel is preparing for the possibility of an Iranian attack during the Jewish holiday period and is ready to respond with significant force if targeted.
Speaking at the “Decision Time: Democracy and Society” conference hosted by ynet and Yedioth Ahronoth in cooperation with the Israel Democracy Institute, Katz said Iran “likes to attack on holidays” and stressed that Israel was prepared.
Asked whether the current exchange of strikes between Washington and Tehran could spill over into Israel, particularly ahead of the Jewish holidays, Katz said Israeli leaders were monitoring developments continuously.
“The prime minister and I are following this on a daily basis together with the IDF, sometimes in the middle of the night on the red phone,” he said. “We are not taking any information lightly. We do not want to be surprised. We are prepared.”
Katz said the IDF, including the Israeli Air Force, was ready to strike Iran if necessary.
“If they attack us, we will respond with great force, independently of anyone else,” he said.
Katz said Israel was currently allowing the United States to take the lead in strikes against Iran because of American interests involving the Strait of Hormuz and energy security.
“For now, they are striking throughout the region except us,” he said. “But there is a possibility that they will attack us. We are prepared for that defensively.”
He added that Iran had a history of timing attacks around Jewish holidays.
“They like to attack on Jewish holidays because they hate Jews,” Katz said. “Look at many things that happened in the past. But we are prepared both defensively and offensively, in coordination with the United States in this area.”
At the same time, Katz stressed that Israel would not accept an attack against it regardless of the trigger.
“If they attack because of Lebanon, because of the West Bank, because of Gaza, or simply because they feel like it, our planes are ready to take off,” he said.
Katz also addressed the possibility that Iran could attempt to rebuild its nuclear program, saying it had been destroyed during Israel’s Operation Rising Lion.
“We destroyed it, the entire production process, all of it,” he said. “There was an active program. We destroyed it.”
Katz said U.S. President Donald Trump later joined the operation with B-2 bombers carrying bunker-busting munitions against Fordow and another site.
“Since then, the nuclear program has not been renewed, and we are monitoring these developments,” Katz said. “Now we need to make sure they do not regain the ability to return to it and that they do not go back to it.”
He said Israel’s policy remained unequivocal.
“We will not allow Iran to have nuclear weapons,” Katz said. “If something like that happens, and President Trump says the same thing, then we will likely attack together.”
Katz argued that Israel’s campaign had significantly weakened Iran.
“We removed an existential threat from Iran, eliminated Khamenei, thwarted their strategic capabilities and set them back by decades,” he said.
He added that Israel had also benefited strategically despite casualties on the home front.
“There were casualties, but when you look at the overall balance, there could have been many more,” Katz said. “We neutralized their launch capabilities. Against Iran, we achieved an enormous gain. Our most dangerous enemy was struck and is now significantly weaker than us.”
The conference brings together elected officials from across Israel’s political spectrum, ministers, former senior judicial officials, law-enforcement figures, academics, Israel Democracy Institute researchers, senior civil servants, economists and representatives of civil society for discussions on major issues shaping the country.

articles.title: China's Xi holds talks with Egypt's Sisi
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
China's Xi holds talks with Sisi in first Egypt visit in a decade
Egypt's President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi on Wednesday received his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping on his first visit to Cairo in a decade, as Beijing seeks a greater foothold in the region against the backdrop of the US-Iran war.
The 21-gun salute at Cairo's Ittihadiya Palace marked the start of a day of talks expected to cover the Middle East war and its fallout, including on maritime trade security, as well as boosting Chinese investment in the Arab world's most populous country.
The two BRICS members are expected to sign a slate of economic agreements, including on artificial intelligence, transport and manufacturing.
Egypt currently estimates Chinese investments at around $10 billion. Beijing has key stakes in the Suez Canal Economic Zone, which are only expected to grow as the US-Iran war threatens global maritime trade.
Beijing has also played a key role in Sisi's megaprojects, the crowning jewel of which is the New Administrative Capital 50 kilometres (30 miles) east of Cairo, large swathes of which have been bankrolled by Chinese investment.
China is a major exporter to Egypt, with its trade surplus reaching $12 billion in the first seven months of 2026, according to Chinese customs data.
Across Cairo, a megalopolis home to over 26 million people, major streets have been lined with Chinese and Egyptian flags, as well as billboards showing Sisi and Xi.
Street signs boast of "generations of Egyptian-Chinese friendship flowing like the Nile River", while residents have been warned to plan for substantial traffic delays on their commutes.
Xi is expected to traverse the entire capital during his visit Wednesday, including a stop at the Grand Egyptian Museum overlooking the Giza Pyramids.
'Independent foreign policy'
According to analysts, Cairo will use the summit to underscore its strategic autonomy, showing it can leverage its close ties with both Washington and Beijing.
Sisi, in an op-ed published in Egyptian media on Tuesday, highlighted Cairo's "independent foreign policy", days after a branch of Egypt's second-largest bank was targeted by US sanctions.
He wrote that Egypt and China were partners in "strengthening the role of the global south" in an increasingly polarised world.
Washington vowed last month to isolate Iran economically, threatening expanded sanctions that could also hit Chinese banks, among others.
China, a major buyer of Iranian oil, has vowed to safeguard its interests.
In the lead-up to an expected meeting between Xi and US President Donald Trump this month, it has also sought to shore up ties with US-friendly regional nations.
Egypt is one of the largest recipients of US military aid, and historically a key Middle East mediator.
Last week, the US Treasury announced sanctions on the Emirati branch of Egypt's Banque Misr for alleged support to Iran.
Egypt—which under Sisi's administration became one of the world's top weapons buyers—hosted major joint air combat exercises with the Chinese military in August, featuring Beijing's powerful J-16 fighter jet.

articles.title: Ukraine urges partners to allocate funds for Ukrainian drone purchases from national budgets – Defense Ministry
articles.body:
Ukraine is urging partners to direct funding toward additional production of Ukrainian drones and to ensure the delivery of air defense missiles before the start of winter, Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara said.
"To counter Russia’s air terror and Russia’s plans to mobilize and ramp up drone production, Ukraine needs an increase in critical weapons as well as additional funding — about $27 billion. That’s why Ukraine is calling on partners to allocate funds for purchasing Ukrainian drones from national budgets, speed up disbursement of the EU loan, and resume discussions on using frozen Russian assets," the Defense Ministry said on Telegram.
Khmara also called on partners to hand over Patriot missiles from their stockpiles to counter ballistic threats, air-to-air interceptors against cruise missiles, and MANPADS munitions against jet-powered drones. Contributions to the PURL and JUMPSTART mechanisms also remain important, he said.
He stressed that the Defense Ministry, together with military leadership, is expanding projects built on asymmetric solutions, and that a war plan based on a shared vision is being prepared and will soon be presented to partners.
Ukraine is now building a win-win model with its partners, Khmara said. "Every euro invested in Ukraine’s defense is an investment in European security," he said.

articles.title: What a new Black Sea grain crisis means for the Middle East
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
What a new Black Sea grain crisis means for the Middle East
Ukrainian drones struck Russian cargo ships carrying stolen Ukrainian grain in the Sea of Azov in April.
Since then, drone attacks by both sides have intensified in the Black Sea region, continuing throughout the summer months.
"For Ukraine, targeting Russia’s oil revenues - and particularly the so-called shadow fleet that enables Moscow to circumvent sanctions - is an important part of increasing the economic cost of the war and degrading Russia’s ability to finance and sustain its military operations," Dr Yevgeniya Gaber, a nonresident senior fellow at the Atlantic Council’s Turkey Program, told The New Arab.
In August, two Turkish-owned civilian ships, the Yaşar and the Nadezhda, were struck by drones after departing from the Russian port of Novorossiysk. In response, Turkey’s Foreign Ministry called for the safe passage of commercial shipping through the Black Sea.
“Russia has fewer sea drones, but it is using both planes and drones to track the Ukrainian navy. For Russia, the Black Sea is now mainly used to strike southern Ukraine and protect their own commercial shipping, since their fleet is now hidden in ports,” Clément Molin, an open-source analyst following the Ukraine conflict, told The New Arab.
“Ukraine’s UAVs are being constantly used to track Russian ships, and more than 200 commercial ships have been targeted, mainly from [Russia’s] ghost fleet,” he said. “Ukraine has barely any navy but managed to create a new dimension of the war at sea with drones.”
No ceasefire in sight
On 13 August, Ukrainian drones hit the Russian port facility of Novorossiysk, damaging two grain export terminals. It wasn’t long before Russia carried out a wave of strikes in Ukraine’s Odesa Oblast, hitting food storage infrastructure.
“Russian forces have targeted Ukrainian ports, grain terminals, silos and export infrastructure throughout the war. What has changed is the scale and intensity of the pressure, including more attacks on civilian commercial vessels, warehouses and food-related infrastructure,” Gaber said.
“The consequences are particularly serious for agricultural exports and, therefore, for food security well beyond Ukraine. Between 1 and 26 August, Ukraine exported only 822,000 tonnes of grain - around 21 percent of what it could normally have exported with functioning logistics," she added.
"Total agricultural exports, including grain, oilseeds, oils and meals, amounted to approximately 1.4 million tonnes, only around one-third of Ukraine’s potential export capacity during this period, according to the Ukrainian government."
On 27 August, The Wall Street Journal reported that wheat prices had reached a three-year high as the Black Sea fighting disrupted grain exports, with Odesa and Novorossiysk losing export capacity.
In late August, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said that Russia was not ready for a ceasefire on grain shipments in the Black Sea. Moscow reportedly sought to include an end to attacks on Russian energy infrastructure in the agreement.
The Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy infrastructure have been a key way for Kyiv to bring the war back home to Russia after four and a half years of the full-scale invasion.
“The problem is not limited to attacks on ships themselves. Russia is targeting the infrastructure that makes maritime trade possible: ports, grain silos, warehouses, railway connections and other logistical nodes,” Gaber told The New Arab.
“In July alone, Russia carried out 67 attacks on Ukrainian seaport infrastructure, 35 attacks on civilian vessels in ports, and 22 attacks on vessels operating through the Ukrainian maritime corridor.”
The attacks come as both Russia and Ukraine are in peak harvest season, and the grain will go to waste unless it is exported soon. Major commercial shipping firms are suspending operations due to the threat of drones in the Black Sea.
“This creates longer-term economic damage as well. Ukrainian farmers lose revenue from exports and face higher logistical costs, reducing the capital available to invest in the next planting season,” Gaber said.
Diplomatic tensions
The Turkish Foreign Ministry warned that the attacks could have “multifaceted negative repercussions”, including for food security.
“We therefore reiterate our call to all relevant actors, particularly the warring parties, to urgently implement concrete measures to ensure the safety of navigation in the Black Sea.”
The collapse of the Black Sea Grain Initiative, which Turkey had helped facilitate, effectively ended in the summer of 2023. However, Ukraine and Russia were still able to ship their agricultural products to the international market by staying close to the coastlines.
To mitigate any diplomatic blowback, Scott Lucas, Professor of International Politics at University College Dublin’s Clinton Institute, told The New Arab that Ukraine could signal that “we don’t want to be in this situation…of having to counter-attack against the Russian vessels in the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea. The Russians put us in this situation”.
The politics surrounding grain shipments from the Black Sea to the Middle East have become an increasingly sensitive issue. The Ukrainian Foreign Ministry noted that stolen grain exported by Russia was reaching Turkey, Egypt, and Algeria.
In April, Ukraine and Israel exchanged accusations over a Russian shadow fleet vessel that arrived in Israel carrying grain from the occupied Ukrainian territories.
“Diplomatically, Ukraine has limited means to stop these attacks as long as Russia is unwilling to respond to calls for de-escalation. Kyiv has repeatedly called for a ceasefire and negotiations to end the war, while Moscow has continued to intensify attacks on critical infrastructure," Gaber said.
"This is why Ukraine argues that diplomacy has to be backed by greater economic, political and military pressure on Russia. Middle Eastern countries also have an interest in making this message clear.”
Russian attacks on Ukrainian ports and commercial shipping are not simply a bilateral Russian-Ukrainian issue, she said, as they directly affect the reliability and cost of food imports and therefore regional food security.
Syria and Egypt's food security
Over 90 percent of Ukraine’s agricultural exports are shipped through seaports, with countries in the Middle East especially vulnerable to prolonged disruptions in the global food supplies. Many have taken steps to mitigate these risks. In the spring, for example, Egypt reached a deal to receive grain shipments from Russia.
“In the case of Egypt, [it depends on] how much backstop they have from the Gulf States. Do they have alternative sources for supply?” Lucas told The New Arab.
Roughly 80 percent of Egypt’s wheat imports came from Black Sea ports in the first half of 2026.
The Emirati company Al Dahra Agriculture Trading and Egypt’s General Authority for Supply Commodities recently signed a five-year, $500 million wheat supply agreement. Egypt’s government has also imposed price controls on unsubsidised bread since March. In mid-August, Egypt expanded a cash subsidy scheme to cover more food items.
“Anytime you get a disruption to grain supplies, especially in countries that are already in a tenuous economic situation, you have to run it on a case-by-case basis on how well these countries prepared for such a shock. 2010 is a reminder of what can happen quickly,” Lucas added.
A poor harvest and high food prices in 2010 contributed to the uprising against the former regime of Bashar Al-Assad in Syria, which lasted nearly 14 years.
“A lot of countries don’t want Syria to fail,” Lucas said, explaining that Syria could likely rely on Turkish and US assistance since the Trump Administration is interested in maintaining Syrian stability.
Likewise, Ukraine has sought to build up its own avenues of cooperation with the new Syrian government.
“During President Zelensky’s visit to Damascus in April, food security was one of the issues discussed with President Ahmed al-Sharaa, alongside broader security and trade cooperation. Ukraine has offered to support Syria through initiatives such as Grain from Ukraine,” Gaber told The New Arab.
Syria has made progress in increasing its own domestic production of wheat. Benjamin Fève, a Senior Consultant at Karam Shaar Advisory Limited, told The New Arab that for now, Syria’s food supply was relatively safe.
“Syria had a very successful harvest. Its strategic reserves have been replenished, and Syria will be much less dependent on imports. Even if the food supplies are secure in the short term, in the medium and long term, they are not, given the huge variability in harvests and wheat production overall,” he said.
“In order to make Arabic flat bread, a staple food in Syria, you need 80 percent of soft wheat and 20 percent of hard wheat,” Fève added.
“Syria exports its surplus of hard wheat at a premium and imports less expensive soft wheat. Depending on where Syria sources its soft wheat, disruptions could cause food insecurity.”
Restarting negotiations
Changing weather patterns, conflicts, and high fuel prices are still significant concerns and could affect the food security of tens of millions of people dependent on the international grain trade. Still, the possibility of talks or a new Black Sea Grain Initiative between Russia and Ukraine appears distant.
“While Ukraine is offering additional grain supplies to countries that need them, Russia is attacking the ports, storage facilities and logistical infrastructure required to produce, store and export that grain,” Gaber told The New Arab.
The risk for the countries in the Mediterranean region and beyond remains present as long as the conflict shuts down the grain transits through the Black Sea.
“For Ukraine to play a stabilising role in food security across the Middle East and Africa, it first needs to be able to maintain production and secure access to the Black Sea. At present, Russia remains the principal obstacle to both," Gaber added.
Lucas noted that Ukraine has to find a way to get Russia to the negotiating table. “That hand was played very well by the Turks in supporting Ukraine in 2022. Can you do the same thing here?”
But while Ukraine has indicated that it wants to negotiate, Russia continues to pursue maximum demands.
The United States and the international community would have to put more pressure on Russia to reach an agreement. “If you can get that type of political strategy, you can put the onus on the Russians,” Lucas said.
Christopher Solomon is a Middle East analyst, researcher, editor, and writer based in the Washington, DC area. He is the author of the book In Search of Greater Syria (Bloomsbury)
Edited by Charlie Hoyle

articles.title: New US ‘precision’ missiles responsible for multiple civilian deaths in Iran – report
articles.body:
New US ‘precision’ missiles responsible for multiple civilian deaths in Iran – report
The US killed multiple civilians in southern Iran using new “precision” missiles with a wide damage radius, conflict monitoring group Airwars has found. Tehran has repeatedly accused Washington of war crimes since the US and Israel launched a war on Iran which has killed up to 3,000 civilians.
In an investigation published on Monday, the London-based watchdog examined three February 28 strikes in the city of Lamerd that killed at least 21 civilians, including seven children. It concluded that the weapons used were likely Lockheed Martin’s Precision Strike Missiles (PrSM), which made their combat debut during the opening phase of the US-Israeli war on Iran.
The PrSM is designed to explode above the ground, spraying tens of thousands of dense tungsten pellets in all directions rather than relying primarily on the blast itself.
Airwars found that civilians were killed at least 50 meters from the estimated detonation points, while damage extended as far as 150 meters. The three missiles exploded over two residential neighborhoods and a sports center.
Among those killed was a two-year-old girl struck while playing outside her home around 50 meters from one blast. Another strike over a sports hall killed seven civilians, most of them children.
No military personnel were reported killed, and Airwars found no evidence that military infrastructure had been hit. A nearby Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps compound appeared undamaged.
The Associated Press separately reviewed the evidence and consulted six weapons experts, including two former military officials, who also assessed that PrSMs were responsible for the strikes.
“You would be hard-pressed to find a reason to use the PrSM in a densely populated area,” former US Army adviser Michael Meier told AP.
US Central Command has acknowledged deploying PrSMs against Iran, describing their use as a “historic first,” but has denied firing any weapons at Lamerd. It has instead suggested that an Iranian cruise missile was to blame, although weapons experts cited by AP and Airwars disputed that assessment.
The PrSM had only recently completed its prototype phase and had not completed operational testing before its combat debut in Iran. A US Army official later said a deployed unit exhausted its entire stock of the missiles early in the war. Washington has since committed billions of dollars to expanding production.
Tehran has repeatedly accused Washington of war crimes over strikes on civilian areas. The Lamerd attack came on the same day as the US bombing of an elementary school in Minab, which killed 175 people, most of them children.
The Airwars findings come as direct US-Iran hostilities resumed over the weekend after a month-long lull. Washington struck Iran’s Larak Island on Sunday, prompting Tehran to launch missiles and drones at US military facilities in Jordan.
US President Donald Trump has since threatened another round of attacks, saying Washington would “hit Iran hard.”

articles.title: Russian Church installs Soviet military veteran to lead occupation-created diocese in Kherson Oblast
articles.body:
The head of the Moscow-based Russian Orthodox Church, Patriarch Kirill, personally consecrated Igor Pashentsev as bishop of Skadovsk and Oleshky after occupation authorities appointed him to lead the Skadovsk diocese, the Ukrainian outlet IPC-South reported, citing Russian sources.
The appointment advances the Russian church’s incorporation of occupied Ukrainian parishes into a Moscow-controlled structure created after Russia seized the area. Pashentsev will oversee churches across five occupied Kherson districts through a diocese IPC-South describes as operating illegally on Ukrainian territory.
Ukraine banned the Moscow-based Russian Orthodox Church from operating in the country in 2024 and established a court process for suspending Ukrainian religious groups that fail to sever Russian control. The measure targets Russian control, not Orthodox Christianity.
IPC-South says Pashentsev graduated from a Soviet military command school of chemical defense and served in the Soviet Defense Ministry’s 12th Main Directorate from 1981 to 1992. The Federation of American Scientists says the directorate stored, maintained, transported, and secured the Soviet Union's nuclear arsenal, but public records do not identify his duties there.
Ordained in 1993, Pashentsev completed the Moscow Theological Seminary in 1998, later led a Tambov diocesan office for relations with the armed forces and detention facilities, and served in the Barysh diocese. Known in the church as Joseph, he held the rank of archimandrite—a senior Orthodox monk—before his consecration.
During a Dormition liturgy—a major Orthodox feast honoring the Virgin Mary—Kirill gave Pashentsev an episcopal staff symbolizing a bishop’s authority and delivered instructions before his ministry began, Russian church accounts relayed by IPC-South said.
The Russian Orthodox Church created the Skadovsk diocese—a regional church administration—on 27 December 2023 after the occupation made it impossible for the existing Kherson diocese to oversee parishes on the Dnipro’s left bank. The new body incorporated parishes across the occupied Oleshky, Hola Prystan, Kalanchak, Skadovsk, and Chaplynka districts. IPC-South describes it as operating illegally on Ukrainian territory.
Russia weaponizes church control while suppressing other faiths
Pashentsev’s appointment is part of the Moscow Patriarchate’s wider effort to control religious life in occupied Ukraine. Religious communities that reject Kremlin authority face interrogations, threats, closures, and confiscation.
Ukraine’s Security Service has accused church structures of recruiting and training mercenaries for Russia’s military. The Institute for the Study of War, a US-based think tank, says occupation authorities also arbitrarily detain clergy and destroy places of worship while suppressing independent Ukrainian religious identity.

articles.title: Japan Modifies ASM-3 Anti-Ship Missile to Destroy Air Targets
articles.body:
Japan is likely to modify the ASM-3 supersonic anti-ship missile into an ultra-long-range air-to-air missile for intercepting aerial targets.
The Japanese Ministry of Defense announced its plans to procure air-to-air missiles for 2027 in a budget document.
Converting the anti-ship missile into an air-to-air interceptor is intended to create a means of countering long-range enemy aircraft — such as long-range radar detection aircraft, aerial refueling tankers, and strategic bombers.
Thanks to its ramjet engine, the upgraded air-to-air version of the missile will be capable of reaching an estimated range of 400-600 km.
Mitsubishi Heavy Industries began developing the basic ASM-3 anti-ship missile in 2003 to replace the obsolete ASM-1 and ASM-2.
The development program lasted more than a decade, and in 2017, test launches from the decommissioned destroyer Shirane confirmed the new weapon’s performance characteristics.
However, the initial version of the missile, with a range of 200 km, never entered serial production because the Japanese Ministry of Defense deemed this range insufficient to penetrate modern naval air defense systems and demanded upgrades.
As a result, an improved version, the ASM-3A, was developed; by reducing weight and optimizing fuel consumption, its range was increased to 400 km or more.
In its basic anti-ship version, the ASM-3 is 6 meters long, has a body diameter of 350 mm, and a total launch weight of approximately 940 kg.
The missile is equipped with a penetrating high-explosive warhead weighing about 150 kg, designed to engage medium- and large-displacement surface ships.
The primary platform for the ASM-3 family of missiles is the Japan Air Self-Defense Force’s F-2 fighter jets.
It should be noted that, starting in 2027, the Japanese Ministry of Defense will begin the procurement process for AARGM-ER anti-radar missiles to counter Chinese air defense systems.

articles.title: Germany blames Moscow for Leipzig drone attack, closes consulate and cultural center among sweeping diplomatic measures
articles.body:
An explosives-laden drone aimed at a Ukrainian cargo aircraft at Leipzig/Halle Airport was part of a Russian state operation, Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said on 1 September.
Germany has moved from suspecting foreign sabotage to formally blaming Russia for the Leipzig attack. The finding has prompted diplomatic and security measures against Moscow while the criminal investigation continues.
Police investigations, the attack pattern, and intelligence findings established Russian responsibility, Dobrindt said. The drones' configuration, components, explosives, and detonation systems resembled those used in other Russian hybrid operations—covert sabotage and disruption below the threshold of open war—and in Russia's war against Ukraine, Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said.
The first drone, carrying explosives, was found near a Ukrainian cargo aircraft on the evening of 4 August and defused. Investigators believe a DHL freighter may have collided with a second drone while aborting its landing after the airport closed; that drone was never recovered. A third drone was found on 14 August in a field at Kabelsketal, where investigators subsequently discovered roughly 50 grams of suspected military explosive.
Leipzig/Halle is an international freight hub used by Ukrainian Antonov aircraft and NATO's strategic airlift program, through which allies charter heavy transport aircraft to move oversized military cargo.
Berlin will close the Bonn consulate on 18 September, end the operating agreement for the Russian House, a Moscow-backed cultural center, tighten entry controls for Russian nationals, seek to add more targets to EU sanctions lists, and pressure Russia's shadow fleet—opaquely owned tankers used to move Russian oil outside Western restrictions. Wadephul also summoned the Russian ambassador. Russia's Berlin embassy will remain open.
Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova told Interfax that Moscow would respond to Germany's “anti-Russian action,” without specifying how.
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said the alliance stood in full solidarity with Germany, and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen described Berlin's measures as a strong response.
Dobrindt said Germany expects further Russian hybrid attacks. The Leipzig incident follows a widening campaign of suspected Russian sabotage across Europe, including a 2024 incendiary-device attack at the same airport that Western security officials suspected Russian intelligence organized.
How the Leipzig attack unfolded
Euromaidan Press reported on 12 August, citing Die Zeit, that footage showed an explosives-laden quadcopter striking the wing of a parked Ukrainian Antonov An-124 before falling without detonating. The article also noted that a US Defense Department official told CNN that Washington assessed the drone belonged to Russian intelligence.
On 25 August, EP reported, citing Tagesschau’s NDR/WDR/SZ investigation, that investigators had expanded the case to three drones and found the third with suspected military explosive nearby in Kabelsketal, 10 days after the original attempt.

articles.title: Russian mobilisation and sabotage – NAF commander explains what Latvia is preparing for
articles.body:
Russia is using intimidation in an attempt to force Latvia and the West as a whole to end their support for Ukraine, Commander of the Latvian National Armed Forces (NAF) Kaspars Pudāns said when assessing Russia’s recent activities in an interview with Latvian Television’s “Rīta panorāma” programme.
A significant part of Russia’s tactics involves acts of sabotage that are easy to organise, require relatively few resources, but can have a considerable impact, Pudāns said. He also stressed that preparing defences against such hybrid activities is difficult because new methods can constantly be devised.
Asked about the reasons behind US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) Director John Ratcliffe’s visit to Moscow and whether it indicates an increased security threat to the Baltic Sea region, the NAF commander said that the United States and Ukraine share intelligence with Latvia, which is used to assess the security situation. According to Pudāns, the available intelligence does not indicate that Russia is concentrating troops near Latvia’s borders.
Mobilisation in Russia is possible, however. Pudāns estimated that it could provide the aggressor state’s military with a relatively large number of personnel, although they would be poorly trained. The NAF commander expects that these troops would primarily be “thrown” into the fighting in Ukraine.
Meanwhile, Latvia’s month-long comprehensive national defence exercise “Namejs” begins today. Pudāns said the Latvian Armed Forces seek to learn from experiences of warfare around the world during their exercises, including by adopting new technologies and tactics and focusing more closely on transforming capabilities into practical action.
Pudāns noted that a significant part of the large-scale autumn exercise “Namejs” will take place outside military training areas.

articles.title: Germany blames Russia for Leipzig plane sabotage attempt, expels diplomats, and restricts visas
articles.body:
Germany blames Russia for Leipzig plane sabotage attempt, expels diplomats, and restricts visas
The German government has officially blamed Russia for an attempted act of sabotage against a Ukrainian An-124 cargo plane at the Leipzig airport. Berlin’s position was presented at a news conference by Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt and Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul.
Dobrindt said the findings of the police investigation, the “characteristic features” of the incident, and intelligence reporting “clearly point to Russia’s involvement in hybrid operations that were planned, that were carried out, and that were also thwarted.”
Wadephul laid out the retaliatory measures: Germany will close Russia’s consulate general in Bonn and the Russian House in Berlin. Russia’s ambassador will be summoned to the German Foreign Ministry. German authorities will also tighten controls on the entry of Russian citizens into the country. Exactly how has not yet been specified.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, for her part, said that the EU “stands in full solidarity with Germany in the face of this attack by Russia.” She said she would take the matter up with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte, and she said the foreign ministers of EU countries would begin preparing additional sanctions.
Rutte himself said that “the evidence is clear.” “I welcome the measures announced by Germany in response,” he said. Finnish President Alexander Stubb, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk, Latvia’s Foreign Ministry, and officials from other EU countries also expressed solidarity with Berlin’s actions and a readiness to continue supporting Ukraine in its war with Russia.
Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova criticized the German government’s moves. “They made up a pretext. And Berlin itself is thoroughly tainted both by inflaming the Ukrainian conflict and by taking part in terrorist attacks against civilians,” she said. Zakharova also said the Russian House had “long been a thorn in the side” of the German authorities, and she said Russia would “respond” to the decision to close it.
Russian presidential spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Germany was “moving further down the path of escalation.” “It’s hard to comment on this, because if accusations this serious are being made, they have to be backed up by something. If I’m not mistaken, no supporting argument was presented,” Peskov told reporters.
A drone with explosives attached to it was found at the Leipzig airport overnight on August 5. The drone was next to a Ukrainian An-124 transport plane that was carrying ammunition. It later emerged that there were several drones — another was found 10 days later, west of the airport, and a third, according to media reports, may have struck the cargo plane, though no trace of that drone was ever found.

The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.
