articles.title: Ukraine’s air defenses down 138 Russian drones, three Banderol UAVs overnight
articles.body:
Ukraine’s air defenses down 138 Russian drones, three Banderol UAVs overnight
According to Ukrinform, the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported this on Telegram.
As noted, starting at 18:00 Tuesday, September 1, Russian forces launched the following at Ukraine:
- two Iskander-M ballistic missiles from temporarily occupied Crimea;
- two Kh-59/69 guided air-launched missiles from airspace over the Black Sea;
- 174 attack drones, including Shahed-type UAVs (about half of them jet-powered), S8000 Banderol loitering munitions, Gerbera UAVs, and Parodiya-type decoy drones. The launches were carried out from the vicinity of the Russian city of Oryol, as well as from the temporarily occupied areas of Hvardiiske in Crimea and Donetsk.
The main targets of the enemy attack were Odesa and Kyiv regions.
The Russian attack was repelled by Ukrainian aircraft, anti-aircraft missile forces, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire teams of the Defense Forces of Ukraine.
According to preliminary data, as of 8:30 on Wednesday, September 2, air defense had shot down or jammed three S8000 Banderol munitions and 138 drones of various types, including Shahed jet-powered drones, and Gerbera UAVs.
Hits by enemy missiles and attack UAVs were recorded at 16 locations. At four more locations, debris from downed targets fell.
The Air Force emphasized that enemy drones are still being detected in Ukrainian airspace.
As reported by Ukrinform, overnight on September 2, Russian forces struck an industrial facility in the Poltava region.

articles.title: “Russian airspace will effectively be closing”: Zelenskyy warns airlines Russian skies are no longer safe
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned airlines, insurers, and other aviation stakeholders on 1 September that Russian airspace is becoming increasingly dangerous as Ukrainian drones operate deeper inside the country.
The warning comes as Ukraine has increasingly carried out long-range drone strikes deep inside Russia, targeting military, energy, industrial, and other infrastructure. Russian authorities have repeatedly reported temporary airport closures and flight disruptions during drone attacks as part of air defense measures.
“We want to warn every airline that uses Russian airspace, every insurer, and everyone who still uses Russia’s key airports: Russian airspace is becoming completely unsafe,” Zelenskyy said.
“Russian airspace will effectively be closing”
Zelenskyy said Ukraine does not intend to threaten civilian aviation or civilian aircraft, but warned that the growing presence of drones over Russia means airlines must account for the risks.
“We in Ukraine do not want innocent lives to be lost. That is why we are warning our partners: the safe days in Russia’s skies are over,” he said.
Zelenskyy accused Russian authorities of failing to properly inform airlines about the risks, saying they have not adequately communicated the growing danger posed by drones in Russian airspace.
“Although the Russian authorities are not properly informing people about this, Russian airspace will effectively be closing,” Zelenskyy said, arguing that Russia’s war against Ukraine is making its own airspace unsafe.
Zelenskyy warned that the growing scale of Ukrainian drone operations over Russia will have to be factored into aviation risks. “There will simply be drones in Russia’s skies on a scale that has to be taken into account,” he said.
He called on foreign ambassadors in Ukraine and Russia to relay the warning to their governments, and said Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry and other institutions would provide international organizations with information about the risks to Russian airspace.
“Drone-infested skies are no place for civilian aviation,” Zelenskyy said.
Ukraine closed its skies in 2022. Russia has kept flying
The warning highlights a stark difference between the two countries. Ukraine has kept its airspace closed to civilian aviation since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
The risk is familiar to Ukraine. Russian forces have repeatedly attacked Ukrainian airports and aviation infrastructure during the full-scale invasion, making the continued operation of civilian aviation impossible.
Russia is also responsible for the 2014 downing of Malaysia Airlines Flight MH17 over occupied eastern Ukraine, which killed all 298 people aboard, showing the danger Russia’s military activities can pose to civilian aviation.
Russia, meanwhile, has continued operating major airports and regular passenger flights despite Ukrainian drones increasingly reaching deep into its territory. EASA has warned that Russian air defenses responding to Ukrainian drone and missile attacks could pose risks to civilian aircraft, including through misidentification, particularly around major airports.
Russian airports increasingly disrupted by Ukrainian drones
Russian authorities have repeatedly restricted or suspended flights at Moscow and other airports during Ukrainian drone attacks. The disruptions have generally come as Russia activates air defenses against drones targeting military, energy, industrial, and logistics infrastructure.
Russia has also moved toward broader restrictions on civilian aviation. In June, Russia imposed new restrictions on light aircraft around Moscow and neighboring regions, while regular passenger and charter flights remained exempt.
The result is a growing disruption to Russian aviation even as Moscow continues to keep its main passenger airspace open: Ukrainian drones are not being used to target civilian aircraft, but their increasing presence is making normal aviation operations more difficult and forcing Russia to restrict or suspend flights during attacks.

articles.title: Meet Sean Parnell, Pentagon's Chief Spokesperson and a Contender to Succeed Army Secretary Driscoll
articles.body:
Prior to Army Secretary Dan Driscoll submitting his resignation Monday, Chief Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell had been suggested by some close to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth as a potential replacement for the Senate-confirmed position.
The Hill reported last week that Parnell’s name was being floated, citing two unnamed sources familiar with the matter.
Asked about the reports, a senior Administration official told TIME: “Sean Parnell is 100% focused on the job he was appointed to by President Trump and Secretary Hegseth.”
News of Driscoll’s departure from the role he held for around 18 months came after months of reported tensions with Hegseth and turmoil within the department.
A person familiar with Driscoll’s resignation is quoted as telling media that for Army Secretary had recently “brought up concerns with the Administration surrounding Army transformation and readiness and Hegseth’s blocking those efforts specifically by firing the generals who were responsible.”
White House spokesperson Anna Kelly did not address the tensions and fallout when approached by TIME, but instead emphasized that the United States Army is “more powerful than ever thanks to [Driscoll’s] work alongside the Commander-in-Chief and Secretary of War.”
Driscoll’s resignation is the latest in a series of high-profile departures within the Pentagon, following the April ouster of the Army’s top uniformed leader, Gen. Randy George, and the June departure of the lead commander in Europe and Africa, Gen. Christopher Donahue.
The firing of George was reportedly a source of contention between Driscoll and Hegseth.
Driscoll openly praised George, referring to him as “an amazing, transformational leader” whom he loved and respected during an April House Appropriations Committee Hearing. Driscoll told lawmakers that after George was fired, his family drove to the former general's house and gave him a hug.
Alongside the reported tensions, Hegseth has also come under serious scrutiny for the duration and mounting cost of the Iran war, which surpassed the six-month mark last week.
“I don’t have any confidence in him anymore. I think he’s all over the place—he’s accelerating the retirement or forcing out some of the most distinguished leaders in the DOD that we have,” Republican Sen. Thom Tillis of North Carolina said in July.
Meanwhile, under Parnell, the Department of Defense has imposed various restrictions limiting journalists’ access in the Pentagon.
In an unprecedented move in June, the department designated its press office a classified area.
“The Pentagon Press Office has been redesignated as a Sensitive Compartmented Information Facility due to speechwriters from the Office of the Secretary of War sharing the facility,” said deputy Pentagon press secretary Joel Valdez. “As a result, journalists will no longer be permitted to enter the office space. There’s nothing controversial about that.”
Now, with talk turning to who may replace Driscoll in the pivotal role of Army Secretary, Parnell's name continues to be floated. Notably, whoever is selected would need to be confirmed for the position by the Senate.
Here’s what to know about Parnell's military record, his past controversies, and more.
Parnell is an Afghanistan veteran who penned a memoir on his experience
Parnell arrived in Afghanistan in 2006 and during his 16-month deployment was awarded two Bronze stars and the Purple Heart. He was deployed alongside his platoon, nicknamed the Outlaws.
He returned home with shrapnel in his leg and a brain injury that had left him with vision problems.
Following retirement on medical grounds, he penned a 2012 war story memoir titled Outlaw Platoon, in partnership with author John R. Bruning, detailing his experiences in the region.
Parnell went on to become a senior advisor for the Concerned Veterans of America and is credited with playing a key role in the passage of the Mission Act in 2018 under President Donald Trump, with the goal of delivering care and support for U.S. veterans.
Parnell previously criticized Trump before becoming a staunch supporter
Parnell backed now-Secretary of State Marco Rubio for the 2016 Republican presidential nomination where he faced off against Trump, who went on to win both the nomination and presidency.
According to Parnell, his support for Rubio, who at the time was a Senator in Florida, was cemented by his vocal backing of matters related to Veterans Affairs (VA).
“There are lots of strong options. But if fixing the VA, rebuilding our military, and doing right by our veterans is a top priority for you, then Senator Rubio should be your first and only choice,” Parnell said in a campaign press release.
In a separate interview, he described Rubio as a "unifying voice” who the country “desperately needs” and labeled him “my guy.”
By contrast, Parnell had called out Trump in 2015, referring to his criticism of the late Republican Sen. John McCain, a prisoner of war, as “the height of arrogance,” arguing that Trump had “no clue what our Vietnam POWs endured.”
However, Parnell had a change of heart once Trump took office, stating in a 2019 interview that the President had earned his respect “because he forces us to talk about issues. Political correctness doesn’t allow us to talk about them.”
At the 2020 Republican National Convention, Parnell further praised Trump, insisting he had “unleashed the economic might of this nation like no other President in our history.”
Parnell suspended his campaign for Senate amid abuse allegations
Parnell, after running unsuccessfully for the House in 2020, went on to launch a bid as the GOP Senate candidate in Pennsylvania. He suspended his Trump-backed campaign in November 2021, after losing a fight for custody of his children to his then-estranged wife, who had accused him in court of abuse.
Laurie Snell had alleged that Parnell choked her and injured their children. Parnell vehemently denied the claims.
Snell also testified in court that Parnell had been unfaithful.
Following Trump’s announcement in February 2025 that Parnell was tapped to become chief spokesperson for the Pentagon, some media coverage saw the abuse allegations revisited.
If Parnell were put forward for a Senate-confirmed position in the future, the historical allegations could be brought up in his confirmation hearing.

articles.title: Petraeus urges UK to lead NATO military overhaul
articles.body:
Britain should become the first major Western country to reorganise its defence institutions around lessons emerging from the war in Ukraine and use that experience to help drive a wider transformation of NATO, General David Petraeus has told the House of Lords.
Delivering the Lord Speaker’s Lecture on 1 September, the retired four-star US Army general argued that the nature of warfare is changing quickly enough to require more than conventional modernisation programmes. Petraeus said Britain’s early recognition of the threat posed by Russia and its sustained support for Ukraine had demonstrated what he described as strategic clarity, giving the UK an opportunity to take a leading role in reshaping how Western militaries organise, train and equip themselves.
Petraeus said: “Britain now has an opportunity to demonstrate that same quality once again. Just as it helped lead the Alliance in recognizing the strategic implications of Russia’s aggression, it can now help lead the Alliance in recognizing the revolutionary implications that Ukraine holds for the future of warfare itself.”
He described Ukraine as “the defining military laboratory of the twenty-first century”, arguing that its importance lies not simply in individual technologies but in the way sensors, software, unmanned systems, electronic warfare, precision weapons and industrial adaptation are being combined. Petraeus said information is being collected, analysed and acted upon at unprecedented speed, while commercial innovation is moving directly onto the battlefield and software, hardware and operational methods are being adapted while fighting is underway.
He told peers: “Much of the discussion has understandably focused on individual technologies—unmanned systems, artificial intelligence, electronic warfare, cyber capabilities, precision strike, battle management systems, and others. Each matters. But the principal lesson is larger: the very concept of warfare is changing.”
Petraeus said Britain’s Strategic Defence Review and Defence Investment Plan showed an appreciation of the changes taking place, pointing to their focus on unmanned and autonomous systems, artificial intelligence, electronic warfare, industrial resilience, procurement reform and accelerated innovation. He cautioned, however, that those measures should be regarded as the beginning of a larger transformation rather than its completion.
He said: “The most consequential military transformations seldom begin with new equipment. They begin with new ideas. Additional resources will clearly be required in important areas, but the greatest obstacle to transformation is rarely money alone. More often, it is the difficulty of questioning long-established assumptions and overcoming institutional inertia.”
Petraeus continued: “And I believe the United Kingdom is unusually well positioned to do precisely that. Not because Britain is free of serious economic, fiscal, or political constraints—it plainly is not—but because, as we have seen in Ukraine, Britain has demonstrated the capacity to recognize strategic reality early and act decisively.”
He added: “That now presents Britain with another opportunity: to become the first major Western nation to organize its defence institutions around the new concept of warfare that Ukraine has been pioneering—and, in doing so, to help lead the transformation of NATO itself.”
Petraeus said NATO itself would also have to change, including the operational headquarters responsible for commanding Alliance forces. He argued that NATO needs a common understanding of the emerging concept of warfare before individual nations can reorganise their forces effectively around it.
He said: “NATO must now summon that spirit again, with far greater urgency, by developing a common understanding of the new concept of warfare and the institutional transformation that must follow.” Referring to NATO’s operational headquarters, he added: “Those headquarters will have to think, organize, and operate differently if they are to lead this transformation successfully.”
Petraeus said the process could not be limited to another incremental modernisation programme, calling instead for changes to force structure, professional military education, training, procurement, personnel policy, industrial engagement and the way battlefield lessons are identified and incorporated.
He said: “The question is not whether this transformation will occur. It is already underway—most visibly in Ukraine, but also in Russia, the Middle East, and elsewhere. The question is whether we will lead it—or be forced to catch up to those who do.”

articles.title: NATO and EU press Spain and Greece to transfer interceptors for Patriot systems to Ukraine, Bloomberg says
articles.body:
NATO and EU press Spain and Greece to transfer interceptors for Patriot systems to Ukraine, Bloomberg says
NATO and the European Union are pressuring Spain and Greece, which hold some of the largest stocks of missiles for Patriot air defence systems, to sell interceptors to Norway so that Norway can transfer them to Ukraine.
Source: Bloomberg, as reported by European Pravda
Details: The requests to Spain and Greece were made this summer and include the possibility of Norway purchasing the missiles and then transferring them to Ukraine, according to Bloomberg sources.
The issue is also expected to be discussed at today's meeting of EU defence and foreign ministers in Ireland, which will also be attended by representatives of Ukraine, the United Kingdom, Norway, Iceland and Switzerland.
Among Ukraine's partners, Spain and Greece hold some of the largest stocks of missiles for Patriots, some of which are also approaching the end of their shelf life.
Greece was one of the first countries to send ammunition to Ukraine after Russia's full-scale invasion. However, it has refused to provide Patriot missiles, citing the need to retain them for its own defence amid its long-standing rivalry with Türkiye.
Earlier this year, Spain said it would provide Ukraine with €1 billion in military aid in 2026.
Some air defence systems are still expected to reach Ukraine in the coming months under the PURL programme, which allows NATO allies to purchase US weapons for Kyiv.
However, the EU is considering whether to allow Ukraine to purchase more Patriot missiles using a €90 billion loan for Kyiv. Countries such as France and Italy want the funds to be directed towards the SAMP/T system, while others fear this could create unnecessary difficulties for Kyiv.
EU member states will vote on the issue on 7 September.
Background:
- On 1 September, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said EU member states should provide Ukraine with the interceptor missiles it needs, including those whose shelf life is about to expire.
- UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said European leaders are considering holding another meeting of the Coalition of the Willing in the United States, on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in September, to discuss supplying Ukraine with Patriot interceptor missiles.
- Earlier, Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen said the Netherlands, which operates Patriot air defence systems and their interceptor missiles, had given Ukraine everything it could from its stocks.
	
Support Ukrainska Pravda on Patreon to help us keep reporting!

articles.title: Budanov on Sept 1 shelling: Ukrainian drones, missiles will rule Russian skies
articles.body:
The Kremlin consciously chose the path of escalation, turning September 1 into another day of terror against Ukrainian children and civilian infrastructure, stated Head of the Office of the President of Ukraine Kyrylo Budanov.
"Guided by the right to self-defense, Ukraine will deliver a harsh and proportionate response. I fully support the decision of President and Supreme Commander-in-Chief Volodymyr Zelenskyy. Russian skies are no longer safe. This is a new reality about which we officially warn international airlines, insurers, and partners. Our long-range assets will systematically strike military targets on enemy territory," he wrote on Telegram on Tuesday evening.
He stated that Ukraine respects the diplomatic efforts of partners and is ready to provide targeted pauses exclusively for real steps toward ending the war. "But as long as aggression continues, Ukrainian drones and missiles will rule the Russian skies," Budanov emphasized.

articles.title: G20 backs final statement despite Russia tensions, China dissent
articles.body:
G20 backs final statement despite Russia tensions, China dissent
G20 finance leaders wrapped up two days of talks in Ashville, North Carolina, on Tuesday with broad backing for a final statement, despite tensions over Russia’s participation and divisions with China. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Moscow’s presence had not disrupted discussions, as ministers also grappled with the war in the Middle East, tariffs, global trade imbalances and continued support for Ukraine.
G20 finance leaders closed their two-day gathering on Tuesday with a statement that all but China backed in full, as Washington insisted that the presence of a Russian minister had no effect on talks.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the fact that nearly all participants agreed to the chair's final statement suggested "there has been no impact" from Russia's attendance.
Ukraine's European allies had expressed frustration after Russian Finance Minister Anton Siluanov was welcomed at the US-hosted meetings in Asheville, North Carolina.
The broiling Middle East war and US President Donald Trump's tariffs also loomed over the gathering.
Read moreWhat to know about Trump's Canada tariffs and the escalating trade war
The chair's statement called for "free, safe, and predictable navigation through the Strait of Hormuz", though China dissented from that section.
The key waterway has been largely blocked by Tehran since the war began in late February with US-Israeli strikes on Iran.
A traditional "family photo" of G20 participants was taken Monday without Siluanov, following European officials' protests.
An EU spokesperson said representatives were only given short notice of Siluanov's attendance.
"It created discomfort, no doubt about that," Canadian Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne told AFP on Tuesday when asked if Siluanov's appearance had a bearing on discussions.
EU economy chief Valdis Dombrovskis told reporters that it was not the time to "normalize" Russia's presence at such events.
He said Moscow's inclusion entails discussing sensitive economic matters with representatives of a government that is "waging an aggressive war" and "killing civilians on a daily basis" in its conflict in Ukraine.
But Bessent countered at a press conference: "I know that some Europeans had a sour taste, but I think it's very important to engage."
"And I will point out that the finance minister who I met with is unsanctioned," he added of Siluanov.
The tension also comes as Germany blamed Russia on Tuesday for an attempted "hybrid attack" involving a drone at a strategic German airport last month, and unveiled diplomatic counter-measures.
Read moreUS Treasury bars certain journalists from G20 meeting in North Carolina
The United States holds the rotating G20 presidency, and Washington was also pushing this week to rally support from partners on Iran sanctions and reducing trade imbalances.
Asked if he also pressured Russia to cut its support for Iran, Bessent earlier told reporters that "many conversations are best done privately".
'Persistent imbalances'
Another topic China took issue with was a declaration that "excessive and persistent imbalances pose risks and can generate economic distortions".
This echoes criticism of excess industrial capacity in the world's second biggest economy, which critics say create unfair competition and drive prices lower.
"We need to discuss and look at collective action, because global imbalances as they are today are not sustainable," Champagne said. "Everyone has to be at that table."
The G20 comprises 19 nations plus the EU and the African Union, and was established in the wake of the 1997-1998 Asian financial crisis to boost global economic and financial stability.
The G20 finance talks also set the stage for a leaders' summit that Trump will convene in December in Miami.
Another issue that came up was support for Ukraine, which was discussed as well on the sidelines of the meeting by the narrower Group of Seven advanced economies.
Moscow has intensified its strikes on Kyiv this summer. US-brokered talks remain frozen while the Kremlin has maintained its maximalist demands to end the war.
German Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil said Tuesday that there has been an "increase in brutal rocket attacks on the civilian population".
"This all has to come to an end," he added.
Klingbeil said that he and other European ministers "made our position on Ukraine absolutely clear". As G7 leaders met late Monday, he said Ukraine's finance minister joined remotely for talks on support for Kyiv.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

articles.title: Germany blames Russia for drone incursion, announces retaliatory measures
articles.body:
Alexander Dobrindt arrives for the first day of a two-day retreat of the federal government coalition cabinet at Schloss Neuhardenberg on Aug. 25, 2026. | Sean Gallup/Getty Images
BERLIN — Berlin squarely placed the blame for an incursion of explosive-laden drones last month on the Kremlin and announced a raft of retaliatory diplomatic measures.
The incident and Germany’s response mark a new chapter in Europe’s fraught relationship with Russia, with EU leaders lining up to support Berlin.
“Russia’s leadership is treating our country with open hostility,” German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said in Berlin on Tuesday. “With the attempted attack in Leipzig, the Russian leadership has, in fact, deliberately chosen to further and significantly damage our already severely strained bilateral relationship.”
Standing alongside Wadephul, German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said the German government determined Russia is responsible even as investigations remain ongoing.
“The attack involved tools such as the drone configuration, various components, explosives and cyber technology that we recognize from other Russian hybrid operations and its war against Ukraine,” Dobrindt said.
Wadephul announced a series of domestic countermeasures, including the closure of Russia’s Bonn consulate on September 18, stricter entry controls for Russian nationals and the termination of the agreement governing the Russian House in central Berlin — a cultural institution suspected of serving as a hub for espionage operations and whose Russian operator is under EU sanctions.
Germany will also propose new EU sanctions targeting Russian individuals connected to hybrid attacks, while pushing to increase measures targeting Russia’s shadow fleet, Wadephul said. A senior German government official also said Berlin would advocate that the EU reduce the number of 90-day tourist visas issued to Russian citizens and restrict the freedom of movement of Russian diplomats.
The announcement comes as EU foreign ministers are set to meet in Ireland on Tuesday night and Wednesday. “The matter, including additional sanctions, will be prepared by Foreign Ministers at their upcoming meeting,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen wrote on social media after the German announcement.
Advertisement
Given the significance of the announcement, it was not immediately clear why German Chancellor Friedrich Merz didn’t make it himself. But the ratcheting up of tensions with Moscow comes at a sensitive political moment ahead of a state election on Sunday in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, where the Russia-friendly Alternative for Germany (AfD) is far ahead in polls.
Dobrindt said the attack was carried out by low-level agents, adding that the technology found at the scene indicated “a high degree of technical expertise and considerable organizational effort in the planning and execution of the attack.”
He also suggested German officials expect more such attacks to follow.
“We assume that Germany is the target of further hybrid attacks by Russia. It can also be assumed that there is a willingness to cause even greater damage through hybrid attacks,” he said. “Thankfully, in Leipzig, this did not happen as had apparently been planned.”
European leaders on Tuesday expressed support for Germany’s retaliatory measures.
Advertisement
“If the gravity of the events is confirmed”, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot told reporters earlier on Tuesday morning, “there will inevitably be consequences, particularly regarding the sanctions that might be imposed on Russia.”
“NATO stands in full solidarity with Germany after the Russian hybrid attack in Leipzig,” the alliance’s secretary-general Mark Rutte said on X. “I welcome the measures announced by Germany in response,” he added.
This article has been updated. Hans von der Burchard contributed to this report.

articles.title: ‘No negotiations with terrorists’ – Putin on Zelensky’s threat to civil aviation (VIDEO)
articles.body:
‘No negotiations with terrorists’ – Putin on Zelensky’s threat to civil aviation (VIDEO)
Russian President Vladimir Putin has said there can be no “negotiations with terrorists,” responding to Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky’s threat against civilian aviation over Russia.
Zelensky warned foreign airlines, insurers and governments on Tuesday that Ukraine’s expanding long-range drone campaign would increasingly endanger civilian flights over the country.
“The safe days in Russia’s skies are over,” Zelensky said.
Putin was asked to respond to the remarks at a press conference on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit in Kyrgyzstan on Tuesday.
“If this was said out loud, then it is simply a move toward state terrorism,” Putin said. 
“I would also draw attention to the fact that they are asking us to resume negotiations; they are asking for face-to-face meetings,” he added.
There are no negotiations with terrorists.
Putin added that Moscow would find a way to respond if Kiev’s threats resulted in any tragedies.
“Let no one doubt that,” he said.
Ukraine has stepped up long-range drone strikes on Russia in recent months, repeatedly grounding flights and forcing prolonged disruptions at airports as air defenses respond to incoming threats.
Kiev’s campaign has also systematically targeted civilian infrastructure, including Russian e-commerce warehouses, prompting Moscow to retaliate with drone and missile strikes on Ukraine’s military-linked infrastructure and shipping facilities. The strikes have effectively crippled Ukraine’s main export route through its Black Sea ports.
In July, Putin warned that Ukrainian strikes on Russian territory would be met with a far stronger response.
“We will respond in kind – only several times more powerfully,” he said.

articles.title: Russian oligarch Yevtushenkov and relatives of high-profile officials profit from construction in occupied territories of Ukraine
articles.body:
Russian authorities have created extremely favorable conditions for developers in the occupied territories of Ukraine, offering tax breaks, nearly free land leases, and loans at 3% annual interest. By August 2026, more than 1.3 million square meters of mortgage-financed housing had been under construction in the Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine’s Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia, and Kherson regions.
Among those profiting from this construction are entities linked to oligarch Vladimir Yevtushenkov, the family of State Duma deputy Sergei Kolunov, major regional businessmen, and a company connected to the brother of a Presidential Executive Office staffer. These individuals and entities are featured in an investigation by the independent outlet Vot Tak, which examined developers’ project declarations and financial statements.
Yevtushenkov’s AFK Sistema holds the controlling stake in construction company Etalon Group, which in turn is closely tied to the Republican Construction Company (RSK). According to Vot Tak’s calculations, Russian state-controlled VTB bank has already allocated RSK more than 26.5 billion rubles ($305.5 million) for construction in occupied Mariupol, Luhansk, and Henichesk, meaning that entities linked to Yevtushenkov are among the largest recipients of mortgage construction loans in the regions seized by Russia. In addition, employees of Yevtushenko’s AFK Sistema can buy RSK apartments through a special program offering a discount and interest-free installment plan.
RSK and Etalon tend to downplay the ties between them. In June 2025, the Russian-appointed head of the so-called “Luhansk People’s Republic,” Leonid Pasechnik, announced the signing of an agreement with RSK, describing the company as part of the Etalon group. Eight minutes later, the mention of Etalon disappeared from the post, and Russian state media later removed the reference as well.
Vot Tak interprets this caution as part of an effort to shield Yevtushenko from Western sanctions. In May 2025, the businessman filed a lawsuit with the EU court seeking to have the restrictions on his business activities lifted — and publicly available information linking his entities to construction in Russian-occupied Ukraine would seriously hinder his chances for success.
Another major developer in Mariupol is the Sadovoye Koltso group, founded by Sergei Kolunov, a State Duma deputy from the ruling United Russia party. Before being elected to parliament, Kolunov transferred his stake in the firm to his wife, and then to his son, Ilya, who now heads the company.
Sadovoye Koltso entered Mariupol in October 2025 and is now building more than 80,000 square meters of housing there — more than any other company. VTB has offered the group a credit line of over 12 billion rubles ($138 million). Its projects include the Dom u Morya residential complex on the Sea of Azov coast and Sadovye Kvartaly near the site of the destroyed Azovstal plant.
Kolunov, meanwhile, serves as deputy chairman of the State Duma Committee on Construction, Housing, and Utilities. As Vot Tak notes, the member of parliament must have been apprised of numerous complaints from Mariupol residents who found themselves unable to obtain equivalent housing after their previous apartment buildings were rendered uninhabitable by the Russian military. Anti-corruption expert Ilya Shumanov called the situation a potential conflict of interest: Kolunov takes part in shaping policy for an industry in which his family’s business operates.
The largest recipient of loans specifically in Mariupol is SU-2007, a company owned by Viktor Budarin, a banker from Russia’s southern Kuban region. According to the investigation, his company received roughly 19 billion rubles ($219 million) for the construction of more than 170,000 square meters of housing.
YugStroyInvest, owned by Rostov developer Yuri Ivanov, ranks second with about 18.4 billion rubles ($212 million) in loans and nearly 150,000 square meters of housing under construction. In the summer of 2026, Ivanov signed an agreement to build housing and infrastructure in occupied Donetsk and Makiivka, with a stated investment volume of more than 100 billion rubles ($1.15 billion).
The top recipients of loans in Mariupol also include the Yevtushenkov-linked RSK and Voronezh-based Proekt Invest, owned by Nikolai Stupin. Other major players include Maxim Radchenko’s Antares, Tatyana Antipova’s Transyuzhstroy, Artem and Natalya Martynov’s Evolyutsiya, Andrei Slashchuk’s Vertikal Yug, and Mirastroy, linked to one of Moscow’s biggest developers, Pavel Te.
In total, according to Vot Tak’s calculations, Russian state banks have allocated at least 61.4 billion rubles ($707.8 million) for the construction of apartments in Mariupol. The outlet estimates developers’ potential combined profit from these projects at more than 18 billion rubles ($207.5 million).
Even more housing is currently being built in the occupied part of Luhansk Region — almost 600,000 square meters. The largest recipient of loans there is Vyacheslav Semenkov’s Zhilstroyinvest, which has been allocated around 18.9 billion rubles ($217.9 million) for building 205,000 square meters of housing in Luhansk. Ukrainian journalists have previously reported on Semenkov’s possible ties to Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) and to Leonid Pasechnik’s inner circle.
Next on the Luhansk list is RSK, with loans of about 17 billion rubles ($195.9 million), and another 15.7 billion rubles ($181 million) was allocated to the Moscow-based company Everest by PSB, the key bank for Russia’s Defense Ministry, in order to build a residential complex of about 136,000 square meters in Luhansk. Before the war, Everest had not built any major residential complexes independently, limiting its activities to capital repairs and installation work.
The company was founded by Begali Nurgushiev, former head of the investigative department of Kalmykia’s Ministry of Internal Affairs, who had previously received a suspended sentence for abuse of power. Everest is now headed by his son, Bulat Nurgushiev.
Bulat’s younger brother, Azamat Nurgushiev, works for the Presidential Executive Office. According to Vot Tak, in 2020 he was an assistant to the deputy head of the Foreign Policy Directorate, and he now holds the position of referent in the secretariat of the head of the Presidential Executive Office. His former boss, Denis Agafonov, heads the Expert Directorate, which prepares analytical materials for Vladimir Putin.
Construction in the occupied territories is not only profitable in itself but is also underpinned by state support, which includes a “free economic zone” regulatory regime that is set to remain in effect until 2050, exempting market participants from property tax and from the federal portion of profit tax for ten years. Developers can obtain project financing at around 3% annual interest and lease land almost for free, without tenders.
According to Vot Tak’s calculations, the profit margin of individual residential construction projects in Mariupol can exceed 30%, compared to the nationwide average of 7–15%, as estimated by experts surveyed by the outlet.
Reconstruction of the seized territories is being overseen by Deputy Prime Minister Marat Khusnullin, who also chairs the supervisory board of the Territorial Development Fund responsible for granting companies free economic zone participant status.
Khusnullin is known for distributing these benefits to his long-time acquaintances, including Pavel Te, whose affiliated entities received more than 1 billion rubles ($11.5 million) for construction in central Mariupol. The Insider previously found that during Khusnullin’s tenure at the Moscow mayor’s office, he and Te made repeated trips to France together on a private jet. Yevtushenkov, who is neighbors with Khusnullin in the upscale suburban Moscow district of Serebryany Bor, received lucrative Moscow city government contracts for years.
The construction boom has coincided with a massive redistribution of property in Mariupol. Homes damaged or destroyed during Russia’s assault on the city have been torn down, and the land has been handed over for commercial residential complexes. Former owners are being offered compensation of up to 70,000 rubles per square meter, while the median price of new housing reaches 170,000 rubles per square meter.
In addition, Russian authorities declare apartments “unclaimed” if their owners have failed to register them with the national Rosreestr property registry. According to the BBC Russian Service, by August 2026 Russian officials in the occupied territories had confiscated or placed on lists for seizure more than 34,000 properties belonging to Ukrainian nationals, including 14,000 in Mariupol.

articles.title: Jordan says air defenses intercepted 10 of 13 ballistic missiles entering airspace: Reports
articles.body:
Berk Kutay Gökmen
02 September 2026•Update: 02 September 2026
Jordanian air defenses intercepted 10 of 13 ballistic missiles that entered the kingdom’s airspace, while three fell in remote areas, the Jordan News Agency reported Wednesday.
The report came amid heightened tensions in the region and a second Iranian missile attack directed toward Jordan in less than 48 hours.
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said earlier that it had targeted a US Marine base in Jordan, known as “Camp Titin,” with ballistic missiles in retaliation for a US strike on a residence hosting a wedding ceremony in Sirik County, in Iran’s Hormozgan province.
The IRGC claimed that numerous US soldiers were killed in the attack, while the US Central Command (CENTCOM) said Tuesday that it had launched strikes against IRGC targets inside Iran. Iranian officials said an initial assessment showed at least four people were killed and 50 injured after a US strike hit a residence and wedding ceremony in Kuhestek.

articles.title: US strikes wedding party in southern Iran: What we know so far
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
US strikes wedding party in southern Iran: What we know so far
Iran accused the United States of striking a wedding gathering in the country’s south, killing five people, including a child, and injuring dozens more in an attack on a residential area near the Strait of Hormuz in Kuhestak, in Sirik county of Hormozgan province, on Tuesday night.
The Red Crescent said shrapnel from a US missile struck the residential property, killing five people and injuring more than 50. Six-year-old Amir Mohammad Karimi was among those killed, it said, adding that those wounded had been transferred to hospital in the nearby city of Minab.
Earlier, Reza Shahidiyan, the governor of Sirik county, told the IRIB state broadcaster that 63 people had been injured, including 50 women and children. Other Iranian reporting has cited as many as 68 wounded.
Videos circulated by Iranian rescue workers showed debris scattered across the site and extensive damage to several buildings, including blown-out walls and windows. Another video posted by the Red Crescent showed a large whole on the roof of a residential building, supposedly from the site of the impact.
Kuhestak lies in Sirik county, on Iran’s southern coast along the strategic Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly a fifth of global seaborne oil trade passes. The attack came during a large new wave of US strikes across Iran, following more than a month without a direct exchange of fire between Washington and Tehran.
US Central Command (CENTCOM) said its forces had launched strikes against targets linked to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, citing what it called recent attempted attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and on US personnel in the region.
But Washington has not publicly identified the precise target near the wedding site, disclosed the weapon used, or explained how a missile strike came to send lethal shrapnel into a home packed with civilians celebrating a wedding. Earlier reports suggested a telecommunications tower in the Kuhestak area may have been among the targets.
US response
The US did not deny carrying out strikes in the area. Asked about reports of civilian casualties, CENTCOM spokesperson Capt. Tim Hawkins said: "We’re aware of the reports, which originated from Iranian state media," claiming that "The US military never targets civilians, unlike the IRGC."
The statement does not address whether the strike hit a civilian residence, whether US planners knew a wedding was under way, whether the house was within the expected blast radius of an intended target, or whether CENTCOM is investigating the deaths and injuries reported by emergency workers and local officials.
The US assertion that it does not target civilians sits uneasily alongside mounting reports of civilian harm from its campaign in Iran. On 28 February, a strike on a girls’ school in Minab, also in Hormozgan province, killed more than 150 people, most of them children, according to Iranian authorities and rights groups.
Washington has yet to publicly accept responsibility or release a final account of that attack. However, a preliminary US military assessment concluded that US forces were likely responsible and that the school was not the intended target. The reported explanation was that outdated intelligence had wrongly classified the site, or the surrounding area, as associated with an Iranian military installation.
Iranian condemnation
Iranian officials condemned the Sirik attack as an assault on civilians and said the country would respond.
Foreign ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said Tehran would respond "with firmness", while Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, Iran’s top negotiator and parliamentary speaker, described the United States as the "Great Satan" and linked the wedding deaths to what he called a broader pattern of US attacks on civilians.
The head of the Iranian Red Crescent Society sent a letter to the Prosecutor of the International Criminal Court on Wednesday regarding the wedding attack, assuring prosecutors that the organisation was documenting the effects of the attack in order to "collect and record (them) for follow-up through legal and international channels," calling for an independent investigation into Tuesday's deadly incident.
Iranian officials also said electricity and telephone services had been disrupted in the area, amid reports that US strikes had targeted telecommunications infrastructure in Hormozgan province. Restoration work was under way, according to Iran’s health ministry.
The strike was followed by Iranian missile and drone attacks directed towards US-linked targets and allies across the region, including Bahrain, Kuwait, the United Arab Emirates and Jordan. The exchange marked one of the sharpest escalations in weeks in the six-month conflict.

articles.title: Xi meets with Sisi in first Egypt visit in a decade
articles.body:
President Xi Jinping on Wednesday met with his Egyptian counterpart, Abdel Fattah El-Sisi as he began his first visit to Egypt in a decade.
The 21-gun salute at Cairo's Ittihadiya Palace marked the start of a day of talks expected to cover the Middle East war and its fallout, including on maritime trade security, as well as boosting investment in the Arab world's most populous country.
The two Brics members are expected to sign a slate of economic agreements, including on artificial intelligence, transport and manufacturing.
Egypt currently estimates Chinese investments at around US$10 billion. 
Beijing has key stakes in the Suez Canal Economic Zone, which are only expected to grow as the US-Iran war threatens global maritime trade.
China has also played a key role in Egypt's megaprojects, the crowning jewel of which is the New Administrative Capital 50 kilometres east of Cairo, large swathes of which have been bankrolled by Chinese investment.
China is a major exporter to Egypt, with its trade surplus reaching US$12 billion in the first seven months of 2026, according to Chinese customs data.
Across Cairo, a megalopolis home to over 26 million people, major streets have been lined with Chinese and Egyptian flags, as well as billboards showing Sisi and Xi.
Street signs boast of "generations of Egyptian-Chinese friendship flowing like the Nile River", while residents have been warned to plan for substantial traffic delays on their commutes.
Xi is expected to traverse the entire capital during his visit on Wednesday, including a stop at the Grand Egyptian Museum overlooking the Giza Pyramids.
According to analysts, Cairo will use the summit to underscore its strategic autonomy, showing it can leverage its close ties with both Washington and Beijing.
Sisi, in an op-ed published in Egyptian media on Tuesday, highlighted Cairo's "independent foreign policy", days after a branch of Egypt's second-largest bank was targeted by US sanctions.
He wrote that Egypt and China were partners in "strengthening the role of the Global South" in an increasingly polarised world. 
Xi's visit is the second leg of his second overseas trip this year, following his participation in a Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Kyrgyzstan where he spoke with Russian President Vladimir Putin and others.
In commentary published by Xinhua, Xi said the two countries were "close brothers standing by each other" in the face of imperialism and colonialism and that he looked forward to exploring a deeper partnership. (Xinhua/Agencies)
Edited by Tony Sabine

articles.title: Inside Taliban-ruled Afghanistan: Five years after US exit (VIDEO)
articles.body:
Inside Taliban-ruled Afghanistan: Five years after US exit (VIDEO)
Five years after the US withdrawal, Afghanistan is no longer a country at war in the way the world once knew it. The streets of Kabul are busy, markets are open, and the booms of airstrikes have faded away from villages that once shuddered under them. But the country that emerged from two decades of conflict is also more isolated, poorer, and firmly under Taliban rule. 
RT India’s head of news, Runjhun Sharma, travels beyond Kabul to see what the new Afghanistan looks like on the ground – seen through the eyes of the people who survived the war, the farmers adapting to sweeping Taliban restrictions, and officials trying to convince the world that the country deserves recognition. 
One of the most haunting encounters in the documentary comes in a village near a former US base, where Mohammed Saabr returns to the remains of his home and recounts losing seven members of his family in an American military operation. For families like his, the war may have ended, but it is hardly history. 
Sharma and her team also follow Taliban officials into former poppy-growing areas near the Pakistan border. Afghanistan’s once vast opium economy has sharply contracted under the Taliban ban – something that years of American military operations could not achieve. It’s something the movement presents as a major achievement. 
Farmers, however, describe the other side of that change: Crops that replaced poppy bring in far less money at a time when poverty and hunger are already widespread.
And there is another story the camera tells almost through the absence of the characters. Women are barely visible on Kabul’s streets. At one point, even the sight of a female journalist traveling in a Taliban vehicle draws attention. Later, questions over women’s education and public life become central to an interview with the Taliban leadership, yet Afghan women themselves remain largely outside the frame. 
The film’s political centerpiece is a rare interview with the Taliban’s chief spokesperson in Kandahar. He speaks about sanctions, frozen Afghan assets, relations with Washington, closer economic ties with Russia, and the group’s demand for international recognition, while rejecting outside pressure to change Afghanistan’s internal laws. 
The documentary ends back in Kabul, where Taliban supporters mark five years in power with the Islamic Emirate’s flags and the weapons the American left behind, outside the old American Embassy – symbols of a war they believe they won, in a country still working out what comes next.

articles.title: Zelensky threatens ‘every airline’ in Russian airspace
articles.body:
Zelensky threatens ‘every airline’ in Russian airspace
Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky issued a warning to every airline that uses Russian airspace, saying any aircraft flying through it will be threatened by Ukrainian drones. President Vladimir Putin called the statement a “declaration of state terrorism.”
The Ukrainian military has been ramping up long-range drone and missile attacks against civilian and infrastructure targets deep inside Russia. The strikes have repeatedly disrupted the work of civilian airports, particularly around Moscow.
On Tuesday, Zelensky claimed that Kiev will close Russian airspace by darkening the skies with drones. “Today, we want to warn every airline that uses Russian airspace, every insurer, and everyone who still uses Russia’s key airports: Russian airspace is becoming completely unsafe,” he said in a video address published on Telegram.
“Safe days in Russia’s skies are over,” he claimed, adding that the threat is addressed to “the airlines currently flying to airports primarily in Moscow, St. Petersburg, and other key destinations in Russia.”
Threats to close Russian airspace amount to a “declaration of state terrorism,” Putin said at a press conference on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan. According to the Russian president, these actions make Kiev’s claims about seeking peace talks with Moscow null and void. “One does not hold negotiations with terrorists,” the president said.
Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said in Bishkek on Tuesday that the increasing strikes against civilian targets in Russia indicate that Zelensky and “the Kiev regime” are “well aware that such statements are proof of their earlier claims about the supposed desire for peace being false.”
Earlier, Zelensky demanded that the number of strikes on Russia be increased to 1,000 per day. The Russian Defense Ministry regularly reports that it downs hundreds of Ukrainian drones targeting various Russian regions. In mid-August, the ministry reported that it repelled one of the largest Ukrainian drone raids since the beginning of the year, when 822 Ukrainian drones were intercepted and destroyed. Two days later, 791 Ukrainian fixed-wing UAVs were downed overnight across the country.
Russia has also conducted long-range strikes on military targets in Ukraine in response to repeated attacks on civilian and energy infrastructure in Russia. Moscow stated that Kiev’s “terrorist” tactics are aimed at diverting the attention of the public from Ukrainian setbacks on the battlefield.

articles.title: Erdogan, Putin discuss Black Sea security, possible Ukraine peace talks in Türkiye – media

Erdogan, Putin discuss Black Sea security, possible Ukraine peace talks in Türkiye – media
Russian officials reported this, according to Ukrinform, citing Türkiye Today.

articles.title: American forces strike IRGC targets in Iran
articles.body:
US forces have carried out a wave of strikes against Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps targets inside Iran, hitting air defence sites, radar systems, maritime assets and other military facilities, according to US Central Command.
CENTCOM announced on 1 September that the strikes had been completed against a range of Iranian military targets. Targets identified by CENTCOM included Iranian air defence positions and radar systems, along with maritime assets and facilities, mine-laying capabilities and communications sites.
CENTCOM stated: “U.S. forces struck Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) targets including air defense sites, radar systems, maritime assets and facilities, mine laying capabilities, and communications sites.”
The command added: “The strikes follow recent attempted attacks by the IRGC against commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and against American service members.”
The Strait of Hormuz is the narrow maritime passage connecting the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman and Arabian Sea. It is used by commercial shipping operating between Gulf ports and international markets and is also regularly patrolled by US and allied naval forces.
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps maintains its own naval, aerospace and ground forces alongside Iran’s regular armed forces. Its naval element operates extensively in and around the Persian Gulf and Strait of Hormuz. The target set identified by CENTCOM covered several elements of Iranian military infrastructure. Air defence and radar installations form part of Iran’s ability to detect and respond to aircraft and other aerial activity, while communications sites support military command and coordination.
CENTCOM also specifically identified mine-laying capabilities among the targets attacked. Iranian forces have long maintained naval mine capabilities for operations in the waters around Iran, including approaches to the Strait of Hormuz.
The United States currently has more than 50,000 military personnel deployed across the Middle East, according to CENTCOM. US Central Command is responsible for American military operations across a region covering the Middle East and parts of Central and South Asia, including the Persian Gulf and surrounding waters.

articles.title: Putin reveals impact of Ukrainian strikes on shipping on Russian GDP
articles.body:
Putin reveals impact of Ukrainian strikes on shipping on Russian GDP
Russian leader Vladimir Putin has stated that Ukraine's armed forces have damaged approximately 100 commercial vessels over the past 40 days in the Black Sea and Sea of Azov, with losses estimated at 1% of Russia's GDP.
Source: The Moscow Times, an independent Amsterdam-based news outlet
Details: "The total losses, according to our early calculations, amounted to, overall, quite a lot – approximately 1% of GDP, but these are not critical losses for us," Putin assured journalists.
"They cannot inflict critical damage on us. But there is damage nonetheless," he said.
"They have inflicted real damage on us, because during the first two weeks they damaged around 40 of our ships. They did not destroy them, they damaged them. And over all these 40 days they damaged around 100 of our ships," Putin said, answering questions from the press.
Putin does not consider Russia's own earlier strikes on civilian shipping to be a crime, claiming that they struck exclusively those vessels that were transporting military cargo.
"Essentially, we did not target civilian vessels. Yes, we carried out precision strikes on some vessels, but these were truly precision strikes," he claims, referring to strikes on "certain watercraft".
Notably, Russian media outlets write about weapons being unloaded from vessels even in Mykolaiv, although unlike the ports of Greater Odesa, the port of Mykolaiv does not receive vessels due to the direct threat from Russian forces at the exit to the sea. All vessels in the port have been blocked since the beginning of Russia's full-scale invasion.
Background:
- The monitoring group of the Institute of Black Sea Strategic Studies previously calculated that over 20 days of August, exports of crude Russian oil from Black Sea ports decreased 3.2-fold to approximately 1.7 million tonnes, compared with 5.5 million tonnes in July.
- Russian grain exports, which bring its economy approximately US$15 billion annually, have been virtually completely paralysed by Ukrainian strikes on the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea ports.
- Russian grain exporters have begun redirecting shipments from the Black Sea and Sea of Azov to the Baltic Sea following Ukrainian attacks on port infrastructure and vessels.
- Russian shipowners have reportedly been refused military risk insurance amid the significant number of Ukrainian drone attacks in the Black Sea and Sea of Azov.
- At Russian ports in the Sea of Azov, vessels have begun returning cargo to shore due to the blockage of exit routes: some shipowners have decided to return cargo until the situation changes.

articles.title: Trump nominates loyalist Hung Cao to be permanent navy secretary – US politics live
articles.body:
Trump nominates loyalist Hung Cao to be permanent navy secretary amid increased attacks on Iran
Hello and welcome to the US live politics blog.
Donald Trump has picked acting navy secretary Hung Cao to take on the job permanently amid concerns that some sailors have been stretched to the limit during his Iran war.
“I am pleased to nominate a true WARRIOR,” Trump wrote on social media, pushing the Senate “to confirm this Warfighter, ASAP.”
Cao has been serving as acting navy secretary since John Phelan departed the job unexpectedly and without explanation in late April. Unlike Phelan, who had not served in the military or had a civilian leadership role in the service, Cao spent 25 years in the navy as a special operations officer and went on to serve with Seal teams and special forces in Iraq and Afghanistan.
Cao on social media called it the “honor of a lifetime to lead the great warriors of the Navy and Marine Corps team”.
Cao’s nomination comes as some, including Democrats in Congress, believe Trump has been overtaxing the navy. The USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier’s nine-month deployment to support the Iran war has included a record-setting uninterrupted time at sea.
It comes as Iran launched a wave of attacks on US sites across the Middle East, with violence surging after an extensive American bombardment. Iran’s Revolutionary Guards announced attacks on US bases in Jordan, the UAE, Kuwait, Bahrain and Iraq’s autonomous Kurdistan region, in the six-month conflict’s heaviest exchange in weeks.
Trump had warned earlier of “much harder and higher” attacks if Iran retaliated to the US strikes, which Iran’s military and state media said killed 18 people.
The renewed attacks deepen the impasse in the war, where Iran maintains a stranglehold on the strait of Hormuz oil export route with the US pressing a counter-blockade of Iranian ports.
In other developments:
Senator Ed Markey won the Democratic primary in Massachusetts, beating back a challenge from Seth Moulton, who argued his opponent was too old to be effective at his job. Progressive lawmakers and the organization Our Revolution hailed the victory.
Democratic leaders in the US House sharply criticized two representatives for defecting and joining with Republicans in order to advance a procedural vote, describing it as a “significant breach of trust,” that requires “a serious response”.
The US House of Representative voted to censure Chuck Edwards, a Republican congressman who the ethics committee found violated rules against sexual harassment in his conduct towards two young female staffers.
The Trump administration seized on House Democrats voting against a resolution denouncing socialism, condemning the lawmakers as “sick [and] dangerous”. The resolution included language calling for the enactment of Trump’s SAVE America Act, a strict voting bill that would ban mail-in ballots and require voters to prove their citizenship.
Kathy Hochul, New York’s governor, criticized Donald Trump for withholding $87m in counter-terrorism funds from the state, describing the move as a betrayal of 9/11 victims.
Donald Trump’s Department of Homeland Security has apparently taken steps to advance the president’s efforts to limit voting.
Ayanna Pressley, a Democrat representative from Massachusetts, celebrated colleague Sen Ed Markey’s victory in the state’s Democratic primary for US Senate.
“Congratulations to my friend and partner, Senator Ed Markey, on his decisive victory as the Democratic nominee for Senate from Massachusetts. Massachusetts voters have once again chosen a senator who gives a damn – who shows up for our communities, fights like hell to lighten their load, and has never wavered in his commitment to workers and families in every corner of the Commonwealth,” Pressley said in a Tuesday night statement.
“Senator Markey is steady, authentic, proven, and consistent. He’s been a committed partner in the fight for justice – from standing up for our LGBTQ+ siblings and immigrant neighbors and advancing fare-free transit, to fighting for racial justice, climate justice, criminal legal reform, housing justice, and more,” she also said. “He centers the people and fights for transformative policies. He is proven and steady.”
Pressley also commented: “With Trump and Republicans moving with malice and enacting widespread harm, Massachusetts sent a clear message: we want Democrats who will defend our communities and never back down.”
Markey’s victory over Rep Seth Moulton has raised questions about the perception of politicians’ ages among voters. Moulton tried to push out Markey by claiming that he was too old at age 80 to properly serve.
Markey nonetheless had broad support among his fellow Democrats and is expected to best his Republican challenger in November. The win may prompt questions about how much age matters if voters feel they’re supporting the right candidate.
Two of the Democratic representatives who defected and joined the Republicans in voting in favor of a resolution condemning socialism and the Democratic Socialists of America organisation have defended their actions on social media.
Democratic leaders in the US House had sharply criticized the representatives for defecting and joining with Republicans in order to advance a procedural vote.
“The decision by two of our colleagues to blindside the entire House Democratic Caucus and join with the Republican majority to pass a procedural rule on the brink of failing represents a significant breach of trust,” Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries, whip Katherine Clark and Pete Aguilar, the caucus chair, said in a statement.
“It is an action that necessitates a serious response, and we have asked the Committee on Caucus Rules to take this up in short order.”
The statement was referring to moderates Marie Gluesenkamp Perez and Jared Golden. The bills included a resolution condemning socialism, which also called for the enactment of Trump’s SAVE America Act, that eight Democrats voted to pass.
Congressman Golden wrote on X:
I just voted to fund government through December 11, preventing a shutdown in October. The bill passed the House 370-48. In an election season without a budget deal, the risk of political games is high. This CR removes the ability for either party to hold the government hostage and gives Congress time to negotiate an appropriations deal.
Representative Gluesenkamp Perez also said:
Working America is hanging on by a thread, trying to feed our families without being beholden to big government or big business. Standing around pointing fingers, debating -isms and making people photocopy their birth certificate every time they cast a ballot is not the job.
The other six Democrats to vote in favor of the resolution were Kathy Castor, Henry Cuellar, Don Davis, Vicente Gonzalez Jr, Darren Soto and Gabe Vasquez.
Teamsters union leaders support Republicans despite members endorsing Democratic candidates
Michael Sainato
The powerful Teamsters union is backing Republican candidates in the 2026 election cycle even after members have voted to support their Democrat opponents.
The 1.3 million-strong union’s president, Sean O’Brien, angered many members and union leaders in 2024 when he became the first union president to speak at the Republican national convention (RNC).
The latest moves by the union’s leadership are further stoking tensions within the union.
“The Republicans have done nothing but take a gun to our head at every turn. And why we think that we can somehow change their behavior, I don’t understand it. It’s not a logical argument,” said John Palmer, who was elected on O’Brien’s slate in 2021 as an at-large vice-president on the Teamsters executive board, but who broke ranks in criticizing O’Brien’s RNC appearance in 2024. “I live in Texas. I’m a moderate guy, but I know when somebody’s trying to cut my throat.”
The national union declined to make an endorsement in the 2024 presidential election for the first time since 1996, claiming a majority of members supported Trump after they supported Biden in 2020, though Teamsters locals and councils representing 1 million members at the union independently endorsed Harris.
So far this election cycle, O’Brien has made two personal contributions – both to Republicans.
O’Brien donated $1,000 to the Republican US Senate campaign of Scott Brown in New Hampshire on 19 February 2026. Brown appeared on O’Brien’s podcast, Better Bad Ideas, on 25 February.
The only Teamsters’ local in New Hampshire, Teamsters Local 633, endorsed Brown’s Democratic rival Chris Pappas for the Senate race in April 2025. Teamsters Local 633 did not respond to multiple requests for comment.

articles.title: Putin says Zelensky’s warning to civilian airlines operating in Russian airspace ‘amounts to state terrorism’
articles.body:
Putin says Zelensky’s warning to civilian airlines operating in Russian airspace ‘amounts to state terrorism’
Russian President Vladimir Putin called Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky’s remarks about threats to the safety of Russia’s skies “amounts to state terrorism.” “And I’d point out that they’re the ones asking us to resume talks, asking for face-to-face meetings. You don’t negotiate with terrorists,” Putin said.
He also said that “if tragedies like this do happen, we’ll find a way to answer.”
In his evening address, Zelensky warned airlines that Russia’s skies are “becoming completely unsafe,” declaring that “the safe days in Russia’s skies are over.”
The Russian Armed Forces have been given orders to prepare and carry out massive strikes on Ukraine’s energy facilities, Putin said at a press conference in Bishkek following the Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit.
“They’re striking ours — they’ll get an answer,” he also said.

articles.title: Putin calls Zelenskyy’s airspace warning “state terrorism” as shares in Russia’s national airline fall 5%
articles.body:
Russian President Vladimir Putin said Moscow would “find a way to respond” if civilian “tragedies” followed President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s warning that Ukrainian drone operations were making Russian skies unsafe. Zelenskyy told foreign airlines and insurers that the “safe moments” in Russian airspace were over.
Zelenskyy’s warning seeks to extend the cost of Russia’s war beyond damaged military and energy facilities to airlines, insurers, and travelers. It does not mean Russian airspace is legally or completely closed. However, carriers that continue flying over Russia face higher costs from repeated airport shutdowns during drone alerts, as well as the danger that military activity in Russian airspace could endanger civilian aircraft.
Putin spoke after a 1 September Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit in Bishkek, where Russia and China coordinate regional security. Zelenskyy’s warning amounted to “a bid for state terrorism” if he had made it publicly, the Russian president said, adding that Russia does not negotiate with “terrorists.” Putin also said Russian forces were preparing massive strikes on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.
In his evening video address, Zelenskyy said Ukraine did not threaten civilian aircraft but would keep striking Russian military targets and parts of the economy supporting the war. Ukraine’s Presidential Office head Kyrylo Budanov backed the decision, saying long-range weapons would systematically strike military targets in Russia while the invasion continued.
“Russian airspace will effectively be closing”: Zelenskyy warns airlines Russian skies are no longer safe
Shares in Aeroflot, Russia’s national airline, fell to an intraday low of 30.36 rubles at about 20:40 Moscow time, down 5.11%, Meduza reported, citing Moscow Exchange data. The timing does not establish that Zelenskyy’s speech alone drove the decline.
Wall Street Journal correspondent Yaroslav Trofimov posted a chart of the decline on X, writing, “Aeroflot shares after Zelensky’s warning.”
European and US carriers already avoid Russian airspace, but airlines from China, Türkiye, the United Arab Emirates, and other Gulf states continue using it, Reuters reported. Aviation-risk firm Osprey Flight Solutions assessed that daily attacks deep inside Russia were nearly certain through 2026 and warned of possible misidentification.
Andrii Kovalenko, head of Ukraine’s Center for Countering Disinformation, said it was “strange” to hear terrorism accusations from “the leader of a terrorist organization masquerading as the Russian state.” Putin’s reaction showed Moscow feared pressure on its airspace, he argued.
Previous closures of Russian airspace due to Ukrainian attacks
Russian airports were repeatedly shut during Ukrainian drone alerts well before Zelenskyy’s warning. On 6 July 2025, Moscow airports canceled 171 flights while airports in five other cities suspended operations.
A 27 May attack closed airports serving Moscow and several other cities after Russia claimed it intercepted 99 drones. Another wave caused flight disruption and mobile internet outages around Moscow, while a 29 May alert again halted flights at Moscow airports.
More recently, Russian authorities restricted operations at Moscow airports during Ukrainian drone attacks, delaying more than 450 flights

articles.title: Russia’s transport minister on Zelensky’s threats to make Russian airspace unsafe — ‘We’re preparing for this’
articles.body:
Russia’s transport minister on Zelensky’s threats to make Russian airspace unsafe — ‘We’re preparing for this’
Andrey Nikitin, head of Russia’s Transport Ministry, said Russian aviation authorities will not allow any “significant disruptions” to civil aviation, responding to threats from Ukrainian President Zelensky to make Russian airspace unsafe through drone attacks.
“Of course, we’re preparing for this and taking all these threats into account. We’re constantly improving flight safety and airport security requirements, and we have answers for all of it. We have answers for all these threats the terrorists are voicing,” the Russian news agency Interfax quoted Nikitin as saying.
The Transport Ministry works “in close contact” with the Defense Ministry and the Russian National Guard, he said.
“I think that we won’t allow any significant disruptions in civil aviation. There will definitely be “Carpets”, of course, because passenger safety is paramount. But we will unequivocally handle this in the coming years,” Nikitin added.
Volodymyr Zelensky warned airlines on the evening of September 1 that Russian airspace “is becoming unsafe,” saying “drones will appear in Russian skies in a way that will have to be reckoned with.” Ukraine, he said, “does not threaten civil aviation as such,” but Ukrainian drone attacks would mean “Russian airspace will de facto be closing.”
Russian President Vladimir Putin called Zelensky’s statement “a bid for state terrorism.”
Turkish airline Pegasus began canceling flights to and from Moscow after Zelensky’s statement.

articles.body:
Iran launched 13 missiles at Jordan, most of which were intercepted by air defenses
Kyiv • UNN
Iran launched a missile strike against Jordan. Jordanian air defenses intercepted 10 of the 13 ballistic missiles; three fell in remote areas.
Iran launched missile strikes against Jordan on Tuesday evening, September 1. At the same time, most of the Iranian missiles were shot down by air defense systems. This was reported by The Times of Israel, according to UNN.
Details
It is noted that at approximately 11:00 p.m., messages warning of possible danger were sent to the mobile phones of residents of Jordan. Shortly beforehand, information emerged that Iran had launched missiles toward the country. A few minutes later, an air raid alert was declared in the country.
Jordanian air defense systems intercepted and destroyed 13 ballistic missiles that entered the Kingdom's airspace, successfully intercepting and destroying 10 of them.
They clarified that three missiles fell in remote areas far from populated areas.
We remind you
