articles.title: Ukraine’s Security Service says it foiled FSB plot to assassinate Russian opposition leader in Kyiv – several wounded in street shootout
articles.body:
A shootout involving Ukrainian security personnel in Kyiv left several people wounded on 2 September, with Ukrainian authorities now saying the confrontation occurred during an investigation into an alleged Russian plot to assassinate a Russian opposition figure in Ukraine.
The incident took place overnight in Kyiv’s Dniprovskyi district, amid reports that Stepan Kaplunov, deputy commander for combat operations of the Russian Volunteer Corps (RDK), had been abducted.
Shootout follows reported abduction
Ukrainska Pravda reported, citing Kaplunov’s lawyer Taras Borovskyi, that law enforcement officers arrived at the serviceman’s home after his reported disappearance.
According to Borovskyi, Kaplunov’s fellow soldiers came to the location after being alerted, after which gunfire broke out. The lawyer also published video from the scene, Ukrainska Pravda reported.
The RDK had previously said that unknown individuals abducted Kaplunov from the courtyard of his home.
Ukraine’s State Bureau of Investigation confirmed to Ukrainska Pravda that it had received a complaint from Kaplunov’s lawyers alleging his abduction and was examining it for possible registration as a criminal proceeding.
Ukrainska Pravda, citing sources in Ukraine’s security services, reported that the confrontation involved the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) and Ukraine’s Main Intelligence Directorate (HUR). Its sources said three HUR personnel had been wounded as of Wednesday morning.
SBU links confrontation to Russian plot
The SBU later said the confrontation occurred during an investigation into an alleged terrorist attack organized by Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB).
The agency said its investigators were conducting a search at one of the addresses connected to the case when a group of people launched an armed attack on them. The group allegedly blocked the investigators’ vehicles with cars and attempted to prevent the search.
The SBU said its Alpha special operations unit was deployed to stop the armed resistance. Officers used their weapons, and several people who resisted were wounded, according to the agency.
The attackers were detained, the SBU said. Initial investigative work found that they belonged to one of Ukraine’s Defense Forces units, while weapons and documents were seized from them.
The agency did not identify the detainees or their military unit.
Alleged assassination attempt
Earlier on 2 September, the SBU said it and HUR had jointly foiled an FSB plot to assassinate a leader of a Russian opposition nationalist political movement who had traveled to Ukraine for Independence Day.
The SBU did not name the alleged target or provide details of the planned attack.
RBC-Ukraine, citing sources, reported that the target was Kaplunov. The outlet also reported that HUR later deleted a statement about the foiled attack.
The SBU’s later statement about the shootout did not name Kaplunov or explicitly identify the armed group involved as HUR personnel.
The Russian Volunteer Corps is a unit operating within Ukraine’s military intelligence structures and composed of Russian nationals fighting against Russia’s invasion.
Budanov calls for investigation
Kyrylo Budanov, head of Ukraine’s Presidential Office, said the incident should be thoroughly and impartially investigated, according to RBC-Ukraine.
He said no one should be allowed to abduct servicemen, open fire in Ukrainian cities, or give or carry out criminal orders with impunity.
The Prosecutor General’s Office has opened a pretrial investigation into threats against and an attempt on the life of a law enforcement officer, the SBU said.
Authorities have not publicly provided a full account reconciling the different reports surrounding the incident. Investigative actions are ongoing.
Ukraine and Russian opposition figures
Ukraine has become a base for some Russian opposition figures and anti-Kremlin activists since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion. Some have joined Ukrainian military units or otherwise supported Ukraine’s war effort.
That has also made some of them targets for Russian intelligence operations.

articles.title: Turkish airline Pegasus cancels flights between Moscow and Turkey after Zelensky’s warning about unsafe Russian airspace
articles.body:
Turkish airline Pegasus cancels flights between Moscow and Turkey after Zelensky’s warning about unsafe Russian airspace
Turkish budget airline Pegasus canceled at least one flight from Bodrum to Moscow that had been scheduled to depart at 12:05 a.m. on September 2, the Russian Telegram news channel Ostorozhno Novosti reported.
Passengers on flight PC1456 said they were told all Turkish airlines had canceled flights because of the “airspace situation.” “We don’t know what to expect. Our Turkish side is prohibiting departures,” the airline stated.
Vnukovo Airport’s departure board also listed several other Pegasus flights out of Moscow as canceled: two to Istanbul, one to Bodrum, and one to Dalaman.
The board also showed at least two Turkish Airlines flights to Istanbul, one Nesma Airlines flight to Sharm El Sheikh, and one Shirak Avia flight to Yerevan canceled overnight and into the morning. Later in the day’s schedule, however, Turkish Airlines flights were listed without changes.
Vnukovo Airport introduced temporary restrictions overnight on September 2 for security reasons. Rosaviatsia announced around 6 a.m. Moscow time that the restrictions had been lifted.
The day before, Volodymyr Zelensky warned airlines that Russian airspace “is becoming unsafe” because “drones will appear in Russian skies in a way that will have to be reckoned with.” “We are warning our partners: the safe moments in Russian skies are over,” he said in his evening address.
Putin, who spoke with journalists in the early hours of August 2 following the SCO summit in Bishkek, called Zelensky’s remarks “a bid for state terrorism.” He also addressed Germany’s decision to close Russia’s consulate general and rumors of a new mobilization after the elections.

US launches new strikes against Iran
TEHRAN — The United States has launched a fresh wave of military aggression against Iranian territory. Four projectiles struck the counties of Chabahar and Konarak in Sistan and Baluchestan, confirmed by provincial security officials and General Ali Khalil Abadi.

articles.title: Kallas Urges Countries to Give Ukraine Expiring Air Defense Missiles
articles.body:
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas urged countries with air defense interceptors nearing their expiration dates to transfer them to Ukraine, where they could be used to protect civilians from Russian attacks.
“The main issue is air defense. They are lacking interceptors,” Kallas said at a press conference ahead of an informal meeting of EU defense ministers on Tuesday, Sept. 1.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“We know that some of the countries have interceptors that will expire soon. So, it would be very good if those would be given to Ukraine so that they can use them to protect their people,” she said.
Russia escalating attacks against civilians
Kallas said July and August have been the deadliest months for civilians in Ukraine.
“Russia is really escalating to hurt the people of Ukraine as much as possible to break them,” she said. “The Ukrainians, of course, are standing strong, and we have to support them.”
Kallas said the EU was also reaching out to countries outside the bloc to obtain more interceptors for Ukraine, although she acknowledged that the effort was difficult.
At the same time, work is underway to develop European interceptor missiles in cooperation with Ukraine, she added.
EU seeks more air defense funding for Ukraine
Kallas said the informal ministerial meeting would not produce direct decisions, but officials were pushing to unblock the European Peace Facility, with an estimated amount of $7.5 billion.
“If that would happen in the coming days, then many Member States have already said that all the funds that they are getting back, they will give to Ukraine,” Kallas said.
Graham’s ‘Sanctions Bill From Hell’ Against Russia Hits House Roadblock
She added that this would provide significant new funding for air defense and other capabilities Ukraine needs.
Ministry to discuss European space capabilities
EU defense ministers will also discuss the bloc’s space capabilities, which Kallas described as a key enabler of defense with both civilian and military uses.
“We really need to step up so that we are still a space power, considering what is going on there,” she said.

articles.title: Italian arms dealer sentenced to 18 months in U.S. prison for supplying ammunition to Russia in violation of sanctions
articles.body:
On Aug. 24, a federal court in the Eastern District of New York sentenced Manfred Gruber, a 61-year-old Italian citizen and former commercial director of an Italian arms company, to 18 months in prison for conspiracy to violate U.S. export laws. Gruber pleaded guilty to the charge on March 30.
According to the U.S. Justice Department, Gruber organized the illegal export of more than $540,000 worth of U.S.-made ammunition produced by a Nebraska company and another supplier in Tennessee, routing it through JFK International Airport in New York. The shipments were declared for export to Italy, where the ammunition was required to remain as per official documents. Instead, prosecutors said, the cargo was routed to Russia via Kyrgyzstan.
The case also involved Sergei Zharnovnikov, the owner of a Kyrgyz arms distributor, who previously pleaded guilty and was sentenced to 39 months in prison. A key piece of evidence consisted of correspondence found on Zharnovnikov’s phone in which the men discussed breaking up shipments of 100,000 rounds into smaller orders in order to avoid attracting the attention of customs officials.
Joseph Nocella, Jr., the U.S. attorney for the Eastern District of New York, said Gruber had been “held accountable for his scheme to send military‑grade ammunition to Kyrgyzstan before reexporting the ammunition to Russia to support its war effort.”
Gruber had served as commercial director of Bignami S.p.A., which bought ammunition for sniper rifles from Nebraska-based Hornady Manufacturing under a U.S. export license, then rerouted the shipments to Russia through Kyrgyzstan, bypassing permit requirements that the ammunition remain in Italy. The Insider previously identified Gruber’s business partners.
From 2022 to 2024, Russian companies including Arsenal, Artemida, Ve-Kasa, Promtekhnologiya, and Tetis received Hornady ammunition. In 2023, Politico Europe found evidence that Hornady ammunition had been used by snipers from the Wagner Group, the Russian state-funded private military company co-founded by the late Yevgeny Prigozhin. The Insider later found that the company’s ammunition was being used by snipers from the 155th Naval Infantry Brigade of Russia’s Pacific Fleet.
Gruber’s case is not an isolated incident. In August 2025, U.S. authorities seized more than $250,000 and dozens of weapons components and accessories after arresting Maxim Larin, a 44-year-old U.S. citizen from Plantation, Florida who owned several small American companies selling firearms parts. On Aug. 25, 2026, the U.S. attorney’s office for the Eastern District of New York accepted Larin’s guilty plea on charges of conspiracy to violate the Export Control Reform Act and the attempted violation of the Arms Export Control Act.
According to prosecutors, Larin and an accomplice in Russia organized shipments of weapons components to Kazakhstan, including trigger mechanisms for semiautomatic firearms, charging handles, and laser rangefinders of the sort used by snipers and artillery spotters.
The investigative bureau Tri Trace Investigations found that from 2009 to 2014 Larin had owned the Russian gun store Shooter’s Shop. In 2012, before leaving the Russian business, he also opened a gun store in the United States. Larin’s former Russian store continues to operate under the iShooter brand. The store’s website has an “international shipping” section listing Express Mail Shipping as its logistics partner. The store’s current owner, Albert Goncharov, is also listed as an employee of Larin’s U.S. company.

articles.title: Ukrainian drones turn on Ozon
articles.body:
Ukrainian drones turn on Ozon
Ukraine continues to strike Russia’s e-commerce companies, escalating its campaign last week to target Ozon, Wildberries’ main rival, for the first time. Seven warehouses were hit in a series of strikes that continued for days. The Russian authorities are clearly concerned about the intensity of these attacks and are using the threat of nationalization to force businesses to invest in their own defenses.
- Ukraine attacked Ozon for the first time on Aug. 22, targeting a logistics center in the Samara region. The warehouse, which has been put out of action indefinitely due to a fire, was one of the biggest in the Volga part of European Russia, covering 135,000 square metres. The next day, a warehouse in the Orenburg region was struck, also forcing it to halt operations. This week alone, drones attacked warehouses in Adygea, Stavropol Region and Bashkortostan. Unlike Wildberries, Ozon is a public company traded on the stock exchange. As trading opened after the strikes, its shares plummeted by 32%.
- At the same time, the attacks on Wildberries have continued. A warehouse in the Tambov region, only just reopened after a drone strike in July, was burned to the ground. This was a clear example of how the state will just be burning through cash if it keeps trying to reopen damaged warehouses.
- Amid the attacks on Ozon, supporters of Alexei Navalny from his Anti-Corruption Foundation (FBK) uncovered how deeply the marketplace is embedded in the infrastructure of Vladimir Putin’s associates. The company is 35% owned by Russian venture capitalist Alexander Chachava who, since 2022, has amassed holdings worth hundreds of billions of rubles in Russia’s biggest internet companies. An FBK analysis of the corporate ownership chain found that Chachava’s Ozon investment was funded by billionaire Gennady Timchenko. In April 2025, The Bell’s sources identified Putin’s close associate Yury Kovalchuk as the ultimate beneficiary of the Ozon deal.
- Ukraine is now targeting the facilities of Russia’s two market-leading marketplaces — but there is a fundamental difference between the companies. Wildberries builds its own warehouses and owns them outright. Ozon prefers to rent. If Ukraine’s aim is to cause problems for Russia’s banks, it makes more sense to target Wildberries. First, the structural difference means Wildberries has much greater debt — reportedly up to 1.3 trillion rubles ($15 billion) — while Ozon’s equivalent costs are lease payments. Second, this concentrates Wildberries’ financial risk among its creditors, especially state bank VTB, which holds 500-600 billion rubles ($6-7 billion) of that debt. Destroying Ozon warehouses creates problems for various owners of individual facilities, whose loans come from multiple institutions. The risks are dispersed, lowering the chances of a systemic crisis.
- According to the latest estimates, Ozon’s losses from the attacks are more than 100 billion rubles ($1.2 billion). Including this week’s attacks, Wildberries faces a bill of 517-580 billion rubles ($6-7 billion) for damage and destroyed goods. Building new warehouses could cost 186-344 billion rubles ($2-4 billion).
- The Kremlin is concerned about the situation and is trying to encourage businesses to invest more in anti-drone defenses. However, the state is not allocating funds due to its already sky-high military spending and expanding budget deficit, so the cost falls on the private sector. This week Vladimir Putin signed a decree allowing critical infrastructure facilities to be placed under external management if their owners could not defend them. The document is hardly a new means to speed up nationalization, which the prosecutor general’s office is busily pursuing via a range of pretexts. Critical infrastructure includes energy and fuel facilities, industrial sites, communications, and transport and logistics infrastructure — including marketplace warehouses. Business owners sometimes prefer to simply shut down altogether rather than risk staff being killed in drone strikes (The Bell’s co-founder Pyotr Mironenko discussed one specific case on a recent Meduza podcast).
Why the world should care
The intensity of Ukraine’s strikes on Russia’s online retail warehouses proves that the Kremlin can do little to protect what it describes as the country’s critical infrastructure. However, there is at least a desire to do so — even if the proposal, once again, lands business with the bill.

articles.title: Ukraine’s SBU says it thwarted FSB plot to assassinate Russian opposition figure
articles.body:
The Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) announced that it worked with the Main Intelligence Directorate (HUR) of the Defense Ministry to foil an assassination plot targeting a Russian opposition figure.
According to a statement from the SBU cited by RBC Ukraine, Russia’s Federal Security Service had planned to kill the opposition figure during his visit to Kyiv for Ukraine’s Independence Day, marked on August 24.
The SBU did not name the target of the plot or disclose further details.
Ukrainian media identified the target as Stepan Kaplunov, deputy commander of the the Russian Volunteer Corps. The group announced on September 1 that Kaplunov had disappeared outside his home several days earlier and that his whereabouts remained unknown.
In December 2025, the Russian Volunteer Corps announced the death of its commander, Denis Kapustin. However, it later emerged that Kapustin was alive, and that reports of his death had been spread as part of an operation by Ukrainian intelligence services.
